exp20v2-pm.empowered:
Empowered teams vs feature teams

Is the team here to hit an outcome or to ship a list, and who decided that?

1. The list on the table

On 6 July 2026, the first Monday of the second quarter of its financial year, Gauri Hebbar walked into the Pune office of Gatiman Fleet Services with a decision she had been avoiding for a month. Gatiman sells trucking fleets GPS trackers, a dispatcher dashboard and a driver app. It had 1,800 fleet customers paying an average of ₹6 lakh a year each, so annual recurring revenue stood at ₹108 crore (1,800 × ₹6 lakh = ₹10,800 lakh). Hemant Gokhale, the chief executive, had left a one-page list on her desk. It named six items, each with a sponsor. Her team of ten engineers, a designer and two product managers had twelve weeks to deliver them.

The difficulty was not that the items were foolish. Fiza Merchant, head of sales, wanted a custom invoice export for Hansa Roadlines, a large customer that had hinted at leaving; Hemant wanted the dashboard redesigned; a fuel-card partner wanted an integration; finance wanted a trip-cost report; support wanted configurable geofence alerts (virtual map boundaries that trigger an alert when a truck crosses them); Pune sales wanted a Marathi driver app.

What worried Gauri was the number that was not on the list. Gatiman had lost 15 per cent of its customers the previous year: 270 fleets, or ₹16.2 crore of annual revenue (270 × ₹6 lakh = ₹1,620 lakh). The board wanted churn at 12 per cent, which meant keeping 54 more fleets. Nothing on the list was tied to that target by evidence. Executing the list would leave sponsors satisfied and churn probably barely moved; declining it would spend political capital against her chief executive.

2. The idea

A feature team is a product team whose job is to build the items it is given. Someone else, usually a senior executive, a sales leader or a customer, decides what is worth building; the team estimates, schedules and delivers. An empowered team is a product team that is given a problem to solve and a measurable result to reach, and that decides for itself which solutions to build. The distinction is about where the decision sits and what the team is judged on: delivery of a list, or movement of a result.

The vocabulary comes from Marty Cagan, a product leader who worked at eBay and Netscape and later founded the Silicon Valley Product Group. In writing and talks from the mid-2010s onward, and in his books Inspired (2008, revised 2017) and Empowered (2020), he argued that most companies run feature teams without admitting it. They treat product teams as a delivery arm for ideas formed elsewhere. The problem it addresses: the people closest to customer data and technology are best placed to choose solutions, yet organisations move that choice to those furthest from both.

Two further terms are needed. An outcome is a change in customer or business behaviour that the team can measure, such as fewer fleets cancelling. An output is a thing that was shipped. The product triad, the product manager, designer and engineer who share a team’s choices, is the unit that holds an outcome.

A sentence Gauri could repeat without sounding glib: “Give us the result you want and the constraints we must respect, and we will bring you back the solutions, with evidence for why they will work.”

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the difference at each box. The first step is the one practitioners leave implicit: someone has to choose the outcome, and it has to be chosen well. Empowerment does not mean the team picks its own goal: leadership sets strategy and outcomes, and the team negotiates how many it can carry. A badly chosen outcome, such as “increase logins”, produces a team empowered to do something pointless.

The second is discovery: finding out which problems are real and which solutions are worth building before committing engineering time. Gatiman’s team would read the exit records of the 270 fleets that left and sort the reasons. Third comes choosing bets. A bet is a solution with a stated guess about its effect, so that the team can check it later. The fourth is shipping in small pieces and measuring. The fifth, which separates practice from theatre, is that the result flows back and changes what the team does next. Leadership must also accept being judged on results; an executive who phones the team about a pet feature turns it back into a feature team.

4. A worked example

Capacity first: ten engineers for twelve weeks is 120 engineer-weeks; reserving 20 per cent (24 engineer-weeks) for bug fixes and maintenance leaves 96 to spend. Table 1 shows what the list costs and what a feature team does with it, taking the items in the order the sponsors ranked them.

Table 1. The list in sponsor order. Items 1 to 4: 28 + 36 + 24 + 8 = 96; items 5 and 6 add 36, giving 132.

Now the evidence the list lacked. Gatiman’s exit records, sorted by main stated reason, gave Table 2.

A feature team never sees this, because for it geofence was never a hypothesis. Meanwhile 36 engineer-weeks remain unspent (96 − 60), and the largest pool of lost fleets, 108, is still largely unexplained.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Empowerment is not the absence of a roadmap

Empowered teams still have plans. What changes is the content: a roadmap of problems and outcomes rather than dated features. Autonomy is not vagueness.

Output metrics wear outcome costumes

“Ship the new onboarding by September” is an output. “Raise the share of new fleets sending data within seven days” is an outcome. The test: could the number stay flat after everything shipped?

Some requests are legitimate constraints

A regulatory change or contractual commitment is a legitimate constraint. If Hansa Roadlines pays ₹42 lakh a year and the export saves it, the item yields ₹42 lakh for 28 weeks, or ₹1.5 lakh per week, against ₹8.1 lakh per week for the original geofence guess (₹162 lakh over 20 weeks). It can still win if leadership names protecting large accounts as a goal.

Empowerment is earned and conditional

Teams need product sense, access to data and a leader who can coach. Handing an outcome to a team that has never run an interview is abdication, not empowerment.

Outcome ownership does not transfer luck

Churn can fall because a competitor raised prices, so a team needs a before-and-after comparison on affected versus unaffected customers.

What the idea cannot tell you

It cannot tell you which outcome is right or whether your estimates are good. The fix rates above are guesses; treating them as measurements merely moves false precision from the roadmap to the spreadsheet.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In B2B products like Gatiman’s, the pull toward a feature team is strongest, because large customers make specific demands. The defence is to treat each request as evidence of a problem and ask how many customers share it. In consumer products, outcomes are easiest to measure because experiments finish quickly. In marketplaces, one team’s outcome (more supply) can damage another’s (buyer experience), so outcomes need paired guardrail measures.

By stage, an early company with eight people is empowered by accident: the founder is the strategy and the company is one triad. The risk comes with scale, when the founder keeps choosing solutions for a hundred people. A large company has layered approvals and a planning calendar built around fixed lists; there the move is gradual, starting with one team that has a measurable outcome and a supportive leader.

7. Common mistakes

Renaming the backlog

Symptom: the team’s “objectives” are the same six features written as sentences. Misunderstanding: an objective that names a solution is a task. Diagnostic: ask what the team would do if its first solution failed; a blank look means the solution was the goal.

Outcomes with no authority

Symptom: a team owns “reduce churn” but needs another department’s approval for every change. Misunderstanding: responsibility was delegated without the decision rights. Diagnostic: list the last five changes the team wanted and count how many needed permission.

Confusing shipped with solved

Symptom: the quarterly review celebrates launches and never shows the outcome number. Misunderstanding: delivery was taken as proof of effect. Diagnostic: ask for the outcome figure before and after the last launch; if no one can produce it, nobody was measuring.

8. What good looks like

Imagine the same morning handled well. Gauri brings Hemant not a refusal but a one-page proposal: the 54-fleet target, the exit evidence in Table 2, three bets with stated guesses, and a commitment to report at week six. She asks Fiza what the Hansa Roadlines export must do, so a smaller build may serve. Hemant keeps a veto on strategy, exercised by confirming the churn target rather than choosing features.

9. What Gauri decided

She took the proposal to Hemant on 8 July. Hemant agreed to a one-quarter trial, with a report on 17 August. After the prototype result, the team spent the remaining 36 engineer-weeks on a second round of interviews about alerts, the largest pool of losses, rather than on the next item down a list. Her reasoning: the list gave a certain output and an uncertain effect, while the bets gave a measurable effect that could be corrected as the quarter went on.

Read next about product organisation models, which shows how companies structure teams around outcomes, and product culture, which explains why the model survives or collapses with leaders’ behaviour when a result disappoints.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own organisation, who chose the last three things your team shipped, and what number would have told them they were right? Second, if Hemant had refused the trial, what is the smallest piece of outcome ownership Gauri could have asked for, and what evidence would she need to earn the rest?
exp40v2-pm.empowered:
Empowered teams vs feature teams

Where the decision sits, what it is worth, and when the distinction stops being useful.

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On Monday 13 April 2026 Damini Borkar put a printed sheet face down on a table at Dhenu Dairy Network, Bengaluru. Dhenu sells milk, curd and staples on daily subscription in nine cities, against Amul, Nandini and the neighbourhood vendor: 1,44,000 subscriptions at ₹1,320 a month, annualised revenue ₹228.10 crore.

Of the 24,000 subscriptions acquired in December 2025, 5,760 were active at day ninety: 24.0 per cent. Acquisition cost ₹1,450 against ₹290.40 a month of contribution, so one had to survive just under five months to repay itself. The board wanted 32.0 per cent.

Under the sheet lay a list from Bikram Dastidar, the co-founder and chief executive: seven items for the thirteen weeks to 12 July, each with a sponsor's name. Damini's three teams, twenty-four engineers, had 312 engineer-weeks less a quarter reserved for on-call, leaving 234. The items cost 246, and none was tied by evidence to the board's number.

Ten days later, on Thursday 23 April, Darshini Chokshi sat through the mirror-image meeting in Hyderabad. Dastoor Expense Systems sells a travel-and-expense platform to large Indian corporates: 410 customers, average annual contract ₹48 lakh, ARR ₹196.80 crore, thirty-one logos lost last year — gross churn 7.6 per cent. Dinkar Chhabria, head of enterprise sales, brought sixty-four committed features across eighteen deals worth ₹38.40 crore of new ARR. Eleven teams had 728 available engineer-weeks after a thirty per cent reserve; the list cost 940.

Darshini's list was signed: three of the eighteen deals carried ₹18.60 crore of the ₹38.40 crore, or 48.4 per cent. Damini's list had no evidence behind it; Darshini's had a price on it.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

A feature team is assigned solutions chosen elsewhere; it owns delivery and quality and is judged on whether they shipped. An empowered team is assigned a problem, a measurable result and constraints; it chooses the solutions and is judged on whether the result moved. The difference is not seniority or process but the location of one decision — which solution — and the evaluation that follows.

The vocabulary is Marty Cagan's, from Inspired (2008) and Empowered (2020); Melissa Perri (2018) and Teresa Torres (2021) supply operating detail. The lineage is older: Drucker's management by objectives (1954) moved evaluation from task to result, Deming held that the person doing the work knows what the planner does not, and Grove (1983) made outcomes a planning artefact. The Agile Manifesto (2001) said architecture emerges from self-organising teams; Scrum then installed a Product Owner who owned a backlog — the ambiguity that produced feature teams in agile clothing.

The most useful academic frame is Richard Hackman's, in Leading Teams (2002): authority is a ladder of four levels, not a switch.

Hackman's finding matters more than his taxonomy: self-managing teams fail without a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive context and expert coaching, and most programmes supply only the first. The strongest empirical leg is narrow: DORA's research in Accelerate (2018) found that a team's ability to make large-scale changes without outside permission predicted delivery and organisational performance — authority over architecture, not over problem choice.

Four positions disagree. The empowerment school signs “a team evaluated on output will optimise output” and refuses “teams choose their own objectives”. The founder-conviction school — Amazon's working-backwards tradition, and Brian Chesky's 2022 return of roadmap authority to Airbnb's centre — signs “coherence is a property of a single taste” and refuses “executives choosing features is inherently a pathology”. The socio-technical school (Conway, 1968; Skelton and Pais, 2019) signs “autonomy without architectural alignment buys coordination cost, not speed”. The contingency school (Hackman, Mintzberg) signs “the right authority level depends on interdependence and uncertainty” and refuses the general claim. India adds a fifth: in a contracted delivery organisation the feature team is what the customer bought.

3. Mechanics, and the arithmetic underneath

The loop — outcome, discovery, bets, delivery, measurement — is easy to name; the implicit steps decide whether it works. The first is attribution. Damini's teams began with the 18,240 December-cohort subscriptions that failed to reach day ninety (24,000 less 5,760). Bhakti Dabholkar, the group's data scientist, joined exit surveys to delivery and payment-failure logs and gave each one dominant cause. No feature team would have produced Figure 2, because it is never asked the question Figure 2 answers.

The second step converts the outcome into a unit tradeable against capacity. Dhenu acquires 24,000 subscriptions a month, so one retention point is 240 subscriptions, and finance values a survivor at eleven further months of contribution — 11 × ₹290.40 = ₹3,194.40, rounded to ₹3,200. The eight-point gap is 1,920 subscriptions a cohort, worth ₹61.44 lakh a cohort and ₹7.37 crore across twelve.

The third step writes falsifiable bets. A bet is a solution, a named cause pool and an assumed recovery rate — the share of that pool it would have retained. Table 1 is what the teams brought back on 24 April.

Table 1. Pools 3,420 + 4,104 + 6,384 + 1,368 = 15,276, or 83.75 per cent of the 18,240 lost. Saved 855 + 513 + 798 + 171 = 2,337, which is 9.7375 retention points. The last column is pooled, 9.7375 ÷ 132 × 10 = 0.74, not the mean of the four rows (0.70).

Read naively, Table 1 promises 9.74 points against a target of 8.0 — 121.7 per cent — for 132 of 234 engineer-weeks. But the rates are guesses, and Ronny Kohavi's work at Microsoft put the share of tested ideas that move the target metric positively at roughly one in three. At that hit rate Table 1's risk-adjusted expectation is 2,337 ÷ 3 = 779 subscriptions, or 3.25 points — 40.6 per cent of target.

That correction is the formal core. Let p be the probability an idea moves the outcome if built, B the engineer-weeks to build one, D the weeks to screen one, C capacity and n the number screened, and give the screen sensitivity s and false-positive rate f. The share passing is ps + (1−p)f, and precision — the chance a passed idea is a real winner — is ps ÷ [ps + (1−p)f]. Expected wins are the smaller of the passes and the builds remaining capacity affords, times precision.

With Dhenu's figures — C = 234, B = 33 (the mean of Table 1's four builds), p = 1/3 — a feature team builds 7.09 sponsor-chosen ideas and, if sponsors are no better than chance, expects 2.36 wins. Table 2 computes the alternative at twelve screened ideas.

Three results follow. First, the advantage belongs not to empowerment but to the ratio D/B: at D = 12 weeks every column in Table 2 is worse than building the list. Setting expected wins equal to the 2.36 benchmark gives the break-even — discovery spend must stay under 114.4 engineer-weeks, 48.9 per cent of capacity, or 9.53 weeks each at twelve ideas, 28.9 per cent of a build. Second, wins can never exceed nps, so the s = 0.75 screen needs at least 9.45 screened ideas and even a perfect screen needs 7.09; screening three buys the cost and none of the benefit. Third, where sponsors beat chance the benchmark rises above anything the team can reach — Darshini's case, since a signed contract puts a sponsor's hit rate near one. Dhenu's measured discovery cost was 7.5 weeks a bet, 22.7 per cent of a build.

The second-order effect practitioners rarely count is decision latency. Of thirty-eight decisions Damini's teams logged, twenty-three needed outside sign-off under the list model, at a median of nine days: 207 team-days, 29.6 calendar weeks of waiting. Under the bet model six did — 54 team-days, 7.7 weeks.

4. Testable conditions, applied

Four conditions are load-bearing, and all are checkable before the quarter starts. The outcome must be observable faster than the team replans. Dastoor passes: median time from submission to reimbursement is computed weekly and stood at 11.4 days. Dhenu fails: day-ninety retention appears ninety days late and the teams replan fortnightly. The remedy is a leading indicator named in advance; Damini chose the day-twenty-one delivery-miss rate, agreed with Bikram on 29 April and reviewed on Monday 25 May; who picks it is the real decision right.

Discovery costs well under a third of a build. Dhenu passes at 22.7 per cent. Dastoor splits: approvals workflows pass at three discovery weeks against a twenty-week build, 15.0 per cent, testing in a sandbox on synthetic reports; enterprise integrations fail at fourteen weeks against a twenty-two-week build, 63.6 per cent, because testing one needs a customer's own system and security review.

The team holds the levers. Dhenu's largest pool — 6,384 subscriptions lost to delivery misses in weeks one to three — moves on route density, rider rostering and crate logistics, none of which sat with product. Dastoor's approvals workflow passes: the lever is in software.

No single customer's committed revenue dominates the period. Dhenu passes trivially; Dastoor fails on 48.4 per cent of its new-ARR pipeline. Where a customer has paid for a solution, that solution is the outcome, and a team that insists on rediscovering it is not empowered but insubordinate.

The idea is actively misleading where a regulator has specified the artefact; where the outcome cannot be measured, so a charter converts accountability into rhetoric; and where cycle time binds, since a quarterly releaser loses to a weekly one whatever its charter.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

Dastoor shows the multi-product seam plainly. “Time to first reimbursement” crosses the expense module, the approvals engine, a partner bank's card ledger and the travel desk — four of nine modules, four owners — so a team handed it alone spends the quarter negotiating. Mature firms appoint a single-threaded owner who borrows capacity: Dastoor gave Bhairavi Chandorkar the journey outcome and a claim on 40 per cent of three teams, while Dhiren Barve's platform group and Bianca Correia, its architect in Porto, held the interface contract.

Two-sided businesses invert the problem: an outcome for one side is reliably achievable at the other's expense, as Dobara Resale Exchange discovered. Chauraha Rentals Exchange pairs every supply-side fill-rate target with a demand-side guardrail; breaching it stops the quarter.

Regulated products bound the space, not the authority: Chhatri Insurance Works sells health cover whose benefit structure requires a filing with the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority, so its teams own conversion and persistency but nothing that changes the filed product inside the cycle. Hardware is the same problem in time: at Dhwaj Instruments Group, which builds laboratory analysers, the bill of materials freezes some fourteen months before shipment, so firmware teams carry quarterly outcomes while the instrument team carries a capability window. At Chintan AI Collective, whose drafting assistant serves legal teams, AI-native answer quality is a distribution, not a rate, so the real decision right is the eval suite.

What mature companies do, as against what they publish, is run a hybrid and decline to name it. Darshini named hers: two of eleven teams in a commitments pod budgeted at 136 of the 728 available engineer-weeks, which forced Dinkar's sixty-four requests to be ranked into 136 weeks rather than 940 and left 592 against three outcomes.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The outcome must be reachable by the team's own levers, and usually is not. Name three things the team could change next fortnight that move the number; if two sit elsewhere, it holds a hope.

Empowerment relocates error; it does not reduce it. An empowered team's bad quarter is three dead bets and a learned constraint; a feature team's is six shipped items and a flat number. No dead bets means nothing was tested.

The asset is the hit rate, not the autonomy. Ask for the last ten bets and their outcomes. An expert team names its misses with dates and the figure that killed them; a team that cannot is running a backlog in new vocabulary. And “we are empowered” usually describes the latest decision, so ask about the one before.

The constraint list is the real charter. Experts write down what the team may not change — price, brand, data residency, a filed insurance benefit — before what it should achieve; unwritten constraints surface at the worst moment.

Making discovery cheap is a capital decision. Table 2 locates the whole advantage in D/B, so experts fund a standing field-test panel, a flag harness, a synthetic-data sandbox. Dastoor's integrations failed condition two for want of a sandbox.

A stakeholder request is data about a problem and sometimes a correctly priced instruction. Ask what happens to revenue this quarter if it is not built: a signed number makes it a constraint, a shrug a hypothesis. Treating all as hypotheses is as naive as treating all as orders.

What leadership does when the number does not move is the only reliable signal. Watch the second review. Any executive tolerates one failed bet; the system shows itself when a team reports no movement twice.

Measurement lag caps how much empowerment is coherent. Where the outcome takes ninety days to observe and the team replans fortnightly, it steers on indicators of its own choosing — a larger grant than the outcome. Leaders who think they delegated a number have delegated the definition of success.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the distinction is sharpest and cheapest to act on: experiments conclude in days and D is small. In B2B and enterprise the pull toward feature teams is structural, not cultural: a signed commitment raises the sponsor's hit rate above the team's, so the honest design is a hybrid with a published commitments budget. In platform products the outcome is another team's productivity, measurable but contested. In marketplaces single-sided outcomes are dangerous; in hardware the time constants differ by an order of magnitude between layers. For AI products only the eval suite is new.

By stage the pattern is less interesting than it sounds. A twelve-person company is empowered by accident: the founders are the strategy. The failure arrives between roughly fifty and three hundred people, when founders keep choosing solutions for teams whose customers they no longer meet. In a large company the obstacle is the planning calendar: commitments made nine months ahead stop a team changing its mind.

8. Three worked examples

Dhenu, the quarter before. From October to December 2025 Damini's group shipped five list items for 198 engineer-weeks, ₹1.98 crore at ₹1 lakh a week. Day-ninety retention of the September 2025 cohort had been 24.8 per cent; the December 2025 cohort came in at 24.0 per cent. Note the windows: the September cohort reached day ninety in December 2025, before most of that work shipped, the December cohort in March 2026, after all of it. Two cohorts are thin evidence for a 0.8-point move, which at ₹3,200 is 192 subscriptions and ₹73.73 lakh across twelve cohorts.

Dastoor's platform team: outcome without decision rights. In 2025 Dhiren's platform group was given a crisp outcome — cut the median customer integration build from nine weeks to four — and no authority over the data schema, reviewed fortnightly by an architecture council. Over twenty-six weeks it requested fourteen changes, waited a median of nineteen days each (266 team-days, thirty-eight calendar weeks in aggregate) and had four refused. The median build fell from nine weeks to 7.6 — 1.4 of the 5 weeks asked for, or 28.0 per cent of target.

Dobara Resale Exchange: empowerment with the wrong outcome. Dobara runs a clothing-resale marketplace in Mumbai. In 2025 Deeya Chandekar gave three genuinely empowered teams one outcome: raise weekly listings from 42,000 to 70,000. They reached 71,400, a rise of 70.0 per cent, and the quarter was celebrated. But sell-through within thirty days fell from 38 per cent to 24 per cent, so weekly items sold rose only from 15,960 to 17,136, up 7.4 per cent, while average order value fell from ₹1,180 to ₹940. Weekly gross merchandise value fell from ₹1,88,32,800 to ₹1,61,07,840, down 14.5 per cent, and the 29,400 extra listings cost ₹11 each to moderate: ₹3.23 lakh a week, ₹1.68 crore a year.

The recovery was not a return to feature teams. Deeya made items sold within thirty days the target, buyer condition complaints per thousand orders a hard guardrail, and gave the teams authority over listing standards, which they tightened. Two quarters later listings had settled at 56,000 a week, sell-through at 35 per cent, items sold at 19,600 and average order value at ₹1,105: weekly GMV of ₹2,16,58,000, 15.0 per cent above the ₹1,88,32,800 it started from. The outcome, not the model, was wrong.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Outcome theatre. Early sign: the objectives name solutions. Diagnostic: “what would you do if this solution failed?” Caught late it costs a quarter plus the credibility of the next attempt.

Accountability without authority. Early sign: a lengthening escalation log. Diagnostic: count how many of the last five wanted changes needed outside permission. Dastoor's platform group reached 28.0 per cent of target.

Single-metric capture. Early sign: the metric moves faster than any plausible mechanism. Diagnostic: name the mechanism and guardrail first, and ask for the last field test's sample size. Dobara's late catch cost ₹1.68 crore a year of moderation and 14.5 per cent of GMV.

Quiet reversion. Early sign: a large escalation ends in a direct instruction. Diagnostic: ask what the team was told to drop last quarter, and by whom. The cost is that honest bets stop.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is about coherence. The founder-conviction position holds that a product's integrity is a single act of taste, and that many teams optimising locally yield a well-measured incoherent product; its evidence is the firms whose best work came from centralised conviction, and Airbnb's 2022 reorganisation. For it to be wrong, coherence would have to be preservable by strategy and interface contracts alone — and the rebuttal rests on cases where the founder was also the strategist.

The second is about what the DORA evidence establishes. Read strictly, Accelerate supports autonomy over architecture and deployment, not over problem choice. The socio-technical school argues that most benefit credited to empowerment is really the benefit of loose coupling, and that autonomy without it buys coordination cost instead of speed. To be wrong, the school would have to see gains where coupling never changed.

The third is about whether the binary is useful at all. The contingency school holds that “empowered versus feature” compresses a four-level ladder and several variables — interdependence, measurement lag, regulatory constraint, revenue concentration — into a slogan; its evidence is that competent organisations run hybrids. The reply is pragmatic: the binary is a teaching device for firms that drifted to level one without noticing, and a continuum would license further drift.

The fourth is about delivery economics. Reinertsen's position is that batch size and feedback latency dominate decision-rights placement, so a feature team shipping weekly beats an empowered team shipping quarterly. Disproving it needs cases where decision rights moved and nothing else did; those are rare, because firms granting autonomy change release cadence too.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a vocabulary and a grievance. Someone who has internalised it arrives with four numbers: the cause decomposition, the cost of screening one idea, the cost of building one, and the list of things the team may not change. They negotiate the charter, not the metric, knowing it is uncollectable without the levers, and will take a feature team's assignment knowingly. They quote the risk-adjusted expectation, and are therefore the only person able to say a target is unreachable — a sentence a feature team cannot utter.

12. What each protagonist decided

Damini went back to Bikram on Wednesday 29 April with arithmetic rather than a position. She accepted one of his seven items as a priced constraint — the pause-and-resume calendar, which Table 1 already carries at 18 engineer-weeks — committed three teams to the four bets at 132 engineer-weeks, and held the other 102 unallocated. Then the uncomfortable argument: at a one-in-three hit rate the four bets carry a risk-adjusted expectation of 3.25 points, so an eight-point move in one quarter would need roughly ten such bets built and twenty-six screened — about 525 engineer-weeks against the 234 she had. She committed to 3.25 points by 12 July, asked for the eight-point target to be re-based to the year ending 31 March 2027, and asked for the one thing that cost Bikram something: a joint charter with Chetna Dighe's city operations over delivery reliability in weeks one to three.

Darshini did not convert Dastoor to empowered teams. She published the pod of two teams and 136 engineer-weeks and told Dinkar his sixty-four requests had to be ranked into it; gave Bhairavi the reimbursement-time outcome across 592 weeks; and declined outcome ownership for enterprise integrations, where discovery costs 63.6 per cent of a build. She signs the contingency proposition, not the universal one — and calling eleven teams empowered while handing them a 940-week list would have cost her both.

Question one. Damini divides Table 1 by three, using an industry-wide win rate. Is that defensible for bets drawn from a measured cause decomposition, and if not, what would she need to observe first?

Question two. Dastoor's pod makes the feature-team model explicit and budgeted. Does publishing the budget strengthen the outcome teams, or create a lane into which every hard request is routed?

Question three. Dobara's teams were empowered throughout and destroyed ₹27.25 lakh a week of GMV. What should Deeya have been accountable for, and would any charter have caught it by week three?

13. Going deeper

The product triad is the prerequisite: joint ownership of the choice is how an outcome is actually held. Product org models turns this page's hybrid into structure: pods, journey owners, platform groups, seams. Product culture answers the survival question: what happens to the team that reports a dead bet. What a product manager does and PM myths vs reality apply the same test to a role, and are where the “mini-CEO” myth dies. Origins of product management supplies the lineage that made the feature team default. PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder matters because outcome ownership gets reassigned to whoever will accept it. PM archetypes shows who thrives at which level; how the PM job changes by company stage picks up the fifty-to-three-hundred transition.
case20v1-pm.empowered:
Jamapunji Merchant Systems: A List or a Problem

A teaching case on empowered teams and feature teams

1. Opening

On Monday 21 September 2026, Jivika Sundaresan sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Jamapunji Merchant Systems' Pune office with two documents open. The first was a one-page roadmap, sent by the head of sales the previous Friday, listing nine features for the October-to-December quarter in a firm order of priority. The second was a spreadsheet of five weeks of results from a small experiment her product team had run quietly on its own initiative.

As head of product, Jivika had until Friday 25 September to lock the quarter's plan. The sales list was not unreasonable. Its first item was tied to a letter of intent from a large distributor, to be signed on 30 September. The experiment suggested that something else mattered more, and the list left almost no room for it. She had to decide whether her team would be handed a list to build or a problem to solve, and she knew that whichever she chose would set how the company behaved for years.

2. Company background

Jamapunji was founded in 2019 by Farhan Lakdawala, a former bank technologist. It sells a UPI soundbox, the small speaker that announces each payment received, to neighbourhood shops, and it layers a working-capital credit line on top, funded by a partner non-banking finance company. A shopkeeper with a Jamapunji box can draw a small loan against the rhythm of her daily QR collections and repay it over a month.

By September 2026 the company had 4,80,000 shops on its soundbox, from Pune and Nashik to Coimbatore, Indore and Guwahati. Paytm and PhonePe sell similar boxes, while Khatabook and OkCredit own the ledger habit. UPI rails and NPCI's merchant-fee rules make the soundbox itself nearly a commodity, so the credit line is where Jamapunji earns its living. The lending partner answers to the RBI, whose digital lending rules shape how money moves between borrower, lender and platform.

Product work is done by 25 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, organised in squads that have, until now, been briefed by the sales and operations teams. Delivery has been excellent; whether the product is improving is another matter.

3. The situation

Jasmeet Bindra's list had grown from deals. The largest was Jaipal Distribution Network, a wholesaler supplying about 1,100 retail outlets, which wanted bulk-order sync between its dispatch system and the Jamapunji app, worth ₹240 lakh a year, or ₹2.4 crore. Eight smaller asks, each from a prospect or a regional sales manager, filled out the rest. Exhibit 1 lays them out. The nine items would consume 236 of the 240 engineer-weeks available, or 98.3 per cent, leaving nothing for learning.

Exhibit 2 shows why Jivika was uneasy. In each of the last three quarters the squads shipped every feature they had been given: 27 of 27. Yet the share of credit-line repayments arriving within seven days of the due date fell from 73.0 per cent to 71.0 to 68.0. Each overdue loan costs the company about ₹600 in calls and field visits, so late repayments cost ₹142.08 lakh in the latest quarter alone. Over the three quarters, the cost was ₹332.46 lakh.

Her product designer, Filip Nowicki, working from Kraków, had spent August interviewing shopkeepers by video. A tea-stall owner in Nashik told him that the monthly instalment fell due on the fifth, when her cash was thinnest, and that she paid late rather than skip stocking. Cash came in daily; the loan asked for it monthly. The team's hypothesis was that deducting a small share of each day's QR collections toward the loan would cut late repayment. Starting 17 August, Jorge Figueiredo, a data scientist in São Paulo, helped run it by hand with 600 merchants on daily deduction and 600 on the usual schedule, assigned by alternate merchant ID. After five weeks, 468 of the 600 on daily deduction repaid on time, or 78.0 per cent, against 408 of 600, or 68.0 per cent, on the old schedule. At the Q1 volume of 74,000 loans, a ten-point gain would mean 7,400 fewer overdue loans and about ₹44.4 lakh saved each quarter. It was a small sample, and productising it would need consent flows built with the lending partner within the RBI's rules.

The view from each location differed. Jorge, eight and a half hours behind Pune, pointed out that five weeks of repayment data could not yet show whether the gain would persist. Filip argued that shopkeepers had told them what they needed and that a ninth feature would not change that.

4. The people

Jivika Sundaresan, head of product, Pune. She is accountable for the credit line's health and has the CEO's authority to set the plan, but not to lose a contract on her own.

Jasmeet Bindra, head of sales, Gurugram. His targets depend on closing Jaipal before Diwali. He argues that a signed contract is the only proof a customer wants anything.

Faisal Ansari, engineering manager, Bengaluru. He leads the 25 engineers and wants predictability. He is sceptical of experiments yet worried that his best people are bored being order-takers.

Farhan Lakdawala, chief executive, Pune. He wants growth and good repayment and will back whoever shows him the numbers. His one stated rule is that no squad should depend on a single customer.

5. The options

Exhibit 4 sets capacity against each option.

Option A: ship the list as sequenced. The squads build all nine items in Jasmeet's order. The upside is certainty: Jaipal's ₹240 lakh is secured and Faisal's planning is simple. The cost is that nothing addresses the falling repayment rate, and 98.3 per cent of capacity is gone before any surprise arrives.

Option B: give the repayment outcome to the team and drop the list. Squads are told to lift the on-time rate from 68 per cent to at least 78 per cent by year-end and are left free to decide how. About 180 engineer-weeks go to daily deduction and related work. The upside is the full force of the pilot and a motivated team. The cost is that Jasmeet loses Jaipal's ₹240 lakh and the goodwill of every sales deal behind it.

Option C: give the outcome to a dedicated squad and turn the biggest request into a problem. Ninety-six engineer-weeks go to the repayment outcome; Jaipal's bulk-order work is kept at 36 weeks but reframed so the team, with Jasmeet, first confirm what Jaipal's outlets actually need; 48 weeks go to other list items chosen against the outcome; 60 weeks are held for what the next test reveals. The upside is that both revenue and learning are protected. The cost is more negotiation, a possibly disappointed Jaipal, and a harder message to sales.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What do Exhibits 1 and 2 together say about how the company's squads are being run, and what would you want to know before deciding that the delivery was the problem?
  2. How strong is the evidence from the pilot, and what would a larger test need to show before the team commits to building it?
  3. In Option C, what separates giving Jaipal a problem to solve from simply refusing the request?
  4. What should Jivika tell Jasmeet and Farhan on Friday, and what measure should she propose to judge her own decision by the end of December?

7. A note for the learner

An empowered team is given an outcome and the freedom to find the way; a feature team is given a list and judged on whether it shipped. The question this topic poses is: is the team here to hit an outcome or to deliver a list, and who decided? Exhibit 2 is the classic symptom. A team that delivers every planned feature while the repayment rate it never owned slides from 73.0 to 68.0 per cent has been held to the wrong measure. The system rewards output.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It separates a customer's stated solution from the customer's problem. Jaipal asked for bulk-order sync, but what it presumably needs is for its outlets to order and pay without friction, and there may be a cheaper route. It treats the pilot as a hypothesis, not proof: 78.0 against 68.0 on 600 merchants each is promising but says little about regulatory design or durability. And it protects the business, since an empowered team still has to earn the trust of sales and the CEO.

One defensible path is Option C. Jivika assigns a dedicated squad the outcome — raise the on-time rate to 75 per cent or more across a 6,000-merchant test by mid-November — and stops the test if the lift falls below five points. She asks Jasmeet and Faisal to spend a week with Jaipal before 30 September, so that the letter of intent commits to a result, such as outlet ordering on credit at delivery, rather than to a feature specification. The reserve of 60 weeks lets the team act on what it learns before Diwali. Option A is rejected because it guarantees the number keeps sliding. Option B is rejected because one lost contract of ₹240 lakh would damage trust in the approach, and a single quarter does not justify handing the whole capacity to a hypothesis on 600 merchants. Option C shows Jasmeet his customer is taken seriously and gives the team a reason to care.
case40v1-pm.empowered:
Chakshu Fleet Systems: Whose Problem Is the Truck Off the Road?

A case for discussion. Empowered teams and feature teams are the lens; the case does not resolve.

1. Tuesday night, Pune

At a quarter past eleven on Tuesday 17 November 2026, Chaitali Zarapkar was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with three documents and a cup of filter coffee gone cold. The board of Chakshu Fleet Systems met on Thursday 19 November; the pack was due by noon on Wednesday. The item against her name read H1 2027 Product Plan — approval.

The first was a one-page roadmap for January to June 2027, circulated by the chief revenue officer, Chaman Zutshi, on 2 November. It listed ten items in a fixed order and claimed, in a column headed New ARR, that they would add ₹1,295 lakh a year to a software business running at ₹1,839.84 lakh. The second was a six-week field study her own designer and data scientist had run among small truck fleets near Nagpur, Hubballi and Raipur, which suggested that what Chakshu sold was not what its customers lost money to. The third was the June 2023 master services agreement with Zamin Haulage Industries, with its annexure of dated deliverables and the exclusivity clause on page nine.

The pack needed a list of what thirty-five engineers, two designers and three analysts would build. What Chaitali had come to believe was that the question underneath it was who at Chakshu decided what the company built, and that nobody had decided it: it had been settled in 2023, by a contract annexure, and had run on its own since.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Chakshu was founded in Pune in 2019 by Zuber Chinoy, a powertrain electronics engineer who had watched his father-in-law run nine trucks on the Pune–Hubballi route with a notebook and a phone. Its first product was a box wired to a truck's diagnostic port, pulling engine, fuel and fault-code data off the vehicle bus over a Jio data SIM. It told an owner where his trucks were, what diesel they drank and — this was the pitch — which of them was about to break down. By 31 October 2026 it had 92,000 trucks under paid subscription across 9,268 fleets, from owner-drivers in Sangli to firms in Ahmedabad. Exhibit 1 shows how little revenue comes from the fleets that are almost all of the customer count.

Two earlier decisions constrain what Chaitali can do now. The first is the hardware subsidy: in 2021, to pull small fleets on, Chakshu began selling the device at ₹1,900 against a landed and installed cost of ₹4,200, a subsidy of ₹2,300 a truck recovered out of subscription. At that band's ₹150 a month and a gross margin of 55 per cent the company earns ₹82.50 a truck a month, so the subsidy takes 27.9 months to repay. At churn of 30.0 per cent a year the average truck stays 40.0 months and yields ₹3,300 of lifetime gross margin, leaving ₹1,000 after the subsidy and about ₹100 after acquisition costs of roughly ₹900. The small-fleet business is break-even, and has been for two years.

The second is the Zamin agreement. In June 2023, needing a marquee logo before a Series A, Chakshu signed a three-year master services agreement with Zamin Haulage Industries, a contract-logistics firm then running 1,900 trucks out of Ahmedabad, Nagpur and Hosur. Zamin insisted on an annexure of dated deliverables; in exchange it took an exclusivity barring Chakshu, until 31 March 2028, from licensing a multi-depot “control tower” to any Indian contract-logistics firm with more than 1,000 trucks. Chaman reads the clause as covering only the module built for Zamin; counsel, on 12 November 2026, called it “arguable in either direction”.

The annexure did something else nobody wrote down: it created the habit of a dated list. From 2023 every planning cycle began with a document sales had written and engineering had estimated, and squads were judged on whether the dates held. They did: Chandrima Zaveri's engineers shipped 47 of the 49 items committed over the last three halves.

3. The industry

The telematics layer on India's trucks stopped being a novelty around 2025. Tata Motors sells Fleet Edge with its vehicles, Ashok Leyland ships iAlert, and Mahindra and Bosch push connected-vehicle stacks into the aftermarket. For a fleet buying new, basic visibility now arrives free in the cab. That has hollowed out Chakshu's pitch and pushed it toward older vehicles, where the data is dirtier but the breakdowns are.

Regulation bears on the product from three directions. The GST network's e-way bill regime gives every consignment a document trail owners must reconcile and nobody enjoys reconciling. NHAI's FASTag turns tolls into transactions a product can match against trips. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, governs the most attractive item on Chaman's list: scoring drivers on braking, cornering and speed and feeding the scores to insurers so a fleet's premium falls. The driver is not the contracting party, and counsel advises that consent must be taken from each driver separately. IRDAI's openness to usage-based motor cover makes the prize real; the consent architecture makes it slow.

Downstream, the repair economy is informal. An owner with a failed turbocharger calls a mechanic he knows, who calls a parts dealer he knows, who may or may not have the part. ONDC's networks have begun to formalise some of this, and a Pune start-up, Chinar Parts Exchange, has a parts catalogue with same-day delivery in eleven cities. None of it connects to anything a telematics box knows. Abroad, exposure is small but loud: Zaawiya Transport Industries, a bulk-haulage group in Muscat, has run a 300-truck pilot since July 2026 out of a fleet of 1,200 and offered ₹260 lakh in year one, contingent on an Arabic interface and Omani compliance reporting by 1 June 2027 and on winning a cement tender due 15 February 2027.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

At each point the company believed something it has since had reason to doubt. In January 2024 it launched Chakshu Alerts, believing small fleets would pay for breakdown prediction. Model precision was 41 per cent at first and 68 per cent by October 2024; acknowledgement in the smallest band did not move. The company then believed the problem was the app: in February 2025 Cornelis Zwaan rebuilt the alert screen, cut the notification to one line of Hindi or Marathi and added a voice call for severe faults, and acknowledgement within 48 hours rose from 14 per cent to 18 per cent, where it has stayed. Then it believed the problem was price: in June 2025 the subscription was cut from ₹199 to ₹150, giving up ₹109.37 lakh a year at today's 18,600 trucks. Churn in that band fell from 34.0 per cent to 30.0 per cent and has not fallen since.

Between 18 August and 28 September 2026, six weeks, Zwaan and Celeste Zamora instrumented not the truck but the incident. With fourteen fleets — 126 trucks, averaging nine each — a field researcher on ₹22,000 a month telephoned the owner, the driver and any mechanic each time a truck stopped, recording the clock: fault noticed, diagnosed, part ordered, part arrived, vehicle moved. Fifty-eight incidents were logged. Over half the time off the road — 52.8 per cent of 208.8 lost days — went on waiting for a part; detection, the thing Chakshu sells, took 9.7 per cent. In the eleven incidents where the alert fired days ahead, the owner saw it, understood it and still lost an average of 3.1 days, because knowing on Tuesday that a water pump will fail does not produce a water pump in Nagpur on Wednesday.

On 2 November Chaman circulated the roadmap. On 10 November, at the annexure review in Ahmedabad, Zubin Chhapgar of Zamin demanded the control tower live by 30 April 2027, mentioning in passing that Zamin's own technology group had built an interim dashboard. On 12 November counsel's note arrived. On 14 November Chandrima sent one line: “Whatever you decide, decide by Thursday. My people are reading the roadmap as the plan already.”

5. The people

Chaitali Zarapkar, vice-president of product, Pune, joined in 2024 from a payments company. She is measured on net revenue retention and roadmap predictability, measures she did not write; she may propose the plan but not give up signed revenue. Unsaid: she commissioned the study without telling Chaman, and is unsure whether she is reading the data or using it to win.

Zuber Chinoy, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, wants a Series C in late 2027 and has told two all-hands meetings that he backs teams which own outcomes. Unsaid: he negotiated the Zamin annexure himself and has promised Chhapgar, verbally, that the control tower ships in April.

Chaman Zutshi, chief revenue officer, Gurugram. Forty per cent of his variable pay rides on bookings this half, and enterprise is where bookings are large. Unsaid: two of the ten items came from regional managers with no deal behind them.

Chandrima Zaveri, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru, thirty-five engineers, measured on delivery against commitment and excellent at it. Three senior engineers resigned in nine months, all saying they had become a queue. Unsaid: she believes an outcome team will miss dates and that she will explain why.

Cornelis Zwaan, principal designer, Amsterdam, on calls with Indian owners from six each morning, believes Chakshu has solved a detection problem for three years because detection is what its hardware measures. Unsaid: he has shown a parts-and-mechanic booking flow, without authority, to Chinar Parts Exchange's co-founder Charulata Zalte.

Celeste Zamora, staff data scientist, Mexico City, eleven and a half hours behind Pune, built the breakdown model and is proud of it. She is also readiest to call the study small: fifty-eight incidents, no monsoon month, one recruiting dealer. Unsaid: her precision figure is computed only on alerts the model fired, and she has never published the recall.

Zarmina Cholia, customer success, Edinburgh, reports 71 per cent acknowledgement at Zaawiya and argues the product works wherever someone is paid to act. Unsaid: every Zaawiya truck has a salaried supervisor, and her bonus rides on that contract.

Zubin Chhapgar, transport operations at Zamin, Ahmedabad, runs 2,400 trucks at ₹130 a month and wants the control tower and the driver scores before a July insurance renewal. Unsaid: his interim dashboard works well enough that April is now a negotiating position. Two voices sit on no committee: Chandrakant Zende, nine trucks in Nagpur, and his driver Chandan Zirpe.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 is the roadmap as circulated. Read as sales reads it, ₹1,295 lakh against a ₹1,839.84 lakh base is an increment of 70.4 per cent inside one plan. Read as finance reads it, ₹200 lakh is one-time fee and only ₹1,095 lakh recurs. Read against capacity, the ten items consume exactly the 180 person-months available, leaving nothing for whatever the company might learn.

Exhibit 3 is the previous cycle's version, with a column Celeste added from the ledger: what each item earned twelve months after shipping. All nine items shipped and realisation was 34.6 per cent, which applied crudely to ₹1,295 lakh gives ₹448.6 lakh — though Chaman objects that a module's first year is not its last.

Together they are the most uncomfortable pair in the pack: one says the plan is worth ₹1,295 lakh, the other that the last plan, built the same way and delivered in full, was worth a third of its claim. Neither says what to build. Exhibit 4 is the one Chaitali returns to: what happens after an alert fires.

Read naively, Exhibit 4 says the product works for large fleets, fails for small ones, and that Chakshu should follow the money upward. Read beside Exhibit 5 it says nearly the opposite: small fleets get the most alerts because their trucks break, and act on fewest because acting needs a part they cannot get.

It was the last two numbers in that footnote that kept Chaitali at the table. If the downtime figure held across bands A and B, 45,000 trucks, the value on the floor would be roughly ₹220 crore a year, against total software revenue of ₹18.40 crore. Celeste had written in the margin: “Do not put this multiplication in the board pack. Fifty-eight incidents cannot carry 45,000 trucks. Give me 1,200 trucks and eight weeks first.”

Exhibit 6 is what the board will read first, and most likely to settle the argument the wrong way. Revenue up 21.7 per cent is a good line in a Series C deck; one in four fleets leaving in a year is a different company.

7. Voices

Chaman Zutshi, planning call, 4 November: “I have four signatures and a tender. Cornelis has fourteen owners in Nagpur and a theory. Tell me which I put in front of the board. And see what I give up: if the list loses 74 of 180 person-months, that is ₹340 lakh of pipeline gone, and in April I explain flat bookings.”

Cornelis Zwaan, email, 8 October, 06:42: “Three years making the alert better, and nobody in the study complained it was late. Chandrakant said something I cannot stop hearing: ‘Madam, the box tells me my truck will stop. I know my truck will stop. Tell me who has the part.’ We sell him a thermometer; he asks for a doctor.”

Chandan Zirpe, a driver in the study, from Marathi: “When the alert comes, the phone rings at the owner's house, not in my cabin. I am the one standing on the highway at night. Nobody has asked me anything.”

Chandrima Zaveri, internal chat, 12 November: “I can staff an outcome team. I cannot staff one and hold April for Zamin and still have Oman. Pick two. And if you pick the outcome, write into the board minute who is accountable when it does not move, because last time it was me.”

Zuber Chinoy, in the car park, 16 November: “You know I believe in empowered teams; I have said it on stage. But Zubin and I shook hands on April. Find me a way to be the company I say we are without breaking our word.”

8. The options as Chaitali sees them

Option A — deliver the list. Exhibit 2 goes to the board as written. All 180 person-months go to the ten items; nothing is reserved for discovery. Squads map to items and are judged on dates, as they are already; the model is merely made explicit. Zamin's April date holds, Oman lands before 1 June, bookings have a number. Against it: Exhibit 3 is what this method produced last time, the churn in Exhibit 6 goes untouched, and Chandrima expects two more resignations.

Option B — hand one squad the downtime outcome. Sixty person-months, 33.3 per cent of capacity, go to a team told to cut unplanned downtime days per truck by 30 per cent across a cohort of 1,200 small-fleet trucks by 30 June 2027, with no specification of how. Zamin keeps its 34 and Zaawiya its 26; 46 go to three list items serving the outcome or a contract — e-way bill reconciliation, FASTag reconciliation and the Chinar parts integration, ₹275 lakh of claimed ARR between them — and 14, or 7.8 per cent, are held for what the team learns. The cost is 74 person-months of list dropped, carrying ₹340 lakh of claimed ARR, nearer ₹117.8 lakh at last cycle's realisation.

Option C — two empowered teams and a contract team. Eighty-four person-months, 46.7 per cent of capacity, go to two teams on the downtime outcome, one on parts and mechanic fulfilment and one on the driver as a user. A third team of 60 takes Zamin and Zaawiya and is explicitly a feature team, staffed and rewarded as one, delivering an annexure. Twenty-four cover FASTag and the parts integration; 12 are reserved. The attraction is honesty: contractual work is called contractual work. The cost is admitting that Chakshu runs two kinds of team with two kinds of career, and Chandrima believes the good engineers will all want the two.

Chaitali had written all three on a sheet of paper, and a fourth line underneath that she had shown no one. All three assume the customer is the fleet owner and the product is software on his phone. If Exhibit 5 is right, the binding constraint is a part on a shelf in a town Chakshu has never visited, and no arrangement of her own teams reaches it. The decision may not be whether to empower a team, but whether this is a telematics company at all, and whether a team can be handed an outcome its business model cannot pay for.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The pack is due at noon on Wednesday 18 November and the board meets on Thursday 19 November; Charusheela Zaidi, the investor director, has asked for a slide on net revenue retention and one on the path to a Series C.

Cash stands at ₹96 crore against a monthly burn of ₹4.8 crore, a runway of 20 months to July 2028, and the board will not approve engineering headcount before the Series C, so 240 person-months is a ceiling. The Zamin annexure runs to 31 March 2028, and its exclusivity clause caps what any control tower can earn outside Zamin until then. Zaawiya's ₹260 lakh depends on a tender result on 15 February 2027, six weeks after the plan starts. The DPDP Act makes driver scoring slower and dearer than its 20 person-months suggest, since consent must be taken from drivers individually and drivers change employers often. The hardware subsidy means every new small-fleet truck costs ₹2,300 up front, so band A growth consumes cash just when the board wants it conserved. And Chinar Parts Exchange, the only partner who could make a fulfilment product real, is in eleven cities; Chakshu's band A and B customers are in more than two hundred.

At twenty past midnight Chaitali opened a new document, typed the heading Recommendation, looked at it and deleted the word. Outside, a loaded truck went down the highway with its hazard lights on, and she found herself wondering, for the first time in three years, whether anyone at her company could say whose job it was to keep it moving.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about who decides what Chakshu builds, and who made that decision?
  2. Exhibits 4 and 6 point opposite ways about which customer Chakshu should serve. Reconcile them, and name the columns you would not rely on.
  3. What would have to be true for Exhibit 5 to justify reorganising half the engineering capacity around it? Design the test Celeste Zamora asks for, including the number you would stop on.
  4. Chandrima Zaveri says an outcome team will miss dates and that she will be explaining it. Is she wrong, and what would have to change in how Chakshu measures engineering?
  5. If the binding constraint is parts and mechanics rather than detection, can any team inside Chakshu be handed the downtime outcome honestly? What would the company have to become, and who must agree?
  6. It is Monday 23 November, the board has met, and Chaitali must tell thirty-five engineers, a chief revenue officer and a customer in Ahmedabad what the next six months are. What does she say to each, what does she tell the board about the half just ended, and what single measure does she offer for June?
exp40v2-pm.archetypes:
PM Archetypes: What the Specialisation Buys, and What It Costs

Foundations › The PM Role & Foundations. Session 1, Introduction to Product Management. Near-expert treatment.

1. Two decisions, eight days apart

On 14 September 2026 Nandita Kulkarni, director of product at Avishkar Grid Industries, was handed a note by her chief executive, Girish Pai. Avishkar built commercial solar inverters and battery packs in Coimbatore and sold fleet monitoring from Pune. FY26 revenue was ₹742 crore: ₹486 crore of inverters, ₹178 crore of battery packs, ₹78 crore of monitoring, the last from 3,120 sites at an average ₹2,50,000 a site a year. Its eleven product managers were all generalists. Should the function be split into named specialisations before the board met on 30 October 2026?

Eight days later, on 22 September, Faraz Siddiqui faced a narrower version of the question at Ekaagra Money Labs in Bengaluru. Ekaagra read a user's bank and investment accounts through the Reserve Bank of India's account aggregator framework and answered questions about them with a language model. It had 62 lakh registered users, 18.6 lakh monthly active, and a distribution commission of ₹4.65 crore in September, or ₹25.00 per monthly active user. Meera Vaidya, his vice-president of product, wanted the assistant given to a dedicated artificial-intelligence PM and the funnel to a growth PM; Faraz had until 9 October to object. The two firms reached opposite answers, and the arithmetic separating them is this page's subject.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees

A PM archetype is a specialisation of one underlying job — deciding what a team builds next, and why — defined by three commitments: who the primary customer is, what unit of value it is measured in, and how long before the PM learns she was wrong; the third does most of the work below.

The vocabulary is an artefact of scale. As consumer-internet firms passed a few hundred engineers in the 2000s, growth teams were carved out around 2008–2012 to run acquisition experiments faster than the core team could; platform teams followed, to stop feature teams rebuilding the same plumbing; data and, after 2015, machine-learning roles followed, because a model's evidence standard is a held-out test set, not a specification. Hardware product management arrived separately. Marty Cagan and Ken Norton codified the distinctions in the 2010s; Harvard Business School and Stanford's CS177 now make students name the archetype before opening a backlog.

Four schools disagree about what to do with the taxonomy. The specialisation school holds that archetypes are real job families; it would sign “a growth PM and a platform PM need different metrics, interview loops and promotion criteria,” but not “an archetype is a career identity.” The generalist school holds that the archetype is an artefact of size and the invariant core is the whole job; it would sign “every PM must state the customer problem and the business case in one page,” but not “a growth PM is measured only on activation.”

The ownership school, visible in Amazon's single-threaded leaders and Intuit's general-manager model, holds that what matters is the surface you own end to end; it would sign “accountability follows the customer outcome, not the technical layer,” but not “platform PMs need no business metric.” The constraint school holds that the right archetype is whatever binds the business now; it would sign “the archetype changes when the constraint moves,” but not “archetypes belong in titles.”

Exhibit 1 states those commitments for eight archetypes, the third as a rate: a role reporting fortnightly gets twenty-six chances a year to be wrong cheaply, one reporting at an annual design freeze gets one.

4. When the taxonomy applies

Specialisation raises throughput inside a lane and latency across lanes, and Avishkar's FY26 decision log priced both: decisions inside one specialism took a median 9 days, those needing two took 31, and a generalist holding several surfaces resolved everything at a median 18. With s the share needing two or more archetypes, average latency under specialisation is 9(1 − s) + 31s = 9 + 22s, so break-even against 18 days is s = 9 ÷ 22 = 40.9 per cent.

The test splits the protagonists. Of 184 decisions Avishkar logged, 63 crossed archetypes: s = 34.2 per cent, latency 9 + 22(0.342) = 16.5 days, saving 1.47 days a decision, about 270 decision-days a year. Of 96 decisions Faraz's team logged, 58 crossed: s = 60.4 per cent, latency 22.3 days, costing 4.3 days a decision, about 412 decision-days. Avishkar should split; Ekaagra should not.

The reason is structural. Avishkar's surfaces are separable — a modem's duty cycle and a trial-to-paid flow share almost no decision — whereas Ekaagra's assistant is its activation funnel, so every question is at once a growth, model-quality and unit-cost event. Separating archetypes there divides the evidence, not the work. The taxonomy misleads outright when the binding constraint sits outside the product organisation, when one PM covers everything, and when the label withholds a business metric, excusing work rather than describing it.

5. Hard edge cases and the seams

Avishkar's most instructive case looked trivial: sales asked for telemetry every 15 minutes instead of 60. There are 24,960 inverters in the field, eight per site across 3,120 sites — hourly, 24 messages each per day, 5,99,040 a day; at 15 minutes, 96 each, 23,96,160 a day, an increase of 17,97,120. At ₹0.002 per ingested message the extra traffic costs 17,97,120 × 365 × ₹0.002 = ₹13.12 lakh a year, the platform work 7 engineers × 6 weeks × ₹72,000 = ₹30.24 lakh. The benefit was renewal protection: 41 sites worth ₹2,50,000 each, ₹102.50 lakh a year, had flagged stale data at renewal, and the account team judged half recoverable, ₹51.25 lakh. Year one nets ₹51.25 − ₹30.24 − ₹13.12 = ₹7.89 lakh; year two, ₹38.13 lakh. Three of the four archetypes would approve.

The fourth killed it. Avishkar's cellular modules are rated for 1,20,000 transmissions. At 24 a day that is 5,000 days, about 13.7 years, inside the seven-year warranty of 2,555 days. At 96 a day it is 1,250 days, about 3.4 years — a warranty breach across the installed base, and at ₹3,400 a module, 24,960 × ₹3,400 = ₹8.49 crore of exposure to protect ₹51.25 lakh of revenue. The constraint was invisible to every software archetype. A compromise rescued it: raise the interval only on the 328 inverters at the 41 at-risk sites. Extra traffic becomes 328 × 72 × 365 × ₹0.002 = ₹0.17 lakh a year, exposure 328 × ₹3,400 = ₹11.15 lakh, and year one nets ₹51.25 − ₹30.24 − ₹0.17 − ₹11.15 = ₹9.69 lakh — exposure cut 76-fold.

Two-sided businesses fail more quietly. Avani Mandi Network, a produce marketplace, gave a growth PM the buyer funnel; requests rose 9 per cent, 48,000 a month to 52,320, while seller fill rate, nobody's metric, fell from 86 to 79 per cent, so matched orders moved only from 48,000 × 0.86 = 41,280 to 52,320 × 0.79 = 41,333 — 53 more, 0.13 per cent.

Regulated and AI-native settings add archetypes the map omits. At Ekaagra, 11 of 34 planned assistant capabilities — 32.4 per cent — needed a change to the consent artefact the aggregator framework governs, so a compliance specialism sits on the critical path of every model change and appears on no chart. The defining act changes too: the PM cannot specify the output, only an acceptance threshold on an evaluation set — Faraz's 600-case set, on which the model scored 71.5 per cent acceptable. What mature firms do here is less tidy than their charts: each charter gets a guardrail metric owned by the adjacent archetype, one archetype is tiebreaker, and people rotate. Avishkar's PMs with two specialisms behind them resolved cross-archetype decisions in a median 14 days rather than 31, a 54.8 per cent reduction.

6. Eight nuances the expert sees

The archetype is a property of the metric, not the title. The tell-tale sign is a job description naming a technology rather than a number. An expert asks for last quarter's review criteria; if nobody has them the archetype does not exist yet, and the PM will be asked to be all of them.

Every archetype has a characteristic overreach, which the expert writes into the charter. Growth's is conversion that produces bad customers; platform's is generality nobody asked for; data's is a pipeline with no consumer; hardware's is gold-plating. The sign is a PM who cannot name the harm her metric misses.

The feedback loop sets the politics, not just the calendar. A two-week loop lets a PM win by accumulated evidence; a fifty-two-week loop forces her to win by credibility before evidence exists. Long loops need a different persuasion strategy, not more patience.

Platform PMs have no revenue, so they must manufacture a demand signal. Experts run an internal adoption funnel: teams aware, evaluating, integrated, dependent. Avishkar's ₹120.96 lakh platform win is worth nothing if only one of three lines adopts, and the weak platform PM's roadmap is justified by elegance.

Most disputes between competent PMs are about evidence standards. A growth PM demanding a significant A/B result and a platform PM offering an architecture argument disagree about what counts as proof, not about the product. The sign is each citing a different kind of evidence without noticing.

The cost of being wrong varies fortyfold at identical headcount. Exhibit 3 shows ₹7.20 lakh against ₹336.96 lakh, 46.8 to one; with the ₹2.40 crore of tooling it is ₹576.96 lakh, 80.1 to one. The sign of an immature organisation is one cadence for both; experts ask how reversible a decision is before how large.

Hardware is irreversible at a date, not at a spend. The sign is a PM tracking budget burn rather than the freeze calendar. The day before freeze a change costs a conversation; the day after, ₹2.40 crore. Software intuition, where cost rises smoothly with lateness, is wrong here.

The archetype is a lease, not a deed. Constraints move every eighteen to thirty months and the archetype moves with them. The sign is a PM declining good work as “not my lane”, or a growth pod still staffed three years after acquisition stopped being the constraint.

7. Differences by product type and stage

In consumer products growth and consumer archetypes dominate: large populations make small deltas valuable and experiments readable. In business-to-business software the payer and the user differ, so the unit of value is a renewal, not a session. In platform and marketplace businesses no single number suffices: Avishkar's platform PM needs an adoption metric beside reliability, Avani's growth PM a fill rate beside buyer requests. Hardware organises around a date and a bill of materials; AI products around an acceptance rate and a unit cost, which makes Ekaagra's ₹11.29 lakh September model spend a product decision.

Stage matters more than product type. Below roughly twenty engineers there are no archetypes, only a generalist whose archetype is whatever Tuesday demands. Between twenty and two hundred they appear as charters without titles, where Avishkar sits. Above a few hundred they harden into job families and the dominant cost shifts from context-switching to seam latency. One asserted difference is not real: discovery, prioritisation and written argument do not vary by archetype — only which evidence is admissible.

8. Three worked examples

Ekaagra's activation chain. Of 4,80,000 September installs, 1,68,000 completed know-your-customer checks (35.0 per cent); 94,080 of those linked an account through the aggregator framework (56.0 per cent); 32,928 of those asked the assistant a question in week one (35.0 per cent); 12,348 of those were still active on day 30 (37.5 per cent). Cumulatively 12,348 of 4,80,000, or 2.57 per cent, were retained. The largest leak by users is the know-your-customer step, 3,12,000 of 4,80,000 or 65.0 per cent; the first assistant question ties it by rate, losing 61,152 of 94,080, also 65.0 per cent. A growth PM without the model could not touch the second.

Ekaagra's model-cost decision. The average question consumed 2,400 input and 320 output tokens at ₹0.022 and ₹0.088 per thousand tokens, so ₹0.08096 a question. At 18.6 lakh monthly actives asking a mean 7.5 questions, September volume was 1,39,50,000 questions and the bill ₹11,29,392, or 2.43 per cent of the month's ₹4.65 crore of revenue. Meera's upgrade raised cost per question to ₹0.284 and the evaluation score from 71.5 to 84.0 per cent. Faraz tested it against the only number that could pay: a retained day-30 user is worth ₹25.00 a month over a median fourteen-month tenure, ₹350 of lifetime revenue.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first dispute is whether archetypes should be formal job families. The specialisation school rests on hiring and review evidence: archetype-specific interview loops predict performance better than generic ones, and one rubric over-rewards whoever has the shortest feedback loop. For this to be wrong, generic rubrics would have to not disadvantage long-loop PMs — hard to argue when a hardware PM gets one reviewable bet a year against a growth PM's twenty-six.

The second is whether the distinction belongs in titles. The constraint school notes that constraints move faster than job architectures: Chinar's changed from funnel to fit inside a year, and a titled growth PM is obliged to keep proposing funnel work. For this to be wrong, constraints would have to be stickier than careers — plausibly true in hardware, false in consumer software.

The third is whether the only real distinction is between owning a number a customer pays for and owning an internal one. The ownership school's strongest form is that every pathology in platform and data product management traces to the absence of a willing payer, so the fix is to let internal customers refuse; it would be wrong if internal markets beat mandates less often than claimed, as chargeback experiments sometimes suggest.

The fourth is new. If model-assisted development compresses cycle times, the learning rates in Exhibit 1 converge and the taxonomy loses its main axis. The counter-evidence is that long-loop cycle time is set by physics, regulation and procurement — a transmission budget, a consent artefact, a tooling lead time — untouched by coding speed. Nobody has three years of data either way.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied archetypes can name eight and place a role on a chart. Someone who has internalised them asks for the metric and review criteria before the title, treating their absence as the finding; computes the cost of one wrong bet before arguing about process, because that number, not seniority, sets the governance a decision deserves; buys the adjacent archetype's veto early rather than meeting it at the seam; and can say what would make her specialism the wrong one to staff.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 28 October 2026 Nandita recommended the split, on the 34.2 per cent cross-archetype share, below the 40.9 per cent break-even and worth about 270 decision-days a year, with three conditions. Each charter would carry a guardrail metric owned by the adjacent archetype, because the telemetry case had put ₹51.25 lakh of benefit and ₹8.49 crore of exposure across one seam. Two of the eleven PMs would stay unassigned and rotate, since dual-experience PMs resolved cross-archetype decisions in 14 days against 31. And the growth charter would be the smallest, because at 3,120 paying sites its 2.22-year payback was the weakest in Exhibit 4 — contradicting every consumer-internet precedent.

On 8 October 2026 Faraz recommended against splitting. At s = 60.4 per cent, specialising would cost about 412 decision-days a year, and the activation chain showed why: 2.57 per cent of installs survive to day 30, and the first assistant question ties know-your-customer as the worst leak by rate. He kept one charter with two metrics — retained day-30 askers and cost per accepted answer — and shipped the targeted configuration at ₹16,39,225 a month, 3.53 per cent of revenue, on one test: retention of askers must reach 41.9 per cent in two cycles or the routing reverts.

Discussion questions. First: Nandita's 40.9 per cent break-even rests on three medians from one log — what would you need to trust it, and how would you argue against her on the same data? Second: if Faraz's experiment returns 40.2 per cent, a real lift short of the 41.9 per cent break-even, what should he do and whose number is it? Third: Chinar's growth PM did good work against the wrong constraint — where should accountability sit, and what would have caught it sooner?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does — the invariant core every archetype specialises. Choosing a PM specialisation — the personal version, including temperament, which no exhibit settles. GM-style versus craft-style product management — the ownership school's home ground. PM myths versus reality — dismantles the mini-CEO framing behind archetype-blind staffing. Origins of product management — why hardware and software traditions never merged. PM versus PMM, TPM, project manager and founder — the roles most often mistaken for archetypes. How the PM job changes by company stage — the variable that split Avishkar from Ekaagra. The end-to-end product lifecycle — where each archetype's leverage peaks. The Six Ps framework — vocabulary for the guardrails.
