PM Archetypes: What Kind of Product Manager Am I Becoming?

Foundations, The PM Role & Foundations. Session 1, Introduction to Product Management.

1. Three offers, eleven days

On 20 July 2026, Aditi Menon, a senior product manager at Manjari Trade Network, opened a calendar invitation from her head of product, Rahul Deshpande. Manjari was a business-to-business marketplace, a platform on which small retailers order stock from wholesalers, with 1,85,000 retailers ordering monthly across fourteen states. Its design owed something to the way Udaan and Jumbotail had shown that kirana stores, the neighbourhood grocery shops that still account for most Indian grocery sales, would order digitally if credit and delivery were reliable. Aditi had spent four years on Manjari's retailer app. Rahul now offered her three roles, each opening on 1 September, and wanted her answer by 31 July.

The first was Growth PM for the ordering funnel, the path from a retailer opening the cart to a confirmed order. The second was Platform PM for the payments and ordering software kit that three internal teams built on. The third was PM for the credit-scoring model that decided how much buying-on-credit each retailer received. The salaries were within 4 per cent of one another. What differed was the working week each would produce, and the metric on which her next performance review would turn.

The stakes were not abstract. Aditi's engineering partners were distributed: Joost van Dam led platform engineering from Amsterdam, and Keisha Warren led machine learning from Austin. A PM who joined the wrong team would spend eighteen months learning to argue in the wrong currency, with Joost counting engineer-weeks saved while a growth colleague counted orders added. Her question was not which job was best. It was which job was best for the kind of product manager she was becoming, and the answer depended on what each role was built to optimise.

2. The idea

A PM archetype is a recognisable specialisation of the one core job, which is deciding what a team should build and why, in order to create value for customers and for the business. The archetype changes three things: who the primary customer is, what the PM is measured on, and over how long a horizon the work pays back. The core craft is shared: discovery, prioritisation, writing a specification, working with engineers and designers. The archetypes differ in what they optimise.

The vocabulary grew out of the large consumer-internet companies of the 2000s and 2010s. As firms such as Google, Facebook and Amazon grew past a few hundred engineers, a single generalist PM could no longer hold the whole product in mind. Growth teams were split out around 2010 to run experiments on acquisition and activation; platform teams were split out to stop dozens of product teams rebuilding the same plumbing; data and machine-learning roles followed. Marty Cagan, Ken Norton and others wrote about the resulting differences in the 2010s, and business-school courses on product management now teach the role through teardowns of such cases.

The sentence Aditi could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: “Every PM does the same job; the archetype is the answer to the question of who is my customer and what number am I willing to be judged on.” Exhibit 1 sets out eight archetypes on that basis.

3. How it works

Exhibit 2. Illustrative positions only; the map carries no measured data.

Exhibit 2 shows the mechanics. Placing a role on the map takes three steps. First, name the customer: whose problem is the PM paid to solve? A growth PM's customer is a retailer who has not yet ordered; a platform PM's customer is Joost's engineer who must integrate payments by Friday. Second, name the feedback loop: how quickly does the PM learn she was wrong? A funnel experiment answers in two weeks. A shared software kit may take two quarters before anyone adopts it. Third, name the unit of value: orders, engineer-weeks, or a point of model accuracy.

Steps practitioners leave implicit matter most here. The archetype also determines the PM's political position. A growth PM competes for traffic and engineering sprints with every other team. A platform PM has no customers who pay and must persuade peers to adopt a shared tool voluntarily. An AI PM spends time writing evaluation sets, the collections of test cases that tell the team whether the model is improving, and cannot promise a date, since model quality arrives by experiment. Aditi concluded that she was choosing a feedback loop and a politics as much as a topic.

4. A worked example

Aditi asked each of the first two teams to put a number on its first six months, using a single measure: rupees recovered per engineer-week spent. She assumed an engineer-week costs Manjari ₹60,000 fully loaded. The growth hypothesis was a one-page reorder button that lifted cart-to-order conversion from 2.5 to 2.8 per cent on 4,00,000 cart sessions a month. The platform hypothesis was a shared payments kit that would save each of three teams five engineer-weeks per quarter.

The result surprised her: on this measure the two archetypes were nearly equal, 5.6 months against 6.4. The difference lay in the character of the risk. The growth figure rests on a conversion lift that may not repeat; the platform figure rests on teams actually adopting the kit. Now the second pass, changing one input at a time.

Exhibit 4. Second pass: one input changed in each case
CaseChangeMonthly benefitPayback
Growth, seasonal dipCart sessions fall to 3,00,000900 orders × ₹1,800 × 6% = ₹97,2007,20,000 ÷ 97,200 = 7.4 months
Platform, fourth team adopts4 teams × 5 = 20 engineer-weeks a quarter₹12,00,000 a quarter = ₹4,00,000 a month19,20,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 4.8 months

At 3,00,000 sessions, orders move from 7,500 to 8,400, a gain of 900.

The second pass reveals the asymmetry. The growth benefit is tied to traffic Aditi does not control; the platform benefit grows with the number of teams, which the platform PM can influence by making adoption easy.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Archetype is not seniority

A growth PM is not a junior version of a platform PM. Archetypes are lateral specialisations; seniority is how much ambiguity and scope the PM carries within one of them.

The labels are used loosely

One company's “technical PM” manages APIs; another's merely requires a computer-science degree. Read the job's metric, not its title.

Archetypes overlap

Most real roles blend two. Manjari's credit-model role is part data, part AI, and part consumer-lending product. Ask which row of Exhibit 1 is the tiebreaker when priorities collide.

Optimising one number distorts others

A growth PM judged only on conversion may push credit offers that raise defaults. Every archetype has a characteristic overreach, and a good PM names it before it happens.

It does not tell you what you are good at

The archetype says what a role rewards, not whether you will enjoy two-week experiments or twelve-month platform migrations. Aptitude and temperament are separate questions that no framework settles.

It is not the same as a general-manager orientation

Some PMs act as mini chief executives of a product line, owning profit and loss; others are craft specialists. Archetype describes the domain, whereas the GM-versus-craft split describes the scope of ownership, and either can sit inside any archetype.

Company stage reshapes everything

A twenty-person start-up has no platform PM; the one generalist does all eight jobs on a Tuesday. The archetypes appear as the company grows, so a newcomer should ask how long the role has existed.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who judges my performance, and with what number? How long until I learn I was wrong? Who must I persuade who does not report to me? Which of the three would the company miss most if I left?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products the growth and retention archetypes dominate, since millions of users generate fast experiments; a Dream11 or Swiggy PM can read a result in days. In B2B the customer who pays differs from the person who uses the product, so enterprise PMs spend time with procurement and integration, and cycles run in quarters. In a marketplace such as Manjari, every decision has two customers, retailers and wholesalers, and a growth lift on the buying side may starve the selling side of margin. The marketplace PM therefore works with a pair of metrics, never one.

Stage matters as much. In an early-stage company, with perhaps eight engineers, the PM is a generalist whose archetype is whatever the week demands. In a large company, specialisation lets each PM go deep but breeds handoffs: the growth PM needs a platform change and waits a quarter for the platform team's roadmap. Large-company PMs therefore need more negotiating skill and less pure discovery skill than their start-up counterparts.

7. Common mistakes

Choosing by title prestige. Symptom: a PM moves to “AI” and within a year is unhappy. Misunderstanding: the title was treated as the archetype. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the hiring manager for last quarter's review criteria for the role.

Applying one archetype's tools to another. Symptom: a platform PM runs conversion-style A/B tests on internal teams, and no one understands the results. Misunderstanding: assuming the feedback loop is the same. Diagnostic: write down how many weeks until the first evidence arrives.

Mistaking the metric for the customer. Symptom: orders rise while retailer complaints rise too. Misunderstanding: treating the optimised number as the goal rather than a proxy. Diagnostic: list one customer harm the metric would not detect.

Assuming the archetype is permanent. Symptom: a PM turns down a good role because it is “not my lane”. Misunderstanding: confusing a current specialisation with identity. Diagnostic: ask which skills transfer, and count how many of last year's tasks were archetype-neutral.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Aditi's decision begins with questions, not preferences. She would interview the three leads about their last quarter's decisions, request the review criteria for each role, and build a one-page estimate such as Exhibit 3 for each. She would notice that the credit role, unlike the other two, had no payback figure at all, and would ask what evaluation set Keisha trusted. She would test her answer against a failure: which role would she regret in a bad quarter? Most of all she would separate what she is good at from what the job pays for, and state both in a page Rahul could read in five minutes.

9. What Aditi decided

On 29 July, Aditi chose the platform role. The arithmetic had not decided it; the base-case paybacks of 5.6 and 6.4 months were too close. Two other facts did. A platform PM's feedback loop was long, and she had spent four years in weekly experiment cycles; she wanted to learn to make decisions whose proof arrived later. And the fourth team Joost mentioned, if it adopted, took payback to 4.8 months, a lever she could pull by making adoption easy, whereas the growth case depended on traffic she could not control. She told Rahul she would reconsider in twelve months, and asked that the role's review criteria be written down in advance.

To go further, study the distinction between GM-style and craft-style product management, which cuts across every row of Exhibit 1, and then the mechanics of choosing a specialisation.

Two questions to sit with. If your next performance review reduced to one number, which number would you want it to be, and what would you stop doing to move it? And in which archetype would you most dislike being wrong slowly?
case40v1-pm.archetypes:
Who Should Own the Rush Hour?

A product case on PM archetypes at Yashasvi Kitchen Systems, Chennai

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday 25 October 2026, Yashika Warrier sat on the floor of her flat in Besant Nagar with four printed decks fanned out in front of her. She had been Vice-President of Product at Yashasvi Kitchen Systems for fourteen months. In the morning she had to tell the executive team which of four product bets the company would make, and, because each implied a different kind of product manager running it, she had to say in the same breath what kind of product organisation Yashasvi was going to become.

None of the decks was hers. Each had been pushed at her over three weeks by a colleague who was certain, and each was internally coherent. The platform deck argued that the integration layer was the only durable asset the company had. The artificial-intelligence deck argued that Yojana, the demand-forecasting module, was the moat. The enterprise deck argued that twelve large chains were asking for things nobody had built. The self-serve deck argued that five lakh independent restaurants were a market Yashasvi had barely touched.

The board met on Friday 6 November, twelve days away; Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. Yashna Yennemadi, the chief financial officer, had capped incremental product and engineering spend at ₹170 lakh a year. Three options fitted inside that cap; the fourth did not. None of the four, Yashika had begun to suspect, answered who the customer was.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Yatin Waghmare founded Yashasvi Kitchen Systems in Chennai in 2018, after four years running operations for a south Indian quick-service chain. The first product, Yashasvi Rasoi, was a kitchen operating layer: it pulled orders from Swiggy, Zomato, the chain's own app and the counter till into one screen, sequenced them by cook station and told the outlet manager what was late. By 2020 it ran in around nine hundred outlets.

In March 2021 Yatin made the decision that shapes every option on Yashika's floor. Chains kept asking whether the fryer had been at temperature when an order went out. Software could not know, so Yashasvi built hardware: the Yantra Hub, a sealed box wired to probes on fryers, griddles and cold storage, reporting temperature and cycle-time telemetry every thirty seconds. It won deals. It also committed the company permanently to a field-service organisation, a manufacturing partner in Coimbatore and a per-outlet installation visit. Hubs are now in 6,120 outlets.

The second constraining decision came in August 2023, with a four-year master agreement with Warsha Foods Industries, a 410-outlet fried-chicken and biryani chain. Warsha was the first genuinely large account and the agreement reflected that asymmetry. Clause 9.4 requires ninety days' notice and Warsha's written consent for any change to a published application programming interface; a separate schedule sets a 99.5 per cent monthly uptime commitment with service credits. The term ends on 31 August 2027. Warsha's 410 outlets are 5.5 per cent of the enterprise outlet base, and the clause applies to the whole platform.

Yashasvi closed a Series B of ₹96 crore in March 2024 and recorded ₹29.62 crore of revenue in the year to 31 March 2026 across the seven lines in Exhibit 1. It employs 186 people: 64 engineers under Yogita Wable in Bengaluru, a 22-person device group under Yamini Waikar in Coimbatore, and five product managers reporting to Yashika — two on enterprise chains, one on device and firmware, one on self-serve, and one half-funded role that has drifted into analytics requests.

3. The industry

Indian restaurant technology in 2026 is crowded at both ends and thin in the middle. Petpooja and a dozen regional point-of-sale vendors sell cheap billing software to independents; UrbanPiper and others move orders between aggregators and tills. Swiggy and Zomato shape demand for almost every restaurant that delivers and both have built partner-facing tooling of their own; Zepto and the quick-commerce entrants have changed what customers consider a reasonable wait. ONDC has opened a parallel channel a few chains take seriously, Razorpay handles the payments, Zoho Books the accounting, and GST e-invoicing makes each seam a compliance surface too.

Two competitors matter specifically. Yugmit Hospitality Labs, in Bengaluru, sells a software-only kitchen display at roughly a third of Yashasvi's per-outlet price and carries no hardware obligation. Waqfa Procurement Exchange, a restaurant supplies marketplace, began bundling a free kitchen display with its ordering app in July 2026, losing money on the software and making it on the groceries. Neither can tell a chain what temperature the fryer was at. Neither, so far, has needed to.

Regulation bears on the product in two places. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India keeps expanding digital record-keeping expectations, which argues for the Yantra Hub; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the customer-level order data in the aggregator feeds, which argues for restraint in what the models retain. Exposure outside India is small but loud: Yashvardhan Yardi, hired in January 2026 to open North America from Austin, sells to Indian-diaspora restaurant groups at roughly five times Indian per-outlet pricing. The largest, Yaadein Hospitality Network, operates 310 outlets across the United States.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

At each point the company believed something later evidence has complicated.

January 2025. A self-serve tier launched at ₹1,250 per outlet per month, on the belief that the enterprise product could be stripped down and sold without a salesperson. A 2024 reseller arrangement had already brought 1,040 outlets in on a legacy ₹500 price, folded into the same segment. The cohorts behave nothing alike, and Exhibit 4 shows that of 14,600 restaurants signed up in the quarter to 30 June 2026, 876 were still paying ninety days later.

October 2025. Yojana shipped in early access at ₹900 per outlet per month. The belief, stated in the Series B deck and repeated since, was that the forecasting advantage came from the Yantra Hub: nobody else had cook-level telemetry. Yatharth Wadhwa's eleven-week study, Exhibit 3, decomposes the gain by data source and finds sensor telemetry contributing 0.5 percentage points of a 15.3 percentage-point improvement.

March to April 2026. A five-week pilot in 118 Warsha outlets measured food waste before and after Yojana. Waste per outlet per week fell from ₹14,800 to ₹11,544, a reduction of 22.0 per cent. Annualised across the 118 pilot outlets that is ₹1.998 crore; a later slide extrapolates to all 410 Warsha outlets and reaches ₹6.942 crore. Neither adjusts for the price promotion Warsha ran in two of the five weeks, and neither is comparable with the eleven-week accuracy window.

July 2026. Waqfa launched its free kitchen display; within eight weeks two mid-market chains gave notice, and Yoonseo Whang's renewal numbers showed it before product noticed.

September 2026. Yamini Waikar's team received an end-of-life notice: the microcontroller inside the Yantra Hub ceases production on 30 June 2027, and a redesign is estimated at ₹186 lakh and twenty-two weeks. In the same month a telemetry audit found that 2,509 of the 6,120 installed hubs had reported in the previous thirty days, which is 41.0 per cent. Yamini has not circulated that number.

5. The people

Yatin Waghmare, 44, co-founder and chief executive, Chennai. He wants Yojana priced and announced before Diwali, because forecasting is the only thing a competitor cannot copy in a quarter. His incentive is a Series C conversation in which an artificial-intelligence narrative carries a better multiple than a kitchen-display one. What he is not saying is that he has already promised Warsha's chief executive a joint announcement.

Yogita Wable, Director of Engineering, Bengaluru. She wants a platform charter, and her argument is structural: eleven bespoke forks for enterprise chains, each with its own release train, and on-call pages tripled in a year. What she is not saying is that two of her strongest engineers have offers elsewhere and she believes the charter is the only thing that will keep them.

Yashvardhan Yardi, Head of Enterprise Sales, Austin. He wants the enterprise suite deepened: approval workflows, multi-brand hierarchies, an on-premises option. His build-up to ₹980.20 lakh of incremental annual recurring revenue at month twenty-four is in Exhibit 6, and ₹513.36 lakh of it, 52.4 per cent, is Yaadein Hospitality Network. His variable pay is on booked revenue, not retained. What he is not saying is that the Yaadein commitment is a non-binding letter of intent, and that their chief technology officer wants a deployment inside Yaadein's own infrastructure, which Yashasvi cannot do.

Yamini Waikar, Head of Device Engineering, Coimbatore. She wants the redesign funded now, because the part dies on 30 June 2027 and twenty-two weeks of engineering has to start somewhere. Her 22-person group exists because of the hub. What she is not saying is the 41.0 per cent reporting rate, nor that she suspects the cause is not failure but that nobody reconnects the probes after a deep clean.

Yatharth Wadhwa, Staff Data Scientist, Amsterdam. He wants a data product manager appointed before any artificial-intelligence bet, because instrumentation and the aggregator data contracts are the real constraint. He authored Exhibit 3. What he is not saying loudly is that his study excluded three chains, 1,920 of 7,480 enterprise outlets or 25.7 per cent, for menu churn — precisely where forecasting would be hardest and most valuable.

Wiktoria Wrona, Principal Designer, Warsaw. From 31 outlet observations she argues that the person the product fails is the outlet manager at seven in the evening, who has eleven minutes of attention across a four-hour shift and reads nothing. Her incentive is a research budget requested for three quarters. What she is not saying is that she has prototyped a customer-facing wait-time feature she privately believes is the company's future, and has shown it to nobody because it belongs to no archetype in the room.

Yoonseo Whang, Customer Success Lead, Seoul, covering Asia-Pacific and Indian mid-market. She argues from Exhibit 2 that nothing new should be funded until retention is fixed; her targets are renewal-based. What she is not saying is that her team manually onboards self-serve accounts above a size threshold, so Exhibit 4's activation rate partly measures her team's effort rather than the product.

Yashna Yennemadi, Chief Financial Officer, Chennai. She holds the ₹170 lakh cap and an eighteen-month payback rule. Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹38.60 crore against net burn of ₹1.42 crore a month: 27.2 months of runway. What she is not saying is that she is modelling a FY28 round at a flat valuation and would privately prefer margin to growth.

Behind them sits Yograj Wandrekar, the Series B investor on the board, who has asked for one thing on 6 November: a sentence naming the customer.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the company as the auditors see it: enterprise software with a hardware line attached, and two lines with no product owner at all, together ₹168.10 lakh. Exhibit 2 is the same company six months later as revenue operations sees it.

Side by side, the company has grown either 6.8 per cent or 25.1 per cent. Exhibit 2's ₹3,164.10 lakh against Exhibit 1's ₹2,962.00 lakh is 6.8 per cent. But Exhibit 1 includes ₹311.80 lakh of one-time hub sales and ₹121.30 lakh of integration fees, absent from Exhibit 2; strip those out and the FY26 recurring base was ₹2,528.90 lakh, against which ₹3,164.10 lakh is 25.1 per cent. Yashvardhan quotes the second, Yashna the first. Both support opposite stories.

Exhibit 3 is the most quietly destabilising document in the set. A 15.3-point reduction against what an outlet manager does by eye removes 48.7 per cent of the error, which is a real product. But 45.1 per cent of the improvement comes from aggregator order history, which Yugmit can also obtain, and 3.3 per cent from the sensor telemetry that cost the company its hardware organisation. The 4,190 outlets studied are 56.0 per cent of the 7,480 enterprise outlets, and the excluded chains are the volatile ones. Read naively, Exhibit 3 says the hub is worthless; read carefully, that nobody tested the hub where volatility is highest.

Exhibit 4 reconciles with Exhibit 2 only once the cohorts are separated. Exhibit 2's 1,870 self-serve outlets at the current price are 876 survivors from this quarter and 994 from before it, with 1,040 legacy reseller outlets apart at ₹500. Yoonseo reads that as proof that self-serve churn is structural. Yashvi Waghela, who owns self-serve and is the only internal candidate for a growth role, reads it as proof that nobody has run a serious experiment on the 9,490 restaurants that signed up and never imported a menu.

Exhibit 5 is the platform argument and the platform problem in one table. The surface carrying the most traffic pays nothing, the one paying most is the newest, two cannot be measured, and the account with a veto over all of them is 5.5 per cent of enterprise outlets. Exhibit 6 prices the options against their sponsors' claims.

7. Voices

Yatin Waghmare, exec review, 14 October: “I am not asking whether the forecasting is perfect. I am asking what else we have that a competitor cannot build by Holi. Name it.”

Yogita Wable, same meeting: “Eleven forks. Every one was a quarter where somebody promised a chain something. Without an owner on the interfaces, options two and four both die in integration work nobody has scheduled.”

Yatharth Wadhwa, in writing, 16 October: “My study says that, given the data we collect, sensor telemetry adds 0.5 points. It does not say the hub is useless. It says we never instrumented the chains where it would matter. The deck has merged two different sentences.”

Yashvardhan Yardi, chat thread, 19 October, 02:41 Chennai time: “Yaadein will sign. I need the multi-brand hierarchy and I need to be able to say the word on-premises without it being a lie. One engineer, one quarter.”

Yogita Wable, 09:12: “It is not one engineer and one quarter. It is a second deployment target for the lifetime of the product.”

Wiktoria Wrona, research readout, 21 October: “In 31 outlets I watched the dinner rush. Nobody opened a forecast or a report. One manager had taped paper over the tablet because of the glare. We are arguing about which specialist should own a product its user does not look at.”

Yoonseo Whang, renewal review, 22 October: “Two mid-market chains left in September. Both said the Waqfa display was good enough. I do not need a new product. I need the one we have to stop being eleven products.”

Yamini Waikar, email, 23 October: “Whatever you decide on Monday, the microcontroller stops shipping on 30 June. Start the redesign in January and we miss it. Do not redesign and we stop selling hubs.”

Yashna Yennemadi, finance review, 24 October: “I will fund one of these. Not one and a half. And I would like to understand why Yashvardhan's growth number is 25 and the one in my board pack is 7.”

8. The options as Yashika currently sees them

Option 1: a platform charter. Appoint a platform product manager over the Exhibit 5 integration surface, publish versioned interfaces, retire the eleven forks and charge partners for access. Cost ₹166 lakh a year; claim ₹420 lakh at month twenty-four. The constraint is Clause 9.4: every interface change needs Warsha's consent and ninety days' notice until 31 August 2027.

Option 2: Yojana as a priced product. Appoint an artificial-intelligence product manager, two machine-learning engineers and a data engineer; take Yojana out of early access and attach it to the base. Cost ₹184 lakh, ₹14 lakh over the cap; claim ₹760.32 lakh. Exhibit 3 is both its strongest and its weakest support, depending which of Yatharth's sentences is quoted.

Option 3: enterprise depth. Appoint a second enterprise product manager and a solutions engineer; build multi-brand hierarchies, approval workflows and an on-premises deployment. Cost ₹148 lakh; claim ₹980.20 lakh, of which 52.4 per cent is one letter of intent. It is the option most likely to add fork number twelve.

Option 4: a self-serve growth engine. Appoint a growth product manager with two engineers, a designer and a lifecycle marketer; attack the Exhibit 4 funnel from sign-up to day ninety. Cost ₹154 lakh; claim ₹1,369.50 lakh. It assumes the 6.0 per cent sign-up-to-paying rate can be moved, not that it is what the market bears at ₹1,250 against a free rival.

Yashika had written a fifth line on the back of the finance deck and crossed it out: none of these says who the customer is. Each option names an archetype and infers a customer from it. A platform product manager optimises for the developer across an interface; an artificial-intelligence product manager for a model's score against a metric somebody chose; an enterprise product manager for a chief technology officer's signature; a growth product manager for a stranger's second visit. The outlet manager Wiktoria watched at seven in the evening is the customer of none of them, and is the only person who touches the product daily.

There is also an option nobody has written down, because it costs political capital rather than money: re-charter two of the five product managers Yashika already has, fund nothing new, and tell two people their job has changed. Exhibit 6 cannot price that.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The executive review is on Monday 26 October. The board meets on Friday 6 November, twelve days after the Sunday night Yashika is sitting through. Diwali is 8 November, and hiring in Bengaluru stops for the fortnight after it, so an approval on 6 November becomes a first working day in January at the earliest.

The money: ₹170 lakh of incremental annual spend, payback inside eighteen months, cash of ₹38.60 crore, net burn ₹1.42 crore a month. The contract: Clause 9.4, to 31 August 2027, with a 99.5 per cent uptime commitment. The hardware: the microcontroller stops shipping on 30 June 2027, 247 days after the executive review, and the redesign is ₹186 lakh and twenty-two weeks that no option includes. The regulation: FSSAI record-keeping argues for the hub, the DPDP Act for restraint in what the models retain. The people: Yogita has two engineers with offers, Yamini has 22 whose work depends on a part being discontinued, and Yashvardhan's pay rewards a signature rather than a renewal.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each archetype in Exhibit 6 optimise for, and for which is the evidence strongest?
  2. Reconcile Exhibit 1 with Exhibit 2. Which growth figure, 6.8 per cent or 25.1 per cent, belongs in the 6 November board pack, and what does the choice reveal about whoever makes it?
  3. Exhibit 3 attributes 3.3 per cent of the forecasting gain to sensor telemetry. What would you have to believe, and measure, before letting it decide the fate of a 22-person hardware organisation?
  4. Who is the customer of Yashasvi Rasoi: the chief technology officer who signs, the outlet manager who uses it, the cook it measures, or the aggregator whose orders flow through it? Pick one and say what being wrong costs.
  5. Clause 9.4 gives an account worth 5.5 per cent of enterprise outlets a veto over the platform. Was August 2023 a mistake, and does that change what you can do before 31 August 2027?
  6. It is Monday morning and you are Yashika Warrier. Which option goes into the room, which archetype do you hire or re-charter, what do you tell Yamini about 30 June 2027, and what sentence naming the customer do you give Yograj Wandrekar on 6 November?

It was past midnight when Yashika stacked the four decks on the chair by the door. She had a page of her own by then, headed what the product needs, and under it a list she kept reordering: one owner for the interfaces; somebody who understands why a cook does not reconnect a probe; somebody who can say no to a chain; somebody whose job is the second week. Four lines, one hire, and a part that stops being made in June. She turned off the lamp without reordering the list again.
case20v1-pm.archetypes:
Who Owns the Silent Meters?

A product case on PM archetypes at Unnati Meter Works, Pune

1. Opening

On Wednesday 14 October 2026, Vandita Kulshreshtha, Head of Product at Unnati Meter Works, sat in the Pune office with a spreadsheet she had stopped being able to ignore. Of the 4,20,000 smart electricity meters the company had installed in homes across three states, only 37,800 households had opened the companion app in the previous thirty days. That is 9 per cent. Two state distribution companies, known in the trade as discoms, had written renewal clauses that required 10 per cent.

The chief executive, Vedant Ghosalkar, wanted a decision by Friday 30 October on how the product team would be organised to fix this, so that hiring approvals could be signed before Diwali on 8 November and work could begin in the second half of the financial year. Vandita had three possible answers and a team of five product managers, each of whom had a different view of what kind of problem this was.

2. Company background

Vedant Ghosalkar founded Unnati in 2016 to build single-phase smart meters for Indian homes. The market opened widely after the government's Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) pushed states towards smart metering. Unnati competes for discom tenders against established meter makers such as Genus Power, HPL Electric and Secure Meters. It wins on firmware reliability and on a software layer that gives discoms consumption analytics. The company has 310 employees, a manufacturing line near Pune and a firmware team in Bengaluru.

The buyer is the discom, not the household. A family in Nashik or Jodhpur receives an Unnati meter because the utility installed it. Unnati also ships a free consumer app, Unnati Ghar, showing daily units used, a bill forecast and outage notices, with a paid plan at ₹1,800 a year. The app competes for attention with the bill-payment screens of PhonePe, Paytm and Google Pay, where most Indian households already pay their electricity bill. Exhibit 1 shows how FY26 revenue splits across the three lines.

The product team has five managers: two hardware PMs at ₹38 lakh a year each, two enterprise PMs at ₹42 lakh each and one consumer PM at ₹36 lakh. That is ₹196 lakh, or ₹1.96 crore, in total. A data scientist sits alongside them but is not a PM. Exhibit 1 explains the team's shape: nearly all the money is made in hardware and discom contracts, and the app, which touches every household, makes under 1 per cent of revenue.

3. The situation

Exhibit 2 breaks down the app funnel. Of 4,20,000 installed meters, 1,26,000 owners downloaded the app (30 per cent). Of those, 75,600 linked their meter (60 per cent), and 37,800 of the linked users were active in the last thirty days (50 per cent). Seventy per cent of households never downloaded anything.

Uma Sundaram, the data scientist, based in Melbourne, ran the pilot. At install, technicians in one group scanned a QR code on the meter that opened the app already paired. Downloads rose from 30 to 40 per cent, but the later steps did not move: 60 per cent still linked, and 50 per cent of those still became active. Pairing lifted the active share from 9.0 to 12.0 per cent, three percentage points. It did nothing to the habit of coming back.

Victor Mwangi, who leads customer success from Nairobi, added a data point from Unnati's small Kenyan pilot. There, 5,600 of 8,000 meters, 70 per cent, are active in the app because customers top up prepaid credit through it. In India, bills arrive by SMS and are paid elsewhere, so the app offers no reason to return.

Exhibit 3 shows what the contracts say. Discom A is above the line. Discoms B and C each have a renewal on 31 March 2027, conditional on 10 per cent of their meters being active in the preceding thirty days.

The stakes extend beyond the fees. Discoms B and C are also expected to place the next meter tranche, provisionally worth ₹38.4 crore, or 40 per cent of FY26 hardware revenue. The renewal question will colour that order.

4. The people

Utkarsh Bhide, enterprise PM in Pune, owns the discom relationships. He argues that discoms are the only distribution Unnati has, and that bill inserts, SMS nudges and field-staff incentives will move more households than any app feature. He wants the work to sit in his team.

Vaishnavi Kamble, senior hardware PM in Pune, owns meter firmware and the QR pairing pilot. She optimises for reliability and cost per unit. A meter lives fifteen years, and she is wary of any change that touches the device in the field. She would extend pairing to every installed meter by revisiting homes.

Uma Sundaram, in Melbourne, believes the numbers show a missing reason to return, not a missing download, and says nobody on the team is paid to experiment weekly. Victor Mwangi, in Nairobi, agrees and points to Kenya. Vedant Ghosalkar, who wants a fix without bloating headcount, listens to all of them.

5. The options

Option 1: a growth pod. Hire a growth PM (₹44 lakh) and form a pod with two engineers at ₹28 lakh each and a designer at ₹24 lakh, reporting to Vandita. The annual cost is 44 + 56 + 24 = ₹124 lakh, or ₹1.24 crore. It would own the funnel from download to weekly habit, running experiments on bill forecasts, outage alerts and tariff-slab warnings. The upside is a team whose job is the behaviour gap. The cost is a new unit, a hiring lag, and no guarantee the gap closes by March.

Option 2: enterprise-led activation. Give the whole problem to Utkarsh, with ₹18 lakh co-funded bill-insert and SMS campaigns through discoms B and C. This costs no new hires and uses Unnati's real channel. The risk is that it relies on discom calendars and goodwill, buys downloads rather than habit, and pulls an enterprise PM away from renewals.

Option 3: hardware-led pairing. Vaishnavi's team sends technicians to the 2,40,000 meters in B and C at ₹85 a visit, a cost of ₹2.04 crore. The pilot gives the upside: the three-point lift. But applied to B (8.4 per cent to 11.4, or 17,100 users) it clears the 15,000 threshold, while for C (4.0 to 7.0 per cent, 6,300 users) it falls short of 9,000. Visits also cost more than the pod.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which step of the funnel is the real problem, and which PM archetypes are built to work on it?
  2. Who is the customer in this case, the discom, the household, or both, and how does that change who should own the problem?
  3. Apply the pilot's three-point lift to Exhibit 3. What does each option deliver for B and C by 31 March 2027?
  4. If you were Vandita, which option would you take to Vedant, what would you ask the others to do, and what result would make you change course?

7. A note for the learner

PM archetypes are specialisations of one core job, and each optimises for something different. A hardware PM optimises for irreversible, reliable decisions and unit cost. An enterprise PM optimises for the buyer's contract and stakeholder trust. A consumer or growth PM optimises for a household's repeated use, and a growth PM does it through fast experiments on funnels and loops. The question is not which colleague is most senior but which archetype's optimisation matches the problem.

The evidence says that acquisition is partly fixed by pairing and bill inserts, but that the later steps, linking and returning, did not move at all. That makes this primarily a growth problem: a behaviour gap among users who never chose the product. Options 2 and 3 are acquisition levers, and both leave the habit untouched.

One defensible path is Option 1, with conditions. Hire the growth PM and pod for ₹1.24 crore, against ₹8.1 crore of fees at risk, about 6.5 times the cost, and a ₹38.4 crore tranche behind them. Name Utkarsh as the partner for discom levers and ask Vaishnavi to ship QR pairing on new installs only, which adds the three-point lift cheaply to what the pod finds. Review progress in January against the 10 per cent threshold. If discom C cannot get near its 9,000 target, Vandita should open the renewal conversation early rather than wait for March. A strong answer names the trade-offs, notes that hiring takes time, and does not pretend the pod alone guarantees the result.
exp20v2-pm.myths:
PM myths vs reality: the mini-CEO, the ticket-writer, and the job in between

1. Opening: a quarter of shipping

On Tuesday, 1 September 2026, Ishita Rao opened the quarterly review pack at Barkha Procurement Exchange, a Pune-based software company whose platform lets mid-sized manufacturers raise purchase orders, match supplier invoices and approve payments. She had been the group product manager for eight months. The pack was, by any visible measure, a triumph: between 1 April and 30 June the team of twelve had shipped 38 features, more than any previous quarter. The chief executive, Hemant Bhatia, had circulated it with a single line: "Proud of this pace."

Ishita was less comfortable. Barkha served 1,200 active customer accounts at an average annual contract value of ₹6 lakh, so annual recurring revenue stood at ₹7,200 lakh, or ₹72 crore. Over the preceding twelve months, 15 per cent of accounts, which is 180 of 1,200, had cancelled. Thirty-eight features had not moved that number. A board meeting was set for 30 September, and Bhatia expected a roadmap for the next quarter that was "bigger, not smaller". Her engineering lead, Tarun Kulkarni, wanted a decision on whether to keep the current rhythm. A colleague in the Amsterdam office had privately asked her a harder question: what is the product manager here for?

If Ishita answered by describing herself as the "CEO of the product", she would be repeating the story the company already believed, and the roadmap would grow. If she answered as a ticket-writer, she would hand Tarun a longer list. Either way, ₹10.8 crore of annual revenue, the value of the 180 cancelled accounts at ₹6 lakh each, would keep leaking while the dashboard glowed.

2. The idea: two myths and a definition

A myth, in this sense, is a belief about the job that is widely repeated, partly true, and costly when taken literally. Two dominate. The first is that the product manager is the "CEO of the product". The phrase gained currency in the early 2000s, popularised in Silicon Valley writing, and it was meant as encouragement: own the outcome, answer for the whole. Its failure is that a CEO holds authority over hiring, budget and direction, while a product manager holds none of these over the engineers, designers and salespeople whose work decides the outcome. A person who behaves as though they do tends to issue decrees, collect resentment and discover that decrees are not followed.

The second myth is the opposite, and more common in service-heavy organisations: the product manager as ticket-writer, who converts requests from sales, leadership and customers into specifications. A company run this way is called a feature factory, a term associated with the product writer John Cutler around 2016, meaning a team that measures itself by output, features shipped, rather than by outcome, a change in customer behaviour or business results. The factory is attractive because output is countable and outcomes are not.

The reality sits between them. Product management, as the practice developed through the 1990s at firms such as Intuit and Microsoft and was later codified by writers like Marty Cagan, exists to solve a specific problem: building the wrong thing well. Engineers can build almost anything; the scarce skill is deciding which problem deserves the quarter. The sentence Ishita could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: "My job is not to decide what we build, nor to record what we are told to build; it is to make sure that what we build changes something a customer does and the business can measure."

3. How the job actually works

The mechanics begin before any feature exists. First, the product manager identifies a customer problem, a difficulty the customer experiences in their own terms, as opposed to a solution the customer requests. Second, she establishes how large the problem is, in accounts and rupees. Third, she brings engineering and design into the problem early, so that the team proposes options rather than receiving a specification. Fourth, she chooses one outcome measure before building, so that success is defined before anyone is attached to a solution. Fifth, after release, she returns to the measure and reports honestly.

Two steps are usually left implicit. The first is saying no, publicly and with reasons, since a team that never declines anything is a ticket queue. The second is influence without authority: because she cannot order anyone, she has only evidence, clarity and credibility with which to persuade. This is why the "CEO" label is a trap rather than a compliment. Her power is entirely borrowed from the quality of her argument.

Exhibit 1 sets the three models side by side. The ticket-writer starts from requests, the mini-CEO from herself, the problem owner from observed customer behaviour; the rest follows from that one choice, which is also the choice the benchmark programmes warn about when they caution against starting from a backlog rather than a customer problem.

4. A worked example: what 38 features cost

Ishita began with arithmetic. Barkha's twelve-person team cost, fully loaded, about ₹9 lakh per person per quarter, so the quarter cost 12 × 9 = ₹108 lakh, or ₹1.08 crore. She then asked product analytics how many of the 38 features had reached 10 per cent of the 1,200 active accounts within 60 days of release (the last window, for a 30 June release, closed on 29 August), which is 120 accounts, her working threshold for "used".

Feature area (Q1 FY27)Features shippedReaching 120+ accounts
Approval workflows92
Reporting111
Integrations81
Admin and settings101
Total385

Exhibit 2. Features shipped 1 April to 30 June 2026 and those reaching 10 per cent of 1,200 active accounts within 60 days..

Five of 38 is 13.2 per cent. The cost per shipped feature was 108 ÷ 38, about ₹2.84 lakh, which looks modest. But only five features were used, so the cost per used feature was 108 ÷ 5 = ₹21.6 lakh, almost eight times larger. The factory's headline figure had hidden this by dividing by the wrong count.

She then ran the more important calculation. Her researcher, Farah Siddiqui, had interviewed 20 of the 180 customers who cancelled. Twelve, or 60 per cent, named the same problem: supplier invoices failed to match purchase orders when quantities differed slightly, forcing manual reconciliation. Applying that share to all 180 cancellations suggests 0.60 × 180 = 108 accounts, worth 108 × ₹6 lakh = ₹648 lakh a year. If a fix retained half of them, 54 accounts, the gain was ₹324 lakh. A three-person squad for one quarter cost 3 × 9 = ₹27 lakh, so the expected return was 324 ÷ 27 = 12 times the cost.

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose the interview sample had been unrepresentative and only 6 of 20, or 30 per cent, named the problem. Then 0.30 × 180 = 54 accounts, worth 54 × 6 = ₹324 lakh. Retaining half gives 27 accounts and ₹162 lakh, against the same ₹27 lakh cost: a return of 162 ÷ 27 = 6 times. The decision survives, but the conversation changes from "obviously" to "probably, and here is how we will find out". A single changed input halved the answer, which is why the share named in interviews deserves as much scrutiny as the arithmetic built upon it.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Ownership is not authority

"Owning" a product means answering for its results, not commanding its builders. A manager who dictates gets compliance on the visible and silence about the risky.

Saying yes to sales is not the same as listening to customers

A request from a salesperson is evidence about what closes a deal this month, filtered through one conversation. It is a signal worth logging, not a priority worth obeying. Count how many different accounts raise the same difficulty before treating a request as a trend.

Output metrics are not worthless

Shipping cadence is a legitimate health measure for engineering. It becomes a myth only when it is the sole measure. Ishita did not propose slowing the team; she proposed adding a second number beside the first.

Data tells you what, not why

The adoption table showed which features failed. Only the interviews explained that the invoice-matching problem was driving cancellations. Behavioural data and conversation answer different questions, and each can mislead when used alone.

The job varies with the company's maturity

Where there is no product-market fit, "problem owner" and "founder" nearly coincide. The ticket-writer failure appears later, as sales and support grow loud. Recognise which stage the company is in before importing a method.

What the framing cannot tell you

Naming the myths does not choose among competing real problems. Should the team fix invoice matching or the approvals complexity that three large accounts keep raising? Judgement, and sometimes a wrong guess, remain unavoidable.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In a consumer product, the customer problem is inferred mostly from behaviour at scale, so the product manager leans on experiments and cohorts; the ticket-writer myth shows up as a mountain of small growth tweaks. In B2B, as at Barkha, the buyer (often the finance head) differs from the daily user (an accounts clerk), and large accounts shout. The myth here is the account-driven roadmap, where the loudest customer defines the quarter. Measuring by breadth, such as the 120-account threshold, is the corrective.

In a marketplace, two sides must be satisfied at once, and an improvement for one can damage the other. The "CEO" myth is especially tempting because trade-offs feel like executive decisions. Early in a company's life, a product manager may legitimately do everything, including support calls. In a large company, the danger reverses: layers of review make a product manager into a coordinator of other people's priorities, and the job survives only if she keeps direct contact with customers.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting the shipped list as the result

Symptom: every review begins with a count of features. Misunderstanding: output is mistaken for outcome. Diagnostic: ask, for any shipped item, "which customer did what differently afterwards?" If nobody can answer, the item was never tied to a problem.

Behaving as the boss of the team

Symptom: engineers stop volunteering objections and the product manager is surprised by late problems. Misunderstanding: accountability is read as command. Diagnostic: count how many ideas in the last quarter originated with someone other than the product manager.

Treating the loudest account as the market

Symptom: roadmap items carry customer names. Misunderstanding: one voice is taken for a pattern. Diagnostic: for each item, list how many distinct accounts raised the underlying difficulty.

Never measuring after release

Symptom: no one can say whether last quarter's biggest feature worked. Misunderstanding: launch is seen as the finish line. Diagnostic: check whether each project had a measure written down before it started.

8. What good looks like

Imagine the morning handled well. Ishita presents two numbers beside the shipping count: five of 38 features used, and 60 per cent of sampled churn tied to one problem. She does not claim to know the answer; she shows Tarun the interviews and asks his team how they would attack invoice matching. She proposes a three-person squad for one quarter, a stated target for retained accounts, and an explicit list of what the team will decline. She tells Bhatia plainly that the quarter will ship fewer features. She also tells him what she will bring back: the count of accounts using the new matching tolerance, and cancellations among them against a comparison group.

9. Closing: the decision, and what follows

Ishita took the proposal to Bhatia on 7 September. He objected for ten minutes, mostly about the board's expectations, then asked what he would say on 30 September. She gave him a sentence: "We shipped 38 features and five were used; we are now fixing the problem that cost us 108 accounts." He kept the shipping count in the pack but placed it second. The squad was approved at ₹27 lakh, the rest of the team continued its existing work, and Ishita scheduled twenty further customer conversations before the next review.

Her reasoning was modest. The 12-times return was an estimate, and the 6-times case showed it could be wrong by half and still justify the work. What she could not know was whether retaining half the affected accounts was realistic; the first release would tell her.

To go further, study what a product manager does in concrete detail, then the practice of problem discovery and outcome measures, since this page only identifies the myths and does not teach the method that replaces them.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own organisation, which number appears first in the quarterly review, and what does that placement teach people about the job? Second, if you had no authority over anyone on the team, what evidence would you need to change what they build next quarter?
case20v1-pm.myths:
Gulmohar Mandi Exchange: The Roadmap Question

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Gunjan Ahluwalia sat in a rented meeting room in Pune's Baner with a printed roadmap and a pen that had run out of ink. She had joined Gulmohar Mandi Exchange as its first full-time product manager eleven weeks earlier. By Friday, 16 October, she had to lock the plan for the quarter ending 31 December, and on 23 October she would present it to the board. Diwali fell on 8 November, the busiest buying fortnight of the year for restaurant kitchens, and nobody wanted a plan that missed it.

The founder and chief executive, Govind Menon, had handed her a list of twelve features on her first day and said, "You are the CEO of this product. Decide, then tell me what you decided." She had since found no customer problem written beside any item. She had three days to choose between shipping the list, stopping to study it, or something in between.

2. Company background

Gulmohar Mandi Exchange runs a mobile ordering app for restaurants and cloud kitchens that buy vegetables, fruit and dairy staples from wholesale mandis. Govind, a former commodity trader from Nashik, started it in 2021 after watching chefs phone traders at five in the morning. The company now connects 1,800 active restaurant buyers in Pune, Mumbai and Hyderabad with 240 mandi suppliers. Monthly gross merchandise value (GMV) is ₹14.4 crore, an average of ₹80,000 per buyer, and the company keeps 2.5 per cent, or ₹36 lakh a month.

The competition is crowded and well funded. Zomato's Hyperpure sells to the same kitchens through its own warehouses, and Zepto and Swiggy supply smaller eateries. Gulmohar's advantage was being the mandi's own channel: suppliers kept their relationships while Gulmohar supplied the order book, invoice and UPI payment. A ₹40 crore Series A in 2024 funded a team of 26, nine of them engineers.

3. The situation

Gunjan spent her first month reading the backlog, which held 38 items. Govind's twelve were at the top, each described by a single line: a supplier-ranking dashboard, loyalty points, voice ordering in five languages, a credit-limit meter, and so on. Several began with a competitor's name: "Hyperpure has this." None began with a customer's.

The team was busy, and proud of it. Exhibit 1 sets out the last three quarters.

Exhibit 1: Features shipped against buyer repeat rate
QuarterFeatures shippedActive buyers at startBuyers who reordered next monthRepeat rate
Q4 FY26 (Jan-Mar)91,50091561.0%
Q1 FY27 (Apr-Jun)111,64095158.0%
Q2 FY27 (Jul-Sep)141,80097254.0%
Total / average34---

Repeat rate = buyers who ordered again in the following month, divided by active buyers at the start of the quarter. No single blended rate is shown because the quarters have different bases. Source: Gulmohar order database.

As the output rose from nine features to fourteen, the repeat rate slid from 61.0 per cent to 54.0 per cent. This did not prove that shipping caused the slide, but releases could no longer be treated as progress. Of the 1,800 buyers at the start of Q2, 828 did not reorder, the people Gunjan most wanted to hear from.

So in her second month she asked Grace Achieng, who leads customer success from Nairobi, to survey lapsed buyers. Grace's team reached 54 of them by phone. Exhibit 2 gives their main reason for leaving.

Exhibit 2: Main reason given by 54 lapsed buyers
ReasonBuyersShare
Vegetables delivered were not the quality quoted2240.7%
Final price differed from the price at ordering1324.1%
Delivery late for the morning service916.7%
App lacked a feature they wanted611.1%
Other47.4%
Total54100.0%

Telephone survey, 21 September to 2 October 2026; one main reason per buyer. A sample of 54 is small and was not randomly drawn. Source: Gulmohar customer success.

Quality and price mismatches together accounted for 35 of the 54, or 64.8 per cent. Only six buyers named a missing feature, and three of those six wanted a way to dispute a delivery in the app, which is the same problem.

The rest of the global team saw the matter differently. In Lisbon, the designer Gonçalo Pereira had prototyped the dashboard and loved the project. In Warsaw, the data scientist Grzegorz Nowak had found in order logs that buyers who complained about quality lapsed far faster, though on a thin sample. Both sit three to four hours behind Pune, so questions arrived overnight and replies were often a day late, which made it tempting to settle things by decree.

Illustration: the decision timeline (not to scale).

4. The people

Govind Menon, founder and chief executive, Pune, wants visible momentum before the board meets. He believes instinct built the company and that a product manager turns instinct into tickets. He has watched the mandis for twenty years.

Gautam Sathe, engineering lead, Pune, runs the nine engineers and wants a plan he can commit to. He has no objection to a different list so long as it is firm.

Grace Achieng, head of customer success, Nairobi, wants the delivery problems fixed, because her team absorbs the calls. She fears quality complaints will be treated as an operations issue.

Gonçalo Pereira, lead designer, Lisbon, wants his dashboard prototypes tested with real users before they are built, but fears a research phase in which nothing is built.

5. Capacity and the candidate list

Gautam's team has 52 engineer-weeks available for roadmap work this quarter, after allowing for support and holidays. Exhibit 3 shows six of Govind's twelve items, those Gautam had already estimated, matched to the lapse reasons in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 3: Estimated effort for six candidate items
ItemEngineer-weeksLapse reason it addresses
Supplier-ranking dashboard6None evidenced
Voice ordering in five languages9Missing feature (part of 6 buyers)
Loyalty points5None evidenced
Photo proof at delivery and quote lock4Quality and price mismatch (35 buyers)
Weekly standing orders7None evidenced
Credit-limit meter3None evidenced
Total34

Estimates by Gautam Sathe, 9 October 2026; the other six items are not yet estimated. Capacity for the quarter: 52 engineer-weeks.

The six estimated items would use 34 of the 52 weeks, leaving 18 weeks for the six unestimated items, which Gautam judged would not all fit. The one item aimed at the leading complaint was among the cheapest.

6. The options

Option A: ship Govind's list in his order. Govind is satisfied and the board sees a long release note. The cost is that only one of the six estimated items touches the problem buyers reported, and the repeat rate may keep falling.

Option B: pause building for six weeks of discovery. Gunjan, Grace and Gonçalo would interview a hundred more people while engineers cleared technical debt. The upside is a deeper understanding of why buyers leave. The cost is that six weeks would run through Diwali, the best selling window, with no releases for the board.

Option C: commit the quarter to one outcome and test the rest. The outcome would be to raise the repeat rate, and the first item would be photo proof and quote lock. Govind's other ideas would be written as hypotheses, each with a cheap test before any build: Gonçalo's dashboard prototype in front of ten buyers, for example. The upside is a plan that is both evidence-led and visibly shipping. The cost is a harder conversation with Govind and a plan with fewer headline features.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 show, and what does it not prove? What else would you want to see before drawing a conclusion?
  2. Which myth about the product manager's role does "You are the CEO of this product" reflect? What does the job look like instead?
  3. How would you read Exhibit 2 given its sample of 54? What would you do to strengthen it in the next week?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 23 October, and how would you prepare Govind for it?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about two familiar myths. The first is that the product manager is the chief executive of the product, deciding alone. In reality Gunjan holds no authority over Govind, the engineers or the suppliers; her influence comes from evidence and clear framing. The second is the feature factory, in which success is measured by what is shipped rather than by what changes for the customer. Exhibit 1 is a small portrait of one: output up from nine to fourteen features, the repeat rate down seven points.

A well-reasoned answer starts with the customer problem and not with the backlog. Option A confuses activity with progress. Option B is right in spirit but wrong in scale and timing: Exhibit 2 is already a usable signal, and a pause would cost the Diwali window.

One defensible path is Option C. Gunjan names a single outcome, a repeat rate back to 61.0 per cent. At the current base of 1,800 buyers, a gain of seven points is 126 additional repeat buyers; at ₹80,000 each that is ₹100.8 lakh of monthly GMV, or about ₹2.52 lakh in revenue at 2.5 per cent. She commits four engineer-weeks to photo proof and quote lock, which addresses 35 of the 54 lapsed buyers, and holds the remainder of the 52 weeks in reserve for what the first release teaches. Gonçalo's dashboard goes to a ten-buyer test, and Grace's team supplies the participants. Govind sees dates, a number and a method, not a refusal. She should also say what would change her mind: if photo proof does not move the rate by the end of November, the weak sample in Exhibit 2 was the problem, and she would return to discovery with more evidence.

The path is defensible because it uses the decision she can actually make, framing the problem and the test, starts from the customer, and keeps the team shipping. Whichever option a reader prefers, the reasoning should be written down and a metric named.
case40v1-pm.myths:
Lagaam Supply Works: What the Command Centre Is For

An ISB reading case. Foundations › The PM Role & Foundations.

1. Opening: Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 7 February 2027, Lipika Mahanta sat at her dining table in Pune with two printouts. One was the fourteen-item roadmap her chief executive had handed her on day one, five months earlier. The other was her engineering lead's note: the thirteen weeks from February to 30 April 2027 held ninety-six engineer-weeks, and seven of the fourteen items had been estimated at eighty-four.

At nine-thirty on Monday the product council expected her to say what the group would build to the end of April. On 18 February the same page went to the board, where Mrittika Capital's nominee would ask again about the subscription line. On 31 March a contract manufacturer in Ho Chi Minh City would decide whether Lagaam supplied its four Indian plants.

What she could not settle was more elementary. She did not know who the Command Centre was for. She had four counts of how many factories used it, no two agreeing. And she had a suspicion recorded nowhere: that the list was a wish, not a plan, and that her job for five months had been to turn wishes into tickets.

2. Company history, and the decision that still binds

Lagaam Supply Works was founded in Ludhiana in 2019 by Lakshay Rathi and Lakhan Pardiwala, both from family trading businesses. Mid-sized factories spend heavily and chaotically on maintenance supplies — bearings, belts, fasteners, abrasives, lubricants, protective equipment — buying from a long tail of traders with no catalogue and no price history. Lagaam offered one catalogue, next-morning delivery, GST-compliant invoicing and thirty-day terms.

By January 2027 it served 412 plant accounts across nine industrial belts from Ludhiana to Hosur. Monthly distribution revenue was ₹27.2 crore, an average of ₹6.60 lakh per plant per month, at a gross margin of 12.5 per cent, or ₹3.40 crore of gross profit a month. Of 318 staff, fifteen sat in product and engineering and eleven of those were engineers.

Two earlier decisions shape what is now possible. The first, in March 2024, was technical: the company built its plant app on its own invoicing system rather than integrating with the plants' own ERPs. It shipped in eleven weeks and was cheap. The consequence, unwritten at the time, is that everything the product knows about a factory's consumption is inferred from what it bought from Lagaam: purchases elsewhere, free issues, returns and the storeroom's buffer are invisible.

The second was financial. In June 2025 the company raised ₹55 crore of Series B led by Mrittika Capital, after a ₹14 crore Series A in 2022, pitched as a software company with a distribution arm. The term sheet carried a milestone: ₹12 crore of annualised subscription revenue by 31 March 2028. At ₹18,000 per plant per month, which is ₹2.16 lakh a year, ₹12 crore needs 556 paying plants. It has 412 accounts in all.

3. The industry

Indian industrial MRO is large, fragmented and contested from several directions. Moglix and Zetwerk have built national catalogues with venture capital behind them; IndiaMART is still where a maintenance engineer in Rajkot goes to find a particular seal; and manufacturers such as SKF, Schaeffler and Grindwell Norton run dealer networks handling the twenty line items that dominate a plant's spend. Lagaam's claim was never price, but that a plant could stop managing forty vendors.

Three forces bear on the product. GST e-invoicing, now mandatory for Lagaam's customers, made invoice data machine-readable, which made a consumption view thinkable in 2024 and makes a schema change unavoidable this quarter. Production Linked Incentive schemes have pushed component assembly into Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, where Lagaam's growth has come from. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act matters in an unexpected place: the Command Centre records which named employee issued which item, and counsel's note of 14 January 2027 observed that letting a plant head read that as a performance record needs a lawful purpose and the plant's own employee notice.

A third of newer accounts are Indian plants of foreign-owned groups, which buy centrally. Phu Sanh Precision, a Vietnamese electronics contract manufacturer with four Indian plants, issued a request for proposal on 22 January 2027 for consolidated MRO supply worth roughly ₹8.4 crore a year of distribution — ₹1.05 crore of gross profit at Lagaam's margin — plus a group software licence quoted at ₹32 lakh a year, which alone would lift annualised subscription revenue by about seventy per cent. Its procurement head, Mai Quoc Hieu, wants one view across all four plants, which the product cannot give.

4. The situation in detail

The Command Centre began as a demonstration. In July 2026 a competitor's dashboard at a Chennai trade show convinced Lakshay that Lagaam's invoice history was an unexploited asset. On 10 August 2026 it went live for 120 plants: a consumption view by item and cost centre, a stock-ageing view, and a reorder engine. Free for sixty days, it made October 2026 the first billed month.

The user was expected to be the plant head, seeing his spend for the first time and paying for the privilege. Lipika joined on 1 September as the first head of product, three weeks into the pilot, handed the list with the remark that she was now the chief executive of the product and should decide. By November plant heads were plainly not the users; Exhibit 2 shows who is.

On 18 November something nobody had designed for happened. The plant head at the Rajkot forging unit opened the stock-ageing view before an appraisal and asked his storekeeper why ₹4.1 lakh of slow-moving abrasives stood against that storeroom's name. Across Rajkot and Hosur, issue slips logged in the app fell from about 310 a week to about 64, roughly seventy-nine per cent, and have not recovered in the eleven weeks since. They had not stopped issuing material, only recording it where the plant head could see.

On 11 December Haruka Shimizu's memo reported 81 per cent accuracy in predicting an item's next purchase, on a holdout of nine plants. Lakshay has quoted it in two investor calls; its third paragraph says the measurement covers only items bought from Lagaam. Between 7 and 19 January Marcela Obando's team in Santiago called the thirty most recent wins; twenty-five replied, and Exhibit 3 sets their answers beside the representatives' record. On 2 February Mrinal Kaushik sent the capacity note that became Exhibit 6.

Illustration 1: events and commitments, not to scale.

5. The people

Lakshay Rathi, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: the Command Centre is the re-rating story. Incentive: the Series B milestone is his to defend. Unsaid: two items came from one prospect he is courting, and he has told Mai Quoc Hieu the group view is being built anyway.

Lakhan Pardiwala, co-founder and head of supply, Ludhiana. Position: distribution pays for everything, so spend the quarter on wallet share. Incentive: his gross-profit line is the only real one. Unsaid: a view exposing how little of a plant's spend comes through Lagaam may cost accounts.

Mrinal Kaushik, engineering lead, Pune, four of his eleven engineers in Coimbatore. Position: he will build whatever is decided, once. Incentive: predictability, with hiring frozen until June. Unsaid: multi-vendor import is the only item he thinks honest, and he has sketched it.

Ishan Kotecha, national sales head, Pune. Position: software wins deals, as Exhibit 3's CRM column shows. Incentive: representatives earn 1.5 per cent of distribution GMV plus ₹25,000 per software attach, a plan he designed. Unsaid: the bonus shapes what gets recorded as a deal's reason.

Kadri Lepik, product designer, Tallinn. Position: three users with opposed interests, and the dashboard serves the one who uses it least. Incentive: she wants her storekeeper flow built. Unsaid: two of the four storekeepers she showed it to asked whether their plant head would see it.

Haruka Shimizu, data analyst, Osaka. Position: the accuracy figure is correct and nearly meaningless, the denominator being Lagaam's own invoices. Incentive: her memo is quoted as she did not intend. Unsaid: Exhibit 5's nine plants were chosen for willingness, which tracks size.

Option B: make the core promise true. Twenty-two engineer-weeks on multi-vendor consumption import, the only item on Exhibit 6 that touches the 62.1 per cent the product cannot see. Phu Sanh decides on 31 March, and Lakshay has told Mai Quoc Hieu the group view is coming. Counsel's note of 14 January stands: named-individual views need a lawful purpose and the plant's own employee notice, which Lagaam cannot supply. Distribution must not be disturbed from May, when plants overhaul their lines and Lagaam books its heaviest fortnights. And the council sits at nine-thirty on Monday, after which the engineers start on whatever is top of the list.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the product, and who is its customer? Use Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 to argue a definition, and say which you would distrust first.
  2. Exhibit 4 holds three counts of adoption and a fourth sits in Exhibit 1. What should Lagaam define, who should define it, and what then changes?
  3. Exhibit 3's two columns describe the same deals. How would you reconcile them, and what would you change next time?
  4. The 81 per cent accuracy and Exhibit 5's 37.9 per cent are both correct. What does the pair tell you about the reorder engine, and what would you measure?
  5. Rajkot and Hosur's slips fell from about 310 a week to about 64. Is that a data-quality problem, an adoption problem, or a statement about what the product does to people?
  6. Lakshay has twice told Lipika she is the chief executive of the product. What authority does she hold, and what does she hold instead? Given that answer, what should she do at nine-thirty on Monday, and what should she tell the board on 18 February about the path from 21 paying plants to 556?

It was past midnight. Lipika turned the fourteen-item page over and wrote three words on the back — engineer, storekeeper, buyer — and under them: which of you is paying, and for what? She knew neither half of the answer, and the council met in nine hours.

PM myths vs reality: ownership, authority and the arithmetic that settles it

1. Opening: two desks, 5 October 2026

On Monday 5 October 2026 Sharanya Iyer had two documents open in Bengaluru. The first, circulated on 29 September by Girish Pathak, chief executive of Hindola Mobility Systems, said she "now owns the P&L of the device line". The second was the field-complaint export. Hindola builds AIS-140-compliant telematics units — the standard notified by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways — for commercial two- and three-wheeler fleets, plus a dashboard subscription. On 30 September it had 1,46,000 devices live across 420 fleets, 348 each on average, at ₹85 per device per month: ₹1,24,10,000 of monthly recurring revenue, ₹124.1 lakh, annualising to ₹14.89 crore.

Exhibit 1. Handling cost: support plus amortised service visits at ₹340.

Those 9,260 complaints against 1,46,000 devices are 6.3 per cent of the base in one quarter. Sharanya's diagnosis was sharper: drift affected about 11 per cent of units, 16,060 devices, yet produced only 4,180 complaints — a 26 per cent rate among affected units. Most had stopped trusting the report. Her largest customer, a Chennai fleet of 9,800 devices worth ₹99.96 lakh of annual recurring revenue, 6.7 per cent of the total, wanted a driver scorecard by 15 December. She "owned" a statement whose two biggest levers sat in other budgets.

In Hyderabad that morning Nikhil Barve faced the mirror image. Group product manager at Ikshana Learning Exchange, a tutor marketplace for Classes 6 to 12, he had been told by his board to deliver five times the paying students in twelve months. His twenty-person organisation made 96 releases between 1 April and 30 September 2026; installs-to-paying moved from 1.52 per cent in March to 1.575 per cent in September — 0.055 percentage points, or 3.6 per cent relative — against ₹3.72 crore of spend at ₹3.1 lakh per person-month. Sharanya had ownership language without decision rights; Nikhil had decision rights without an outcome account.

2. The idea, its history, and five schools

Output is work released: features, releases, tickets. Outcome is a measured change in customer behaviour; impact is its business consequence. A myth here is a claim about the role that is widely repeated, locally true, and destructive when generalised. Two matter: the mini-CEO, which overstates the product manager's authority, and the feature factory, which substitutes output for outcome accounting.

Neil McElroy's 1931 memorandum at Procter & Gamble created the "brand man", accountable for a brand's results and the arithmetic behind them. The CEO phrasing entered software through Ben Horowitz and David Weiden's 1996 Netscape memo "Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager": in context a demand for accountability where nobody would answer for a release, out of context a licence to act as though one had reports. Marty Cagan's Inspired (2008) and Empowered (2020) replaced it with teams "given problems, not solutions"; John Cutler's 2016 list of feature-factory signs named the second myth, and Melissa Perri's Escaping the Build Trap (2018) gave it an economics.

SchoolWill signWill not sign
Empowered teams (Cagan, Perri, Torres)Teams get problems, not features; the PM owns value and viability risk.That she decides the roadmap, or holds the P&L.
General manager (Amazon single-threaded ownership)Hold the budget and headcount or stop saying "own".That influence without authority is a healthy steady state.
Agile product owner (Scrum, SAFe)The ordered backlog is the single source of truth, ordered by one person.That the role reaches architecture or pricing.
Betting / founder-led (Shape Up)A dedicated role follows scale; shaped bets beat roadmaps.That every squad needs a PM.
Jobs-to-be-done (Christensen lineage)The unit of analysis is the job, not the user or feature.That a conversion rate is an outcome, not a proxy.

Exhibit 2. Five positions as signable propositions.

Pathak's memo came from a general-manager instinct, Sharanya's training from the empowered-team school. The memo is incoherent only because it moved accountability without the resources that school requires.

3. Mechanics: decision rights and marginal value

Experts begin by mapping where money and decisions sit.
