Exhibit 3. Engineering at ₹2.6 lakh per person-month: 6 × 3 × 2.6 = ₹46.80 lakh; 5 × 3 × 2.6 = ₹39.00 lakh.

Hence the authority gap: she directs ₹39.00 lakh of ₹139.70 lakh, 27.9 per cent of the money said to be hers. The mini-CEO reading says act as though the other 72.1 per cent is hers too, whereupon Vaze's team routes her requests through Pathak and every technical question becomes an escalation. The general-manager reading says demand the budget — a twelve-month project. The practitioner's move is narrower: find the one lever evidence alone can move.

The second mechanic decides whether an improvement is worth making at all — a marginal condition, not a target. Where c is the cost saved per unit automated, e the error rate on the automated path and L the average loss per error, automating the marginal unit pays only while e × L < c. The factory never writes this down; its unit of account is the release. The mini-CEO writes an automation target instead, which section 8 shows costing ₹1.73 crore a month.

The third is denominator discipline. Nikhil's 96 releases are a numerator: 96 out of what, changing what? In September 2026, 2,40,000 installs produced 72,000 student profiles (30.0 per cent), 25,200 booked trials (35.0 per cent of profiles), 18,900 attended trials (75.0 per cent of bookings) and 3,780 paid packages (20.0 per cent of attended trials) — a compounded install-to-paid rate of 1.575 per cent. At ₹7,400 per twelve-session package that is ₹2,79,72,000, or ₹279.72 lakh, of which a 22 per cent take rate retains ₹61.54 lakh and tutors take ₹218.18 lakh.

4. When the framing applies, as testable claims

One: the mini-CEO myth bites when the share of required spend under the product manager's control falls below about half. At Hindola it is 27.9 per cent. Nikhil's squads own the student application end to end, so his problem is not authority.

Two: the factory myth bites when release count rises while no behavioural rate moves. Ikshana: 96 releases, install-to-paid up 3.6 per cent relative. Hindola shipped 11 dashboard changes in the same six months and its complaint volume rose, so its diagnosis is a defect, not a factory.

Three: both myths need a measurement lag long enough to hide the truth. Where the loop is hours — a pricing page, a bidding algorithm — neither survives the dashboard; where it is two quarters, as with Hindola's firmware train, both flourish.

The framing misleads in three cases. In a crisis someone must direct work without consensus. Without product-market fit, "problems, not solutions" dissolves: the founder's solution is the hypothesis. And where contractual feature coverage decides revenue, as in government tenders, feature count is not vanity.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the myths migrate upward: a group product manager is handed a revenue line without power to move engineers between products. At Hindola a device sold at ₹2,400 against a ₹1,850 bill of materials yields ₹550 of hardware margin, trivial beside 36 × ₹85 = ₹3,060 of subscription over three years — yet the lines sit under different owners.

In two-sided businesses the factory becomes almost undetectable, because supply-side and demand-side work can each look productive while cancelling out. At Ikshana, 18,900 attended trials across 6,800 active tutors is 2.78 trials per tutor per month; 3,780 paid packages means 0.56 conversions per active tutor and a payout of ₹218.18 lakh ÷ 6,800 = ₹3,209 each. Only 16.6 per cent of 41,000 registered tutors were active, and demand-side releases added unpaid trial labour.

In regulated contexts statute settles the question. At Hemkund Pharma Systems, a Pune firm building pharmacy dispensing software, no product manager owns a release touching schedule-H logic, which needs sign-off against Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation requirements. Mature firms make the compliance reviewer a named team member with a five-working-day commitment, so the constraint is schedulable.

In hardware-plus-software firms the seam is cadence: dashboard weekly, firmware quarterly, tooling annually. In AI-native products it is the model — behaviour comes from training data and thresholds held by a research group, so owning the outcome means owning what one cannot specify. What mature companies do, as against what they publish, is name one arbiter and fund them — the general-manager school quietly winning inside firms whose blogs endorse empowerment.

6. Nuances that separate expert from competent

Accountability and authority are separable

The competent practitioner reads "ownership without authority" as a grievance; the expert reads it as the job description and asks what substitutes — evidence, sequencing, and making a colleague's success depend on the same outcome. The tell: blockers named as people, not decisions.

A silent defect is worse than a loud one

Drift affected 16,060 units and produced 4,180 complaints, a 26 per cent rate. The obvious reading is that the other 74 per cent are content; the expert reading is that they have written the feature off, so complaints flatten as churn accelerates. The tell: a support queue falling while renewals fall faster.

Sole output metrics, not output metrics, are the problem

Release cadence measures engineering health and leads batch size. The expert never argues for slowing down, only for a second column. The tell: a deck opening on a count and carrying no denominators.

The loudest account is sometimes also the market

Hindola's Chennai fleet is 6.7 per cent of recurring revenue and the densest deployment in the country — one voice, and the best sample of where the product breaks at scale. The tell that discounting has become dogma: a roadmap with no named account.

Outcome metrics are gameable too

Replacing "features shipped" with "straight-through processing rate" relocates the trap: any number issued with a target becomes a thing to achieve rather than measure. The tell: a scorecard with no guardrail row.

Average rates hide marginal rates

The most expensive statistical blind spot in the role. Automation rising from 41 to 82 per cent while the average error rate rises from 1.9 to 6.4 per cent looks mild; the marginal rate on the new work is 10.9 per cent. The tell: metrics reported only as averages.

Discovery is a cost, and its cost should be stated

Thirty customer conversations a quarter at two hours each, including synthesis, is 60 hours — 10 per cent of a 600-hour working quarter. The tell: a discovery plan with no cost line.

Naming the myth does not rank the problems

Diagnosing a factory tells Nikhil nothing about whether to work on trial conversion or tutor earnings. The tell of maturity: saying which problem she is not working on. Influence is likewise a stock — Sharanya can divert Vaze's team perhaps twice a year, so experts budget the asks.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the problem is inferred from behaviour at scale, so the factory failure appears as a long tail of defensible experiments. In B2B and enterprise buyer and user differ — at Hindola the fleet owner signs and the dispatcher uses — and the myth becomes the account-driven roadmap. In platform businesses the customer is another engineering team that can build its own, so the mini-CEO pose is costly; in marketplaces both compound.

In hardware the irreversibility of tooling changes the calculus honestly: a bracket redesign cannot be rolled back on Friday, so up-front specification that would be called waterfall in software is correct. In AI products the specification is a threshold and an error rate, not a behaviour. By stage: before product-market fit the role often should not exist separately; from thirty to three hundred people it exists to stop sales becoming the roadmap; beyond that, to hold a line to customers that the organisation's structure works against. Differences by geography are mostly not real.

Of November's 3,254 erroneous approvals, 483 belong to the original 25,420-claim cohort at its unchanged 1.9 per cent rate, leaving 2,771 among the 25,420 newly automated claims — a marginal error rate of 10.9 per cent, nearly six times the 1.9 per cent baseline rate and 1.7 times November's reported average. By the marginal rule, automating one of those claims costs 0.109 × ₹7,100 = ₹773.90 in expected over-payment against ₹95 of review saved. Exactly: 2,771 × ₹7,100 = ₹1,96,74,100 of over-payment less 25,420 × ₹95 = ₹24,14,900 of review is ₹1,72,59,200 — the ₹172.59 lakh gap in Exhibit 8.

The recovery matters more. Sane reverted the threshold in December, restoring the ₹69.04 lakh baseline, then argued what no target could have told him: because ₹7,100 of loss per error is about seventy-five times the ₹95 saved per automated claim, automation pays only while the error rate stays under 95 ÷ 7,100 = 1.34 per cent. At the inherited 1.9 per cent, every level of straight-through processing destroyed value; the project was never automation but error reduction. Two quarters with the model team, led from Warsaw by Katarzyna Wójcik, took the rate to 0.8 per cent, where each automated claim nets 95 − 56.80 = ₹38.20. Expanding to 70 per cent gave the June 2027 position of ₹42.31 lakh a month, ₹26.73 lakh below baseline.

9. Failure modes and the cost of lateness

Accountability without decision rights. Sign: status updates containing the word "waiting". Diagnostic: what share of the money your plan needs sits in a budget you control? Caught late, it costs a capable person who leaves after two quarters of guaranteed failure.

Output accounting. Sign: the review opens with a count and no denominator. Diagnostic: for the largest thing shipped last quarter, which customer did what differently? Ikshana caught it at ₹3.72 crore and six months.

Target fixation. Sign: a number in an objective with no guardrail. Diagnostic: what would it look like to hit this number while the business got worse? Ishanya caught it in month four, at ₹172.59 lakh a month.

Average-rate reporting. Sign: every metric is cumulative. Diagnostic: what is the rate on the units added most recently? This is what makes target fixation expensive.

Silent-defect blindness. Sign: complaints falling. Diagnostic: among accounts that stopped complaining, has usage also stopped? Hindola's cost roughly 20 fleets.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the role need formal authority? The empowered-team position is that authority corrupts the work: a product manager with budget and headcount stops persuading and starts directing, and decision quality falls as engineers withhold objections. The general-manager position is that influence-only roles are a tax paid to dodge an org-design decision. For the first to be wrong you would need empowered teams out-shipping resourced ones at equal scale; for the second, resourced product managers making worse calls, controlling for stage. Neither observation exists cleanly.

Is the feature factory always a mistake? The steelman is a portfolio argument. Twelve small bets, each with a 15 per cent chance of ₹40 lakh at ₹5 lakh of cost, are worth 0.15 × 40 − 5 = ₹1 lakh each: ₹12 lakh on ₹60 lakh of spend. Three large bets at a 35 per cent chance of ₹200 lakh for ₹20 lakh each are worth 0.35 × 200 − 20 = ₹50 lakh each: ₹150 lakh on the same ₹60 lakh, twelve and a half times as much. But the chance all three large bets fail is 0.65³ = 27.5 per cent, against 0.85¹² = 14.2 per cent for all twelve small ones. The factory buys variance reduction, which with two quarters of runway can be rational, and collapses only if the small bets' success probabilities are lower than claimed.

Does the role survive AI-native development? If a small team can specify and generate software quickly, the scarce activity becomes deciding what is worth building — an argument for more product management and fewer product managers. The betting school says the function disperses into founders and engineers; against that, probabilistic products need someone to own an acceptable error rate, which Ishanya shows is neither engineering nor general management. Underneath sits a third dispute: whether product managers should own metrics at all, given Goodhart's law. Ishanya says no; Ikshana says unmeasured accountability is none.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this says "we are a feature factory" and proposes a process. Someone who has internalised it computes a denominator first, states the marginal condition under which the work pays, names what she will not do, and says which number would have to be wrong for her recommendation to flip. She treats her authority as a measured quantity — 27.9 per cent of the relevant spend — not a grievance, reports the marginal rate beside the average, and separates what she knows from what she has sampled and what she is guessing.

12. Closing: the two decisions

On 9 October 2026 Sharanya took both options to Pathak with Exhibits 3 and 5 and the flip calculation, and made an unusual request: not the firmware budget but a written statement that the drift fix was a company commitment, with Vaze as owner and herself reporting the outcome. She also committed to the scorecard, descoped to the three fields the Chennai dispatchers used, inside the ₹15.60 lakh. Pathak agreed, conceding that "owns the P&L" had been a figure of speech. Nikhil, on 12 October, told his board five times was unreachable, presented Exhibit 6, and asked for a two-quarter mandate on trial-to-paid conversion and tutor earnings with the install budget flat at ₹52 lakh. The board gave him one quarter.

Discussion questions. First: was asking for accountability clarity rather than budget Sharanya's strongest move, or acceptance of a structure she should have challenged? Second: Ishanya's 90 per cent target was an outcome metric, not an output metric — what distinguishes a good one, and who should have caught it in August? Third: when should Nikhil keep shipping 96 releases a half-year rather than two bets?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does is the prerequisite: no myth is visible without an account of the work it distorts. Origins of product management explains why P&L language keeps returning; PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder settles the boundary disputes behind most authority confusion. PM archetypes names the version a company is hiring. How the PM job changes by company stage is the highest-value follow-on, most nuances above being stage-dependent. The end-to-end product lifecycle places discovery and delivery in proportion; The Six Ps framework widens the frame to price, placement and promotion.

Raftaar Forecourt Systems: What Is the Job?

Pune, October 2026. A hardware obligation, a software business, and nobody who owns the question.

1. The night before

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Shrinidhi Vaze was at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with a page carrying one line: What the company needs next is…

By nine next morning she owed Vikhyat Dharmadhikari, Raftaar Forecourt Systems' founder and chief executive, a one-page recommendation on how to spend the two senior headcount the board had released. Fifty days remained on the Series B term sheet.

Shrinidhi had joined in March 2025 as Senior Product Manager, hired to "own the product". What she owned was the schedule of 38 field technicians — none employees, all staff of contracted install partners — and the order in which 534 metal boxes in a Coimbatore warehouse would reach petrol pumps.

Four people had told her that week what Raftaar needed: Balaji Seshadri, her VP of Engineering, a technical programme manager; Shireen Contractor in Mumbai, a product marketing manager; Debashis Hazarika, the Series A investor's board observer, a general manager owning the hardware P&L; Vikhyat, "a proper PM who can run the hardware programme". At least two of the four, she suspected, described her current job and one his own.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Raftaar was founded in February 2018 by Vikhyat, a former engineering manager at Zoho who grew up above his family's fuel outlet on the Pune–Solapur road. Its first product, Raftaar Flow, is subscription software for a pump dealer: shift reconciliation, wet stock loss, credit ledgers, GST e-invoicing. By 30 September 2026, 4,120 outlets across eleven states were live on Flow at a list price of ₹3,200 per outlet per month, realisation after dealer-group discounts averaging ₹3,100 — annual recurring revenue of ₹15.82 crore on list or ₹15.33 crore on realisation, and nobody had ruled which was the company's. Thirty-one people were on the payroll.

The decision that governs October 2026 was taken in 2023. To see what the pumps did rather than what a dealer typed, Raftaar built Sense, a retrofit kit reading existing dispensers' pulse output without touching the Legal Metrology–sealed measuring chamber. Dealers paid ₹38,000 a kit plus ₹12,000 for installation.

On 1 October 2023, to cut the kit's landed cost from ₹31,000 to ₹24,500, a reduction of 21.0 per cent, Vikhyat signed a forty-eight-month exclusive supply agreement with Ponni Precision Works in Coimbatore: a minimum purchase of 9,000 kits by 30 September 2027, with a shortfall fee of 40 per cent of contract price, ₹9,800, on every kit not purchased. On the 4,920 kits bought in the thirty-six months to 30 September 2026, Raftaar saved ₹3,19,80,000. But 4,080 remained for the final twelve months, and the fee on purchasing none came to ₹3,99,84,000 — netted crudely, the 2023 decision was ₹80,04,000 under water at worst.

3. The industry

India's roughly ninety thousand retail fuel outlets are mostly run by dealers under the brands of Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, each of which automates the equipment it owns. Private retailers including Jio-bp, Nayara Energy and Shell have expanded alongside them.

Raftaar lives in the gap. The dispenser and tank belong to the oil company; the shift ledger and the ₹4 lakh of fuel that evaporates or walks away in a quarter belong to the dealer, unreported by any oil company's system. UPI, cleared through NPCI, now carries much of forecourt collections; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bears on Raftaar's loyalty application, which has no data protection officer.

The force nobody could size was electrification. Public charging at forecourts, pushed by PM E-DRIVE and by EV volumes from Tata Motors, Ather and Ola, competes for the capital a dealer might spend on a kit — visibly in Pune, not at all in Punjab or Telangana.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The 2023 plan rested on one belief: a kit sold would pull a subscription behind it. Hardware was the wedge; software, at 87 per cent gross margin, the business. Vikhyat had written 60 per cent on a slide — the share of hardware-first outlets expected to subscribe within a year.

By September 2026 the chain had resolved. Of 4,386 kits installed, 2,822 went into outlets already on Flow and 1,564 into outlets that were not; of those 1,564, exactly 118 subscribed, a conversion of 7.5 per cent against the 60 per cent believed. The other 1,446 were hardware-only: a box, a support line, nothing per month. Meanwhile 2,940 of the 4,120 live Flow outlets, 71.4 per cent, had a kit — the wedge had worked backwards.

Three things came apart quietly. First, 534 kits bought from Ponni never reached an outlet, ₹1,30,83,000 of inventory at contract cost. Second, installation became a business in itself, billed at ₹12,000 and costing ₹10,700 — a margin of ₹1,300, a partner network of 38 technicians, and Shrinidhi's day. Third, Orla Brennan, a data scientist in Dublin reporting to Balaji, built the first honest funnel in September: under half of installed kits produced usable data.

Customer counting came apart too. Finance reported 4,120 paying accounts; sales, 5,566 outlets, being 4,120 plus the 1,446 hardware-only; the board pack, "over 6,400 forecourts", being 4,980 ever activated on Flow — 860 since churned, 17.3 per cent — plus the same 1,446. All three were used interchangeably in the data room.

5. The people

Shrinidhi Vaze, Senior Product Manager, Pune. Position: the hardware programme and the software product are two jobs; she does the first badly instead of the second well. Incentive: her review measures kits installed. Unsaid: a Bengaluru payments company has offered her ₹62 lakh.

Vikhyat Dharmadhikari, founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: hire "a proper PM" to carry the hardware programme and free him to fundraise. Incentive: the ₹12 crore milestone. Unsaid: Exhibit 3 shows he took 11 of 14 roadmap and 10 of 12 pricing decisions last quarter.

Balaji Seshadri, VP Engineering, Pune, 17 engineers including a four-person firmware cell. Position: a programme manager would fix the slippage; his dashboard shows 86 per cent milestone adherence. Incentive: dates. Unsaid: his team changed the Sense specification 11 times last quarter, and two firmware engineers are on notice.

Shireen Contractor, Head of Marketing, Mumbai. Position: no positioning, no pricing discipline, no launch process; a product marketing manager is the gap. Incentive: a second-half lead target. Unsaid: it is her decks that carry 5,566 in one place and 6,426 in another.

Senthil Arumugam, programme director, Ponni Precision Works, Coimbatore. Position: Raftaar must commit volume. Incentive: plant utilisation. Unsaid: Ponni will supply at ₹22,900 a kit, ₹1,600 or 6.5 per cent below contract price, on a firm order for 2,000 before 31 December 2026 — never in writing.

Orla Brennan, data scientist, Dublin. Position: the only number that matters is the 46.3 per cent in Exhibit 4, and no one owns it. Incentive: she wants it given to somebody. Unsaid: her funnel has never reached the board.

Camila Undurraga, partner lead, Santiago. Position: her 184 signed Chilean outlets need Spanish-language loyalty and a tax-invoice module. Incentive: commission on new outlets. Unsaid: Vikhyat promised loyalty by Diwali; nothing was built.

Debashis Hazarika, board observer, Bengaluru. Position: hardware is a business needing a general manager who owns its profit and loss "the way a founder does". Incentive: the fund's mark depends on the round closing. Unsaid: his portfolio-operations team already has a candidate.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the half-year the board reads on Thursday. Hardware — kits plus installation, ₹553.00 lakh — was 42.9 per cent of revenue but 20.9 per cent of gross margin; software, 80.7 per cent of margin on 56.4 per cent of revenue.

7. Voices

"We are not confused about roles. We are behind on a programme. Give me one person whose week is the Ponni schedule, the firmware drop and the install partners, and I will give you 340 kits a month."

"Two headcount is a luxury we will not get twice. Spend them where the ₹12 crore is, not on tidiness."

Vikhyat Dharmadhikari, WhatsApp, 10 October

She had written four, aware that all answered "whom do we hire" and none "what work is not being done".

Option A — product and programme. A senior product manager in Pune at ₹54 lakh and a technical programme manager at ₹48 lakh, ₹102 lakh, breaching the envelope by ₹6 lakh and needing a waiver. Option B — product and market. A senior product manager at ₹54 lakh and a product marketing manager at ₹42 lakh, exactly ₹96 lakh. Option C — a business owner. A general manager for hardware at ₹92 lakh, holding the Ponni relationship, the kit price and the P&L, leaving ₹4 lakh. Debashis would support it and may supply the candidate. It is the only option that puts whether hardware should exist inside one person's job — and it splits a thirty-one-person company in two, giving a stranger the right to stop buying kits.

Option D — delivery, cheaply, and wait. She had also written, and deleted, a fifth line: that what was missing was not a role but a decision — whether Raftaar is a software company selling a sensor or a hardware company with a dashboard — and whoever must make it is already employed.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Only the board, meeting on Thursday 15 October, can waive the ₹96 lakh envelope. The term sheet lapses on 30 November 2026, fifty days from tonight, carrying the ₹12 crore FY27 hardware milestone. Hardware revenue in the first half was ₹5.53 crore, leaving ₹6.47 crore, which at the H1 realisation of ₹50,000 per installed kit is 1,294 installs in the second half against 1,106 in the first — 1.17 times, nothing like the 2.49 times in Figure 1, because the milestone counts installations and the agreement counts purchases.

Cash is ₹740.00 lakh against a burn of ₹33.63 lakh a month: twenty-two months of runway, less under scenario C. Senthil's ₹22,900 offer dies on 31 December 2026. Two of four firmware engineers leave in November. A senior hire in Pune has taken Raftaar 94 days on average from brief to joining, placing a Monday decision's joiner on about 14 January 2027, three and a half months into the twelve remaining on the Ponni clock.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 4 only, state Raftaar's product problem in one sentence; now state it from Exhibits 2 and 5 only. Which sentence is a product manager's job, and which is not?
  2. Exhibit 3 was written by one of the people it describes. Which rows would you trust, which discount, and what one further source would you collect before letting it drive the hire?
  3. Balaji's dashboard says 86 per cent and Orla's funnel says 46.3 per cent, and both are accurate. What is each measuring, and what is the title of the person who should own the gap?
  4. The ₹96 lakh envelope was set against Pune salaries, yet Exhibit 6 prices the same five roles between ₹26 lakh and ₹168 lakh by city. Does location change which role to hire, and should Shrinidhi raise that with the board?
  5. Option C hands the Ponni decision and the kit price to a general manager — in effect a second founder for one line. What does Vikhyat lose that he is not counting, and when is that loss worth taking?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday. What does Shrinidhi send Vikhyat, and what does she say to the board on Thursday, including about her own title? If the missing role is one Raftaar cannot hire for, how does she tell a founder with fifty days to close a round?

At ten past midnight the four options were still four. Underneath them sat what she could not put on one page: that the job she was being asked to define might be the one she was already failing at, and that whoever was best placed to say which of the five questions in Figure 2 was really unowned had taken thirty-five of last quarter's eighty-four decisions himself. She made tea and did not begin writing.

When Someone Says “We Need a PM”

Five roles that share one job title in conversation, and the decision of which one Gulmohar Payments Network actually needed

1. Four requisitions, one word

On Monday 2 March 2026, Kavitha Subramanian, Head of Product at Gulmohar Payments Network, opened the hiring tracker and found four requisitions, all titled “Product Manager”, all approved, all unfilled. Gulmohar, a Bengaluru company, had spent six years building a QR-code and UPI acceptance service used by 3,20,000 small merchants, from kirana stores to pharmacies. UPI is the Unified Payments Interface, the real-time payment rail run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). Gulmohar’s next product was a countertop “soundbox” that announces each payment aloud so a shopkeeper need not check a phone. Paytm and PhonePe already sold such devices, so the hardware was a commodity.

The plan was to put 40,000 devices in merchants’ hands in the first quarter, renting each at ₹125 a month. Thus 40,000 × ₹125 = ₹50,00,000, or ₹50 lakh a month, and ₹600 lakh, or ₹6 crore, over twelve months once every device is deployed. The hiring budget was ₹2.00 crore, which is four people at an assumed ₹50 lakh each in annual cost. The pilot launch was fixed for Monday 29 June 2026, twelve weeks after the new team would start on 6 April.

Kavitha had read the job descriptions that Ananya Rao, the recruiter, had drawn from the requisitions. One asked for someone to “own the go-to-market”, another to “work with the firmware team in Austin”, a third to “keep the launch on track with the contract manufacturer in Noida”, a fourth to be “a customer-obsessed owner of the merchant experience”. Four jobs, one title. Ramesh Iyengar, the founder and chief executive, had been acting as the product manager himself for eight months.

If she hired four people called product managers, she would pay more than the budget, leave pricing and vendor schedules to people trained for neither, and leave the founder in the middle of every decision. A wrong mix risked a slip, and each month of slip deferred up to ₹50 lakh of rental. The question was not “how many PMs?” but “which of five roles is each of these jobs?”

2. The idea: five roles, five different questions

A product manager (PM) is the person accountable for deciding what the product should do, for whom, and why, and. The role traces to a 1931 Procter & Gamble memorandum in which Neil McElroy proposed a “brand man” to own a soap brand end to end. A product marketing manager (PMM) decides how the market will understand the product: positioning (the claim the product makes against alternatives), pricing, messaging and sales enablement. A technical program manager (TPM) coordinates work that spans several engineering teams, owning dependencies and integration risk; the title grew in large software firms as systems outgrew single teams. A project manager owns the schedule, budget and delivery of a defined piece of work, a discipline formalised by the Project Management Institute (1969). The founder owns the company itself: funding, the decision to bet, and the final call when functions disagree.

These roles exist because one decision-maker cannot do everything well once the work grows. Each answers a different question.

The sentence Kavitha could repeat in a meeting was this: the PM decides what is worth building and for whom, the PMM decides how the market will hear of it, the TPM decides how the pieces fit, the project manager decides when and in what order, and the founder decides what the company is willing to lose. It turns an argument about titles into a question about decisions, and decisions can be counted.

3. How it works: from titles to decisions to hours

Kavitha’s method had four steps. First, list the decisions the launch requires, not the roles. Second, assign each decision to the role whose question it is. Third, convert each decision into weekly hours. Fourth, and this is the step usually omitted, check the interfaces: the points where one role’s output is another’s input.

For the soundbox she identified six workstreams. Merchant discovery meant sitting in shops to learn what a shopkeeper does when a payment arrives. Prioritisation and specification meant deciding which of forty requests entered version one. Pricing, positioning and enablement meant fixing the ₹125 rental, the pitch and the field team’s training. Technical dependencies meant firmware, the UPI switch and the mobile SDK (software development kit, a bundle of code other teams build against). Schedule and vendor tracking meant the Noida factory’s production slots. The sixth, funding and final trade-offs, belonged to Ramesh.

The implicit fourth step matters most. Every boundary has a handoff: price is set by the PMM but constrained by what the PM decides to include; the order of technical work is set by the TPM but must follow the PM’s priorities; dates are kept by the project manager but only mean something if the PM agrees which features may be cut to hold them. Where a handoff has no owner, the most senior person in the room takes it, and at Gulmohar that was usually Ramesh.

4. A worked example: hours, cost and one changed input

Kavitha estimated the weekly effort in each workstream during the twelve-week build, using 45 focused hours a week as one person’s capacity.

Table 1. Exact sums: 24+18+34+32+28+14 = 150; 36+27+51+48+42+21 = 225. Both plans total 1,800 hours (150 × 12 = 225 × 8).

Now the costs. Using Gulmohar’s compensation bands, the loaded annual cost is ₹55 lakh for a PM, ₹46 lakh for a PMM, ₹60 lakh for a TPM and ₹32 lakh for a project manager.

Plan B costs ₹27 lakh less than Plan A (220 − 193). Hours tell a more interesting story. Under Plan B on the 12-week plan, the PM carries 24 + 18 = 42 hours, or 93.3 per cent of capacity (42 ÷ 45); the PMM 34 hours, 75.6 per cent; the TPM 32, 71.1 per cent; the project manager 28, 62.2 per cent. Plan A has four people with 180 hours of capacity (4 × 45) against 136 hours of non-founder work (150 − 14), which is 75.6 per cent. On raw hours Plan A looks fine. It fails because four people trained as PMs would do pricing and vendor scheduling without the training, while the PM’s 42 hours of discovery and specification still needed doing.

Plan C leaves the founder 42 + 14 = 56 hours, 124.4 per cent of capacity: cheap and unsustainable.

Now change one input. Suppose the board brings the launch forward from 29 June to Monday 1 June, eight weeks instead of twelve. The same 1,800 hours fit into fewer weeks, so each workstream scales by 1.5. The PM now needs 63 hours (140.0 per cent), the PMM 51 (113.3 per cent), the TPM 48 (106.7 per cent) and the project manager 42 (93.3 per cent). Three of four roles are overloaded, the PM by 18 hours (63 − 45).

Compressing the schedule did not create a need for more project managers; the project manager is the one role under capacity. It created a need for the PM to decide to do less. Removing 18 hours means halving merchant discovery, from 36 to 18, a judgement about how much to learn before shipping. No hire fixes that.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The boundaries are drawn by company, not by nature. At some firms the PMM owns pricing; at others the PM does. Ask what a role decides.

A TPM is not a senior project manager. The project manager asks whether the work is on schedule; the TPM asks whether independently built systems will fit when joined, and needs the engineering depth to judge a design.

The PM has authority by persuasion. A PM usually has no reporting line over engineers, designers or marketers.

The founder as PM works, then stops working. Founders are often excellent early PMs because they hold the customer problem and the authority together; the limit appears when decisions queue. In Plan C the founder is at 124.4 per cent of capacity before anything goes wrong.

The PMM is not the launch-week role. Price shapes what is built, since a ₹125 rental constrains the bill of materials; a PMM engaged in the final fortnight can only describe decisions already made.

The framework cannot tell you the quality of the people. It assigns decisions to roles but not whether the person in the role is good. Nor can it say whether the soundbox is the right bet; that stays with the founder.

6. How it differs across product types and company stages

In consumer products the PM and PMM work closest, because positioning is tested in the app itself. In B2B products, which sell to organisations, the PMM carries more weight: sales enablement, competitive claims and procurement conversations are part of the product’s success, and the TPM matters when the product must integrate with customers’ systems. In marketplaces, which must grow two sides at once, the PM’s job divides by side, and the PMM messages each side differently while one side’s pricing subsidises the other.

Stage matters as much as type. In a ten-person start-up the founder is the PM, the PMM and the project manager, and that is correct. By two hundred people the roles separate as the founder’s hours run out. At very large firms the roles specialise further: a TPM may coordinate fifteen teams, and a PM may own a fraction of one product.

7. Common mistakes

Hiring from the title. Symptom: four interviewers ask four different questions of the same candidate. Misunderstanding: that “PM” names one job. Cheapest diagnostic: ask each interviewer to write down the first decision the hire would own, and compare.

The PM as scheduler. Symptom: meetings are status reports and the roadmap is a Gantt chart. Misunderstanding: that coordination is the same as decision. Diagnostic: ask what the PM decided not to build last month.

The late PMM. Symptom: the positioning document arrives after the price is fixed. Misunderstanding: that marketing begins when building ends. Diagnostic: compare the date of the PMM’s first meeting with the date of the pricing freeze.

The founder bottleneck. Symptom: unanswered messages to the founder. Misunderstanding: that holding every decision is the same as leading. Diagnostic: count decisions waiting more than 48 hours for one person.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Gulmohar’s decision would begin with a one-page list of decisions, not titles. Each decision would have one named owner. Each hire would be told at interview which question they were hired to answer. The PM and PMM would agree the price band before the specification froze, and the TPM and PM would agree the cut-list before firmware work began. The founder would keep the 14 hours only a founder can spend.

9. What Kavitha decided, and what to learn next

On Friday 6 March, Kavitha took Plan B to Ramesh. She asked him to rewrite the four requisitions as a PM, a PMM, a TPM and a project manager, at ₹1.93 crore, ₹7 lakh inside the budget. She rejected Plan C: a founder at 124.4 per cent of capacity could not also be the final decision-maker. She asked Ramesh to hand over the 42 hours of product work gradually, over the first six weeks. If the board moved the date to 1 June, she would not ask for more hires; she would ask which 18 hours of PM work to stop. Ramesh agreed. Her reasoning: the cheapest plan that leaves a question unowned is not cheap.

Next, study what a PM does in detail, since each boundary above is drawn from the PM’s own scope, and then prioritisation and pricing, where the PM and PMM interfaces are most contested.

Two questions to sit with. First, in an organisation you know, name the one decision that no role currently owns, and say who makes it by default. Second, if Gulmohar’s launch moved to eight weeks and Kavitha could add exactly one hire, which role would you pick, and what would that person actually do on their first Monday?

Five Questions, One Title

Product manager, product marketing manager, technical program manager, project manager, founder — why the boundary moves by company, and why counting interfaces beats counting people

1. Two companies, one week, the same confusion

On Tuesday 7 April 2026, Nandita Deshmukh left a board review at Prayukti Factory Systems in Pune holding an approval she had not asked for in the form she received it. Prayukti sells shop-floor intelligence software to auto-component plants in the Tata Motors and Maruti Suzuki vendor base. At 31 March 2026 it carried annual recurring revenue of ₹74 crore across 148 plants in 42 customer groups, an average of ₹50 lakh per plant per year, with 310 employees and sixteen engineers in Kraków.

The approval was five headcount, all titled “Product Manager”, against an envelope of ₹2.90 crore: five slots at Prayukti’s loaded PM cost of ₹58 lakh. Dilip Wagle, the co-founder and chief executive, had argued it himself. Prayukti was no longer one product but three: the uptime product; Inspect, a camera module bolted to a press line and built with a contract manufacturer in Hosur; and Classify, a defect-recognition model retrained per customer. Inspect was planned into 60 plants at ₹14 lakh each — an ₹8.40 crore annual run rate, ₹70 lakh for every month it arrived late.

She did not need five product managers. She needed one product manager, one owner of pricing and positioning, one to own the seam between camera firmware and the Kraków platform team, and one to hold Hosur to a schedule.

Two days later Tanvi Khosla had the opposite problem at Shehnai Wedding Exchange in Gurugram. Shehnai is two-sided: 18,400 verified vendors — venues, caterers, photographers — in 24 cities, matched to couples. In the year to March 2026 it brokered 10,000 weddings worth ₹1,240 crore in gross merchandise value, an average booked value of ₹12.4 lakh, on which a 4.5 per cent take rate produced revenue of ₹55.80 crore. Here 9 of the 140 employees carried “Product Manager” in their title, 6.4 per cent of the company, yet her co-founder Vikramjeet Sodhi still settled the two arguments a week that mattered.

Nandita had too few titles for her questions; Tanvi had too many titles and too few answers.

2. The idea: five questions, and a history of splitting them

The five titles are not five kinds of person but five decision rights, each defined by a question. The product manager: what should we build, for whom, why — and what will we therefore not build? The product marketing manager: how will the market understand this, and at what price? The technical program manager: how do independently built pieces fit, and in what order? The project manager: by when, at what cost, with which dependencies tracked? The founder: what will the company risk and fund, and who wins when two competent people disagree?

The history is a history of splitting. Neil McElroy’s three-page memorandum at Procter & Gamble in May 1931 asked for “brand men” with full responsibility for one brand; Toyota arrived independently at the shusa, or chief engineer, with end-to-end authority over a vehicle programme. Project management was codified separately: the Project Management Institute was founded in 1969, the first PMBOK guide published in 1987. Microsoft created the program manager in 1984, when Jabe Blumenthal was moved onto Excel to hold specification and schedule across a growing team; the TPM of the 2000s is that role pushed outward to span teams.

No single authority designed the set, so the boundaries are conventions, not natural kinds; and every split happened because a decision one person used to make became too slow or too specialised to keep in one head.

The schools disagree about where splitting helps. The empowered-team school, argued by Marty Cagan and the Silicon Valley Product Group since 2001, holds that a team needs a PM owning value and viability alongside design and engineering; it signs a team without one owner of value and viability is a feature factory and refuses coordination deserves its own career ladder. The program-management school holds the reverse: beyond some dependency count, integration risk is first-class work, owned by someone with the depth to reject a design. The go-to-market-primacy school, visible in April Dunford’s work on positioning, signs positioning and price decide enterprise outcomes more than feature choice and refuses the PM should set the price. The founder-mode school — Paul Graham’s lineage, sharpened by Brian Chesky in 2023 — signs for years the founder alone holds both the problem and the authority and refuses there is a headcount at which the founder hands over product.

3. Mechanics: count decisions, then count interfaces

Expert practice does not start from roles. It lists the recurring decisions, assigns each one named owner, and then — the step usually left implicit — counts the interfaces: the pairs of owners whose outputs feed each other. With k owners on one product surface there are k(k−1)/2 pairs, so five owners make 10 and thirteen make 78. Decisions grow with the product; interfaces grow with the square of the owners. That is why role confusion seems to appear overnight at a particular size, and why the instinctive remedy of adding a coordinator makes the arithmetic worse before it makes it better.

Nandita listed the decisions that recur every planning cycle, tagging each with the question it answered.

Decision familyQuestionDecisions per quarterHad one named owner, March 2026

Table 1. Exact sums: 6+5+4+3+3+5+4+4 = 34 decisions; 4+3+1+0+2+3+4+4 = 21 with a single named owner.

So 13 of the 34 recurring decisions — 38.2 per cent — had no owner. Nandita then timed them. From her calendar and Prayukti’s escalation thread, a decision with one named owner closed in a median of 4 working days; one without closed in 19, having to be noticed, escalated and scheduled into Dilip’s week. The quarterly load therefore cost 21 × 4 + 13 × 19 = 331 decision-days, a mean of 9.7 days. With owners named for 11 of the 13 orphans it would cost 32 × 4 + 2 × 19 = 166 decision-days, a mean of 4.9 — 165 decision-days removed per quarter.

Decision-days are not additive to the schedule; most run in parallel and cost only irritation. Three orphans, though, sat on Inspect’s critical path: the hardware price point, the firmware-to-platform contract, and which of six camera placements version one would support. Each lost the 15-day gap between an owned and an unowned decision — 45 working days, nine weeks, about two calendar months of slip at ₹70 lakh a month. That is ₹1.40 crore pushed out of the year against a staffing difference of ₹22 lakh: the latency term is 6.4 times the salary term.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

It rests on three testable claims. First, the five questions are genuinely distinct here: the skill that answers one does not answer another. At Prayukti this is plainly true: nobody who can negotiate a camera price in Hosur is the right person to decide which press-line defects matter to a Bajaj supplier. At Shehnai it is partly false, since the couple-side PM and the marketing lead work from the same cohort data, and splitting positioning from product on a surface tested inside the app creates an interface where none existed.

Second, the cost of an unowned decision exceeds that of a named owner. Nandita passed this at 6.4 to 1. It fails in low-latency settings: in a ten-person company, 4 days and 19 days collapse into one afternoon.

Third, the owner can actually decide rather than recommend. This claim is least often tested and most often false. Shehnai’s nine product managers recommended; Vikramjeet decided. Naming an owner who cannot decide yields an orphan with a frustrated custodian, and adds an interface in the bargain.

The framework misleads twice over. When the real constraint is capability, a company whose PMs are weak does not improve by giving them cleaner mandates; the ownership map will cheerfully certify well-bounded poor judgement. And when the bottleneck is one scarce person, decisions queue behind them whoever owns them, so redrawing boundaries moves the queue without shortening it.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware, AI

Prayukti is a multi-product company pretending to be one product. Three lines with their own PM, PMM and TPM would be nine owners plus Dilip — ten owners, 45 interfaces. Nothing says that is wrong; the arithmetic says it is costly. They say they “share a platform team”; in practice one senior person, often with no relevant title, settles platform conflicts by reputation.

Shehnai is two-sided, which breaks the PM question specifically. “What should we build, for whom?” has two answers that trade against each other: vendor tooling that raises listing quality, and discovery that raises conversion. One PM across both sides internalises the trade-off and becomes a bottleneck; one per side externalises it into an interface neither can settle, so it rises to the CPO. Pricing is worse: the 4.5 per cent take rate is at once a PMM decision, a supply lever owned by Pooja Chandiramani, and a founder-level bet on share.

Regulation relocates the boundary rather than blurring it. When the product is a licensed object — a medical device under CDSCO rules, a payment flow under NPCI and Reserve Bank of India circulars, a securities interface under SEBI — a class of decisions becomes legally non-negotiable, and the TPM’s seam work absorbs compliance evidence as a dependency. The failure mode is a PM who treats regulatory constraint as a feature to prioritise.

Hardware plus software, Prayukti’s Inspect case, is where the project manager stops being optional: a software cut-list can be revisited weekly, an injection-moulding slot booked eleven weeks out in Hosur cannot.

AI-native products move feasibility into the PM’s lap. For Classify, “can the model do this reliably enough for a plant to act on it?” is not an engineering question answered once but a scope question answered continuously against an evaluation set. The test: ask who owns the eval set. If the answer is “the data science team”, the PM question is unowned.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

The unit is the question, not the title. An expert refereeing a role dispute asks three people to write down independently the first decision the role owns. The tell is three different answers — and the obvious reading, that they need aligning, is wrong. One needs to be told they do not own it.

A technical program manager is not a senior project manager. The tell is whether the person can reject an architecture. A project manager asks whether work is on schedule; a TPM asks whether two independently built systems will fit when joined. Confusing them produces a well-tracked integration failure.

Product marketing’s leverage sits upstream of the build. The diagnostic is one subtraction: the pricing-freeze date minus the date the PMM first joined a product meeting. At Prayukti the gap was negative — Inspect’s ₹14 lakh price had been quoted to three customers before anyone owned pricing. A PMM engaged after the bill of materials is fixed can only narrate.

A product owner is not a product manager. Scrum’s product owner is a role inside a delivery framework: it guarantees a ready, ordered backlog. The tell is a calendar of refinement ceremonies. The PM question is unowned while someone sequences work nobody chose.

Decision rights are not the org chart. Dotted lines resolve nothing. The expert reads the last ten escalations and asks who closed each. At Shehnai nine PMs reported through Tanvi, yet Vikramjeet closed seven of the last ten. That is the real organisation; the chart describes payroll.

The founder’s scarce resource is tie-breaks, not hours. A founder who answers questions is a search engine; one who settles conflicts between competent people is irreplaceable. Sort a fortnight of founder decisions into first-resort and last-resort: a high first-resort share means the organisation routes around its own owners.

Boundaries follow the bottleneck, not the function. Where the PMM owns pricing in one company and the PM in another, the difference usually traces to which function last caused a crisis. That is local knowledge, not incoherence. Ask what went wrong here three years ago before proposing a boundary.

Every coordinator is a tax on the thing coordinated. Adding the kth owner adds k−1 interfaces: Shehnai went from 6 owners and 15 interfaces to 13 and 78, so seven more people brought 63 more interfaces, 9 apiece. Overload is visible and self-correcting; split ownership is invisible, and its tell is a recurring meeting for alignment between two people who both believe they decide.

In AI products, reliability is a scope decision. When behaviour is learned rather than specified, the line between “what we build” and “whether it works” dissolves, and the PM must decide what error rate the customer will tolerate before the feature can be said to exist. The tell is a review where accuracy is reported as status rather than argued as a trade-off.

7. How it changes by product type and by stage

Four differences by type are real. In consumer products the PM and PMM questions genuinely overlap, because positioning is tested in the product itself; splitting them early buys an interface and little else. In B2B and enterprise the PMM question carries independent weight — a competitive claim and a price list are not derivable from the feature set — and the TPM question becomes real once the product integrates with customers’ systems. In platforms and marketplaces the PM question splits by side, and the scarcer side gets the senior owner. For hardware the project-manager question is non-negotiable; for AI products the PM question absorbs feasibility. Other differences practitioners cite are cultural, not structural.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Prayukti: the reallocation. Nandita costed three options against the approved ₹2.90 crore, scoring each on question coverage: how many of the five questions had a named owner.

Option A is the most expensive plan that answers the fewest questions. Option C fails on Hosur: without a schedule owner, hardware commitments return to Dilip.

Shehnai: the partial fix. Tanvi audited 28 recurring decisions: 9 on the couple side, 8 on supply, 5 on trust and payments, 4 on pricing and positioning, 2 on platform sequencing. Only 12 of the 28 had a single named owner, 42.9 per cent, despite nine people holding the title. At a 5-day owned median and a 16-day unowned median the quarter cost 12 × 5 + 16 × 16 = 316 decision-days, a mean of 11.3 days; naming owners for 11 more, leaving 5 contested, gives 23 × 5 + 5 × 16 = 195 decision-days, a mean of 7.0. The stakes were seasonal: the two booking peaks, November to December and January to February, carried 6,200 of the 10,000 weddings — 62 per cent — worth ₹768.80 crore of GMV and ₹34.60 crore of revenue at the 4.5 per cent take rate. A decision not closed by 15 October waits a year.

The recovery came not from better coordination but from someone being allowed to decide what not to build.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Hiring from the title. Early sign: four interviewers ask four unrelated questions. Diagnostic: have each write down the first decision the hire will own. Late cost: a year of a well-regarded person in the wrong job, the orphan still orphaned.

The product manager as scheduler. Early sign: the roadmap is a Gantt chart and reviews are status reports. Diagnostic: ask what was decided not to be built last month, and why. Silence means the PM question is unowned. Late cost: a backlog-driven product, what the benchmark programmes warn against on day one.

The late product marketing manager. Early sign: positioning arrives after price. Diagnostic: the subtraction in section 6. At Prayukti the cost was a ₹14 lakh price quoted before the bill of materials was known, which then constrained the hardware rather than the reverse.

Coordination mistaken for progress. Early sign: coordinators outnumber deciders. Diagnostic: Pratibimb’s ratio, eight coordination roles to one decider. Late cost: ₹56 crore for ₹3.10 crore of ARR.

The founder bottleneck. Early sign: decisions waiting more than a week on one calendar. Diagnostic: first-resort versus last-resort founder decisions over a fortnight. Late cost: the organisation stops routing decisions to owners at all, which only visible refusal by the founder reverses.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether the project-manager role belongs on a product team. The empowered-team position rests on a real observation: in software, dates are an output of scope decisions, so a person paid to defend dates defends them by quietly removing scope, without the customer knowledge to choose well. For this to be wrong there must be commitments whose cost of movement is independent of scope — Prayukti’s Hosur tooling slot. The camps rarely notice they describe different industries.

The second is whether pricing belongs to product or to product marketing. The go-to-market camp points to enterprise outcomes decided by packaging and list price, and to PMs who price by intuition and lose margin. The product camp answers that price is a design constraint, and that a PMM setting price after scope is fixed is only discovering someone else’s choices. For the go-to-market position to be wrong, price would have to be substantially determined by what is built: in consumer subscription it largely is, in enterprise it largely is not.

The third is the founder question, and it is least settled. The founder-mode argument is that product judgement rests on a thousand unarticulated facts about customers, and that companies which hand it to a hired executive decline in ways nobody can point to for two years. Its opponents answer with latency: both audits above show a founder as de facto owner of a double-digit share of decisions, with the 15-day penalty attached. What would settle it is a measurement nobody has — the quality of decisions, not their speed.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite the five definitions. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They talk about decisions where others talk about people, and will ask “who decides the cut-list?” in a meeting about headcount. They are reluctant to add owners, treating every new title as a request to add k−1 interfaces someone must service. And they will leave a question deliberately unowned, loudly, with a date attached — as Tanvi did with the take rate — because an acknowledged orphan behaves differently from a hidden one.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Friday 10 April 2026, Nandita took Option B to Dilip: two product managers, one product marketing manager, one technical program manager, one project manager, at ₹2.68 crore, ₹22 lakh inside the envelope. Her argument was not the saving but that the three orphans on Inspect’s critical path were worth ₹1.40 crore of deferred run rate, 6.4 times the staffing difference. She asked one further thing: that Dilip keep his four tie-break decisions and give up the eleven he had absorbed by default.

Tanvi’s decision was narrower. She did not hire. She moved two of her nine product managers to engineering programme work, named owners for 11 of the 16 orphaned decisions, and wrote on one page the 5 decisions she was leaving with Vikramjeet, with the 15 October date beside them. Her open headcount went to a product marketing manager, the company’s first, because a 4.5 per cent take rate had never been owned by anyone whose job it was.

Three questions. First: Nandita’s case rests on a 15-day penalty from her own calendar. If the true penalty were 5 days, would Option B still win, and what would you measure to find out? Second: Tanvi cut owners from 13 to 11 while naming more decisions; when would the opposite be right? Third: Pratibimb recovered by narrowing from 31 hospitals to 9. Was the error the staffing mix or the belief that integration was the hard problem?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does comes next, because every boundary here is drawn from the PM’s own scope; without it the other four roles are defined by subtraction. PM myths vs reality unlocks the diagnostics in section 9; Origins of product management extends section 2 and explains why conventions differ by industry lineage; PM archetypes addresses what this page omits, whether the person in the role is any good; How the PM job changes by company stage turns Table 2 into a career question; The end-to-end product lifecycle supplies the decisions behind Table 1; and the Six Ps framework gives a vocabulary for section 10.

Gehna Ledger Systems: Which Hire?

1. Opening

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Harinder Sachdev sat in the Indiranagar office of Gehna Ledger Systems in Bengaluru with a blank job description on his screen and a board instruction in his inbox. The board had approved exactly one new senior headcount, with an annual cost-to-company ceiling of ₹45 lakh. The recruiter needed a written brief by Wednesday, 21 October, if the person was to join before the new year.

The difficulty was the title. His head of engineering wanted a "TPM", his marketing lead a "product marketing manager", and an investor "a proper PM". Harinder, the founder and chief executive, had been doing parts of all three jobs himself. He had to decide which of them the company actually needed first.

2. Company background

Gehna Ledger Systems sells subscription software to independent jewellery retailers: billing, gold and silver stock by weight and purity, old-gold exchange, customer ledgers, and GST and hallmarking records. It was founded in 2019 in Bengaluru by Harinder, a former Infosys engineer whose family ran a jewellery shop in Thrissur. In October 2026 it had 31 employees and 1,800 paying shops, 1,680 in India and 120 in East Africa, where many Gujarati and Kerala-origin jewellers trade. The average subscription was ₹2,000 a month, so annual recurring revenue was ₹4.32 crore (1,800 × ₹2,000 × 12 = ₹4,32,00,000).

Its competition was the habit of the trade. Many shops still ran Tally or Marg ERP, adapted by a local consultant, while others used Zoho Books with spreadsheets alongside. The Bureau of Indian Standards' HUID hallmarking rules had created Gehna's best growth year, because small shops suddenly needed a tool that could log a unique hallmark identifier against every piece.

3. The situation

Gehna's product organisation had never had a product manager. Harinder decided what was built, wrote the tickets, set the prices and approved the launch emails. He also chased the engineers about dates, which, he admitted, consumed more of his week than he had imagined. In September he asked his assistant to log every working hour for four weeks, 60 hours a week, and to tag each hour to a kind of work. Exhibit 1 is the result.

She wanted someone to own the schedule. Girish read the same table and saw twelve unused features and a sales team that could not explain the product.

The distributed team saw it differently. Duarte Matos, the product designer in Lisbon, four to five hours behind India, received requests as one-line messages and often redrew screens after engineers had started. Wanjiru Kariuki, who led customer success from Nairobi, two and a half hours behind, heard East African jewellers ask for the same stock-by-weight fix three times, and had no one to take it to except the founder.

4. The people

Harinder Sachdev, founder and CEO, Bengaluru, wanted relief from the hours he could not afford, but feared hiring someone who would take over decisions he considered his own.

Gayathri Murugesan, head of engineering, Pune, managing nine engineers in Bengaluru and five in Pune, wanted a stable scope and a named owner of dates. She thought a TPM would give her both.

Girish Ponnappa, marketing lead, Kochi, wanted a product marketing manager. He had been writing launch copy for features he had never seen before the release note.

Wanjiru Kariuki, customer success lead, Nairobi, wanted someone to take customer problems to engineering and tell her what would be fixed, and when.

5. The adjacent roles, and their cost

Harinder wrote down what each role owned, because the labels were being used loosely. A product manager owns which customer problems are worth solving and what the product should do about them. A product marketing manager owns who the product is for, how it is priced and positioned, and how it is launched. A technical programme manager coordinates large pieces of work across several engineering teams and their dependencies. A project manager owns the schedule and budget of a defined piece of work with an end date. The founder owns the company's direction and its money. Exhibit 3 gives the annual cost-to-company he had been quoted for each.

The TPM would breach the ceiling by ₹1 lakh, while the project manager would leave ₹21 lakh unspent. Exhibit 1 shows that 19.2 per cent of the founder's time went on coordination, 21.7 per cent on marketing and 15.8 per cent on product. Time alone therefore pointed at marketing.

6. The options

Option A: hire for delivery. Appoint a TPM at ₹46 lakh, which needs a board waiver, or a project manager at ₹24 lakh. The upside is a visible owner of dates. The cost is that nobody would be deciding what ought to be on the schedule, and the Exhibit 2 adoption rate suggests that is where value leaks.

Option B: hire a product marketing manager at ₹34 lakh. This takes the largest delegable block of the founder's time, 52 hours, and gives sales a clear story for the Dhanteras and Diwali buying season. The cost is that better positioning of features few shops use will not raise adoption, and the product decisions would stay with Harinder.

Option C: hire a senior product manager at ₹42 lakh. This puts one person on customer problems, the hand-off to Duarte's design and to Gayathri's engineers, and the priority order Wanjiru needs. The cost is that it relieves the smallest of the three blocks a hire could take over, 38 hours, and demands that Harinder genuinely share decisions. Pricing and launch work would stay with him.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which hours are inherently the founder's, and which belong to a role someone could be hired for? What would you need to know before treating hours as the hiring signal?

2. Exhibit 2 shows an on-time rate of 55 per cent and an adoption rate of 29.4 per cent. Which of these is a delivery problem, which is a problem choice, and how would you tell them apart?

3. Gayathri says scope changed in seven of nine slipped items. Does that make a TPM the answer, or is it evidence of something upstream?

4. Which option would you write into the recruiter's brief on 21 October, and what would you do about the work that option leaves with the founder?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as a question about work, not titles. When someone says "we need a PM" they may mean any of five roles, and the first task is to say what job is not being done. The boundaries are drawn from the product manager's own scope: the PM owns the customer problem and what to build. The product marketing manager takes that product to market. The TPM and project manager make delivery predictable. The founder decides direction and funds it.

A well-reasoned answer reads Exhibit 2 before Exhibit 1. Exhibit 1 shows where the founder's hours go, but Exhibit 2 shows which failure costs the company most. Only 5 of 17 shipped features were adopted, so most of the engineering effort was spent on things customers did not use. A TPM would make that waste arrive on time, and a PMM would announce it more clearly. Slips matter, yet seven of nine followed scope changes, which suggests the schedule is unstable because nobody owns the decision upstream.

One defensible path is Option C. Hire the senior product manager at ₹42 lakh and write the brief around customer problems, prioritisation and a written scope that locks at sprint start. Use the ₹3 lakh of headroom (45 minus 42) to retain a freelance launch writer for three months at ₹1 lakh a month, covering Dhanteras on 6 November and Diwali on 8 November while the founder keeps pricing. Review at six months using the Exhibit 2 adoption rate and the founder's coordination hours; if the schedule is still unstable, a project manager or TPM follows, and if sales still cannot explain the product, a PMM. The reasoning is sequence: decide the right work first, then deliver it, then sell it.

Hypothesis-driven product development

Running a plan as a register of claims evidence can overturn — and finding that the hard part is the grain at which a result is read.

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Devyani Marathe, vice-president of product at Dhanak Imaging Works in Ahmedabad, held a quotation for tooling, board bring-up and a Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation submission: ₹3.6 crore, or ₹360 lakh. Dhanak makes a handheld retinal camera that photographs the back of the eye without dilating drops, with software grading the image for diabetic retinopathy. The second-generation unit her founder, Nachiket Limaye, wanted would halve the bill of materials and run the model on the device. Poornima Hegde held the tooling slot until 19 October; Ashwin Mascarenhas, in Kochi, had the regulatory file half-drafted.

The plan rested on revenue nobody at Dhanak had yet collected. District vision programmes would not buy cameras; they would pay per screening. At the benchmark a state tender had set, ₹38 a gradable screening, the entire ₹3.6 crore turned on one number: how many screenings a unit performs in a day, month after month, once the inauguration photographs are taken. Marathe's predecessor had written 42 into the business case. Nobody could say where 42 came from.

Five days earlier, Raghav Khandekar sat through a different meeting at Tagada Recovery Systems in Bengaluru. Its largest customer, a mid-sized non-banking financial company, wanted a module scoring each delinquent account by its probability of paying, so agents visited likely payers first; Jyotsna Mirashi, the chief executive, costed it at ₹2.4 crore. Manas Pattnaik had back-tested a model on 18,400 accounts in the 31-to-60-day bucket, carrying ₹84.64 crore of outstandings, and the lift curve was the cleanest Khandekar had seen. His objection was that it answered a question nobody had asked.

2. The idea, and the five positions people hold

Hypothesis-driven product development decomposes a plan into falsifiable claims — statements specific enough that a stated observation would oblige the team to abandon them — ranks them by the damage each would do if false, and tests them in that order with the cheapest instrument that could disconfirm them. Three elements do the work: a claim that forbids something, a threshold fixed before the data, and a named person with authority to stop.

The lineage has three strands: Karl Popper's 1934 demarcation, that a theory earns scientific standing by what it rules out; the decision-analytic tradition, Raiffa on the value of information and Dixit and Pindyck on investment under uncertainty, which prices a test rather than recommending it; and the operational translation in Blank's customer development and Ries's build-measure-learn loop, alongside the experimentation platforms at Amazon, Microsoft and Booking, whose published hit rates (about one idea in three moves its target metric) are the strongest evidence that plans do not predict outcomes.

The problem it solves is not ignorance but agreement: a plan accumulates conviction in proportion to how many have reviewed it, and review tracks consensus, not behaviour. Dhanak's 42 had survived four quarterly plans because it had been repeated four times.

Five schools disagree. The lean school signs that an untested load-bearing element is a liability, but not that a passed test licenses a build. The jobs-and-design-research school signs that the unit of inquiry is the customer's job rather than the feature, but not that a number should arbitrate a qualitative insight: thresholds on small samples manufacture false precision. The experimentation-platform school signs that most ideas fail and the answer is industrial-scale randomised testing, but not that twelve interviews or a fourteen-site pilot are evidence. The conviction school — Thiel's definite optimism, Cagan's product vision — signs that some products cannot be discovered by experiment, because no customer can evaluate them before they exist, but not that results outrank founder judgement. The real-options school signs that a test's value is the option value it buys net of delay, but not that every assumption deserves one.

3. Mechanics: the register, the threshold, the price of knowing

Expert practice begins with a hypothesis register: the load-bearing claims, each with the observation that sinks it, ranked by damage.

₹4,200.00 divided by ₹15.608 is 269.09 screenings a month and, over 26 operating days, 10.3497 per operating day. That is the 10.35 in H1: the point at which the programme stops paying for itself over the camera's life.

On an honest prior of 70 per cent for the good branch, committing blind is worth 0.7 × 316.83 − 0.3 × 180.72 = ₹167.57 lakh: positive, so build. With a perfect oracle Marathe takes the good branch and walks from the bad, worth 0.7 × 316.83 = ₹221.78 lakh. The gap, ₹54.22 lakh, is the value of perfect information, and equals the downside avoided, 0.3 × 180.72 — four times the register's cost.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, stated as claims and checked against each protagonist. The decision is costly and hard to reverse. True of Dhanak's tooling, false of its capture prompts; partly true of Tagada, where code is reversible but a quoted model is not. A cheap instrument can produce the disconfirming observation. True for Dhanak, whose H1 pilot alone cost 1.8 per cent of the commitment and whose whole register cost 3.7 per cent; for Tagada only if the instrument is right, and a back-test cannot see what the module claims to change. Someone may act on a negative result. Marathe could release the tooling slot; Khandekar had no authority to refuse his largest customer, so his first move was to buy it. The behaviour the economics depend on is observable inside the window. True of utilisation over six weeks; false, as Dravya shows, of anything turning on month-four persistence.

Where the method misleads is narrower than critics claim and wider than advocates admit. It misleads when the test population cannot behave as the real one will: a concierge service is more attentive than software, so pilots flatter. It misleads when the outcome is bounded by something the test holds constant, as with a feature that tests well then fails licensing. And it misleads in new categories, where the repair is to shift the claims to mechanism.

5. Hard edges: two sides, regulators, hardware, models

On two-sided systems the hypothesis must be stated for both sides, and supply hand-seeded before demand can be tested. Dharti Equipment Exchange, which rents tractors between farmers near Nashik, recruited 46 owners across two talukas before taking an enquiry; co-founder Aniruddha Gokarn fixed in advance that fewer than 45 per cent of enquiries matched within 24 hours would stop expansion. Over eight weeks it matched 612 of 1,180 enquiries eventually (51.9 per cent) but only 487 of 1,180 within a day (41.3 per cent). The pre-committed metric failed; the comfortable one passed. Gokarn densified one taluka, partly because 289 of the 388 rentals completed (74.5 per cent) came from seven owners.

In regulated settings the instrument becomes the constraint. Tagada's holdout meant deliberately not sending an agent to some delinquent borrowers; counsel read the Reserve Bank of India's fair-practices expectations as permitting a withheld discretionary visit where statutory notices and call-centre contact continued. Dhanak faced the mirror image: a device change altering a diagnostic claim cannot be A/B tested on patients, so before submission the only testable claims are engineering ones.

Hardware inverts the loop: software hypotheses are tested by building something thin, hardware hypotheses by not building, substituting people for the thing that costs steel. Dhanak's pilot used gen-1 cameras and overnight human grading so no gen-2 commitment preceded the utilisation answer. Model-native products add a subtler edge: Tafteesh Audit Labs, which extracts figures from scanned invoices, found a fortnight of prompt and retrieval work moved accuracy more than that fortnight's model upgrade, so any result older than three weeks describes a vanished system.

In multi-product firms a shared claim must be assigned to one product's economics, or two teams test it twice. At the seams, the honest account diverges from the published one: large firms run far more experiments and act on far fewer, because a negative result arrives attached to a headcount plan. What works is pre-commitment — criterion, date and decision-maker fixed before the quarter opens.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The average is not the decision grain

Dhanak's pilot averaged 13.96 screenings per centre-day against a 10.35 line, a pass with 35 per cent to spare. The tell-tale sign is one statistic standing in for a quantity the decision consumes over time. The obvious reading makes the average the estimate and the weeks noise; expertise inverts that.

A back-test contains no counterfactual

Pattnaik's lift curve is real and irrelevant: historical data hold no observation of a treated account untreated. The tell-tale sign is a model judged on an outcome rather than a difference. No sample size repairs that; the quantity was never recorded.

Rank by incremental effect, not outcome level

A propensity-to-pay model ranks borrowers by how likely they are to cure, which includes everyone who would have cured unvisited. The tell-tale sign is a targeting proposal whose top segment has a high base rate; the obvious reading spends the scarce resource where it changes least.

The window must cover the behaviour the economics need

If the margin comes from month-four persistence, a three-week trial measures the wrong thing however cleanly. The tell-tale sign is a threshold in the only unit the instrument could produce. The repair is a longer window, or a proxy population already showing the behaviour.

A surviving hypothesis promotes the next one

Passing H1 does not validate Dhanak's plan; it moves the weakest point to H3. The tell-tale sign is the word "validated" with no mention of what is now most likely wrong. Experts keep the register visible afterwards, so the new weakest link is named rather than met in month nine.

Information has no value where nobody may act

Khandekar's first act was not an experiment but asking Mirashi, in writing, what result would let Tagada decline the module. The tell-tale sign is a test whose negative branch has no owner: evidence persuades only where the authority to stop predates it.

Blended rates hide failing segments

Dhanak's gradable share cleared its 78 per cent threshold at 81.19 per cent overall while three of its five clusters fell below that line. The tell-tale sign is a pass on a weighted rate with no segment view beside it: clusters arrive one at a time, so a blended pass forecasts a mix that does not exist yet.

Read the verdict at the pessimistic end

A point estimate is not a verdict. The expert habit is to restate the result at the unfavourable end of its interval, then name the assumption which, moved plausibly, flips it: for Dhanak, fleet size; for Tagada, the value of a cure.

7. What changes by product type and by stage

In consumer products samples are large and cheap, so the constraint is threshold discipline. In business and enterprise products the sample is nine lenders or eleven school chains; statistics are unavailable and the instrument becomes the structured commitment — a paid pilot, a signed order — because only that separates interest from intent. On platforms and marketplaces every hypothesis is two, and liquidity thresholds must be time-bounded, as Dharti's 24-hour rule was. In hardware the test is a substitution, not a build; in model-native products the subject drifts, so thresholds carry dates. Register, threshold and stop authority, though, are identical in all five.

Stage changes the dominant risk, not the method. Before product-market fit a company tests existence and runway binds, so cheap and crude beats clean and slow. A scaling company tests magnitude, where thresholds from unit economics matter more than direction. A large company tests marginal change against a base it must not damage, so its obstacle is political. The recurring error is importing the previous stage's instrument.
