9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Threshold drift. Sign: after a weak result, talk turns to what the number "really means". Diagnostic: show me the dated document stating the threshold. Cost if late: the full build, since permitting it is drift's purpose.

Proxy substitution. Sign: the threshold is in the unit the instrument happens to produce. Diagnostic: which line of the business case does this number occupy? Cost if late: Dravya's ₹43.24 lakh shortfall, found post-launch.

Level in place of difference. Sign: a targeting claim evidenced by a lift curve. Diagnostic: where is the untreated group? Cost if late: a negative-value programme that reports beautifully, harder to kill than a visible failure.

Pilot theatre. Sign: a launch date but no stop criterion and no owner of the negative branch. Diagnostic: what do we do differently on Monday if this fails? Cost if late: the credibility of every later experiment.

Over-testing the reversible. Sign: a six-week test on a decision reversible in four days. Diagnostic: what does it cost to do and watch? Cost if late: the calendar, which nothing recovers.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether small-sample evidence is evidence. The platform school's strongest form holds that judgement about product outcomes is barely better than chance, and that anything short of a powered randomised comparison is a story. For it to be wrong, the decisions that matter most would have to be those where randomisation is unavailable — enterprise, hardware, regulated, zero-to-one — which is the counter-claim: a commitment from three of nine buyers is statistically weaker and decision-theoretically stronger than any test they will never be in.

Whether conviction should outrank evidence. The conviction school's steel version is not anti-empirical. It holds that customers evaluate only within the frame they inhabit, that the most valuable products redefine that frame, and that early negative evidence about them is biased. It would be wrong if the cases usually cited carried early signals the founders did not seek.

Whether most assumptions deserve a test. The real-options position is that a register is a cost, that the option value of most tests falls below it once delay is priced, and that the default for cheap reversible decisions is to act. Opponents answer that teams misjudge reversibility, tooling and public pricing being the examples.

Whether holdouts are ethical where the treatment may help. Tagada's counsel permitted its design; a reasonable colleague would argue that withholding a visit from a borrower it might have helped is not neutral, and that benefit must be shown first.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this runs experiments. Someone who has internalised it spends most of the effort before any experiment, on three questions: which claim, at what grain, and who may act. The register fits one page and names a person per row. Thresholds are odd numbers, derived rather than chosen for comfort. Results arrive with the segment view beside the headline. And the practitioner can say, without hesitating, when their own proposal was last stopped by a number they wrote down in advance.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Marathe neither released the tooling slot nor cancelled the programme. She took the sixth week's 10.33, not the 13.96 average, as the planning figure, and showed the board that at 600 units the project needs 10.35 and at 300 units 14.46 — so the live hypothesis was not utilisation but fleet size, which depended on H3. She asked for ₹26 lakh and eleven weeks to convert two state programmes into signed per-screening orders with volume floors, tooling contingent on 400 committed units.

Khandekar declined to build what his largest customer had asked for, offering instead a four-week extension of the holdout at Tagada's cost, to estimate uplift within the mid stratum by region and balance band, and a module priced on incremental cures rather than seats. Mirashi backed him: the alternative was a ₹2.4 crore build whose own test valued it at minus ₹6.89 lakh.

Three questions. First: under what conditions would you approve the gen-2 tooling with no test, and what does that say about your prior? Second: Dravya's process was faultless and its outcome a ₹43.24 lakh hole — was the error in the threshold, the instrument or the plan? Third: if a clean negative result on your largest initiative arrived tomorrow, name the person who could act, the document authorising them, and the days needed.

13. Going deeper

The end-to-end product lifecycle is the loop these tests run inside. What an MVP is supplies the craft assumed here: the smallest artefact that can carry a real test. Zero to one asks what falsification means when no customer can yet evaluate the category. What a product manager does and PM myths vs reality turn on authority: a register without a stop owner is decoration. Origins of product management explains the inherited planning habits; PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder matters because the register crosses all five roles and one owns the threshold; PM archetypes shows which temperaments over-test; and how the PM job changes by company stage extends section 7.

Hypothesis-driven product development

Treating a product plan as a set of claims that evidence can overturn, and testing each with the smallest product that can overturn it.

1. The Monday meeting

On Monday 3 August 2026, Pallavi Sardesai, head of product at Gyanodaya Learning Labs, a Pune company that sells exam-preparation video lessons to class 10 students, sat across from her founder, Sandeep Kolhatkar, and the engineering lead, Lokesh Brahme, who had joined by video from Nagpur. On the table was a plan the company had carried for a year: a live doubt-solving service in which a student photographs a stuck problem and a tutor answers within ten minutes, sold as a premium tier at ₹499 a month.

Gyanodaya's free app had 2,50,000 monthly active users, most of them in towns such as Indore, Coimbatore and Nagpur. Lokesh had estimated six months and ₹180 lakh (₹1.8 crore) to build the service properly: tutor scheduling, a queue, a photo-upload pipeline, quality review. Sandeep wanted a decision by the board meeting in the first week of September. No one had asked a student to pay for it.

Pallavi's difficulty was not that the plan was bad. It was that the plan was written as a set of certainties: students want faster doubt resolution, they will pay for it, tutors can deliver it at an affordable cost. If the first claim was wrong, the company would find out after six months and ₹180 lakh. She proposed something less comfortable: write the plan as claims, decide in advance what evidence would sink each, and spend about one-thirtieth of the budget finding out.

2. The idea

Hypothesis-driven product development is a way of running product work in which each important belief behind a plan is stated as a falsifiable hypothesis, a claim specific enough that an observable result could prove it false, and is then tested with the cheapest experiment that could produce that result. The product team builds only what the experiment needs, reads the result against a threshold fixed beforehand, and lets the result decide whether to continue, change direction or stop.

The problem it was invented to solve is familiar to anyone who has watched a funded team ship for a year to indifferent customers. A plan feels strong in proportion to how many people have agreed with it, and agreement is not evidence. The intellectual root is the philosopher Karl Popper's argument, from the 1930s, that what separates a scientific claim from an opinion is that it forbids something and can therefore be caught out. Steve Blank, in his early-2000s work on customer development, pushed founders to leave the building and test their guesses on customers. Eric Ries, in The Lean Startup (2011), turned this into an operating loop for software teams: build the smallest thing, measure, learn.

The sentence Pallavi could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "We are not deciding whether to build the service; we are deciding which belief to test first, and what result would make us stop."

3. How it works

The method is a loop with five steps, shown below. Teams usually skip steps 2 and 4.

Step 1 is the belief, usually phrased as a feature: "students will love instant doubt solving." Step 2, the implicit one, is converting it to a hypothesis with a number attached. Pallavi wrote: "If we offer the doubt service at ₹499 a month to a random sample of free users, at least a stated share will pay after a trial." The share is the threshold, the result below which the team commits to not building. Without it, any outcome looks encouraging.

Step 3 is the smallest test: the cheapest arrangement that could produce a believable number. Pallavi chose a concierge test, in which humans deliver by hand what software would eventually automate. Six tutors would answer doubts sent through WhatsApp to 5,000 randomly chosen free users, from Monday 10 August to Sunday 30 August, three weeks in all. The test would cost ₹6 lakh. Step 4, also implicit, is committing to how the evidence will be read before it arrives. Step 5 is the decision, and it feeds a new belief: if students pay, the next question is whether tutors can sustain the price.

4. A worked example

The threshold has to come from the plan's own economics, not from optimism. Table 1 sets out the economics.

Table 1. Economics of the doubt-solving service, as planned

Paying students needed (15,00,000 ÷ 289 = 5,190.3, rounded up)5,191Computed
Required conversion (5,191 ÷ 2,50,000)2.08%Computed

The last row is the threshold: if fewer than about 2.08 per cent of active free users would pay, the build does not recover its cost within a year. Pallavi rounded it to 2.1 per cent and wrote it on the whiteboard before the test began.

The test ran. Of the 5,000 users offered the service, 1,250 started the free week and 150 paid for the first month. Table 2 shows the chain, and Figure 2 draws it to scale.

The observed conversion is 150 ÷ 5,000 = 3.0 per cent, above the 2.08 per cent threshold. But 150 payers from a sample of 5,000 is an estimate, not a fact. Its standard error is the square root of (0.03 × 0.97 ÷ 5,000), which is about 0.24 percentage points, so a 95 per cent interval (1.96 standard errors) runs from roughly 2.53 to 3.47 per cent. Even the pessimistic end clears 2.08 per cent. The first hypothesis survived a test that could have killed it.

The second pass changes one input at a time. Table 3 shows what happens if the trial-to-paid rate had been 8 per cent instead of 12, and separately if tutor cost per student turns out to be ₹290 instead of ₹210.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A hypothesis is not an idea with a question mark

"Maybe students want faster doubt resolution" cannot be wrong, so it cannot teach. A usable hypothesis names a population, an action, a number and a time window. Whenever a team cannot say what result would make it stop, it holds a hope.

The threshold must precede the data

If the threshold is chosen after the result, people unconsciously pick one the result clears. The discipline is to write the number down, with a date, before the first student sees the offer. The 2.08 per cent line was set before 10 August for exactly this reason.

A test is not an MVP, and neither is a prototype

A test exists to answer a question; an MVP is a product a customer can use. They overlap, but a landing page that measures sign-ups tests demand without being usable.

Behaviour beats opinion, and payment beats behaviour

What students say in a survey, what they click and what they pay are three different strengths of evidence. The cost of a false positive rises as you move down that list.

Evidence cannot tell you what you did not test

A passed test says the tested claim survived. It says nothing about retention in month four, about a competitor's free alternative, or about whether a different product would have earned more. Hypothesis-driven work narrows uncertainty; it does not remove it.

When the method does not apply

If the decision is irreversible or regulated, such as a payments licence, small tests may be impossible or misleading. And if no one has the authority to act on a negative result, the test is theatre. The question to ask before relying on any experiment is: what will we do differently if this fails?

6. How the idea changes by product and by stage

In consumer products such as Gyanodaya's, samples are large and tests are quick, so the discipline is mostly threshold-setting. In B2B products, a sample might be eleven school chains, each negotiated over months; statistics are useless, and the test becomes a structured set of conversations ending in a signed pilot or a refusal, with a paid pilot counting as stronger evidence than praise. In marketplaces, there are two sides that each need the other. A hypothesis must be stated for both, and the supply side, here the tutors, usually has to be hand-seeded before the demand side can be tested honestly. That is why a concierge test suits Gyanodaya: six hired tutors stand in for a marketplace that does not yet exist.

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company has few customers and little to lose, so it tests the existence of demand itself. A large company has customers to protect and brand risk to manage; its tests are more often run on small slices of live traffic, and its main enemy is not scarcity of data but the political cost of a team stopping something it announced.

7. Common mistakes

Testing the feature rather than the belief. Symptom: the team reports that "users liked the demo" and moves straight to a larger build. Misunderstanding: liking a demonstration is not the behaviour the plan depends on. Cheapest diagnostic: ask, "which line of the business case does this result change?" If the answer is none, the test was decoration.

Moving the goalposts. Symptom: after a weak result, the discussion turns to "what the number really means" or to a different metric that looks better. Misunderstanding: the threshold was a hope rather than a commitment. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether a dated, written threshold existed before the data; if it did not, treat the result as exploratory.

Treating one pass as proof. Symptom: a single 3.0 per cent result is quoted as "validated." Misunderstanding: uncertainty has been mistaken for certainty. Cheapest diagnostic: write the interval beside the number and re-run the verdict at the pessimistic end, as Table 3 did.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of the Gyanodaya decision has a one-page document before any work starts. It lists three or four hypotheses in order of how much they can hurt the plan (demand, tutor cost, retention, quality), a threshold for each, the cheapest test for each, the date by which each will be read, and the name of the person who may stop the project. The sign of health is not that hypotheses pass; it is that they are sometimes failed, and the organisation acts on it.

9. Closing: the decision, and what comes next

On Tuesday 1 September, Pallavi presented the figures: 3.0 per cent against a 2.08 per cent line, a 2.53–3.47 per cent interval, and the unresolved tutor-cost risk. She did not ask for the ₹180 lakh. She asked for a second test, a four-week paid run with the tutor cost measured per answered doubt, before committing the full build, and she asked the board to accept a stop line of 2.87 per cent. The reasoning was not that the first test proved the plan good, but that it moved one belief from "assumed" to "survived", and exposed the next belief, which was more dangerous.

To go further, read next about what an MVP is, because choosing the smallest test is the craft this page assumed, and then zero to one, which asks what changes when the product category itself is unproven. Two questions to sit with. First, think of a plan in your own work that everyone believes in: what is its weakest belief, and what number would make you abandon it? Second, if your organisation received a clean negative result tomorrow, who would be permitted to act on it, and how long would they wait?
case40v1-pm.lean:
Ogha Materials Exchange: Three Doors, One Sorting Line

A case on hypothesis-driven product development, set in Ahmedabad, October 2026

1. Sunday night, Narol

On the evening of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Shalaka Vartak sat on the loading dock of her own sorting facility in Narol, on the southern edge of Ahmedabad. Navratri had emptied the industrial estate. Diwali was four weeks away, and with it the packaging surge that had, both previous years, doubled the material her trucks could pick up and halved its price.

In her lap was a memo for the board of Ogha Materials Exchange, which met on Thursday, 15 October. It had to answer a question the company had circled for a year without naming: who, exactly, was Ogha’s customer.

Behind her, the line stood idle. It had been built to take 300 tonnes of plastic a month. In September it had taken 142.6.

2. How Ogha came to own a sorting line

Ogha was founded in October 2023 by Shalaka, formerly a category manager at a Mumbai packaging firm, and Pritesh Mogre, an engineer in Pune. Their first thesis was a software thesis: India’s dry waste was not scarce, merely unaccounted for. If a housing society could schedule a pickup in an app and receive a weight, a receipt and a small payment, the material would surface in an orderly stream and Ogha would hold the ledger of record. The app launched in March 2024. An angel round of ₹1.1 crore was followed in November 2024 by a seed round of ₹7.4 crore led by Aparna Vaidyanathan of Palash Ventures, Mumbai, taking the total raised to ₹8.5 crore.

A software company can abandon a hypothesis on a Friday; a company with a sorting line has an appetite. The decision that shaped everything afterwards came in January 2025. Buyers would not pay for sacks of mixed material; they wanted washed, graded flake to a specification. Rather than depend on processors in Vapi, Ogha took a five-year lease on a shed at Narol at ₹2.4 lakh a month, with a break cost of ₹14.4 lakh, and spent ₹1.85 crore on a wash-and-granulate line rated at 300 tonnes a month. From that month it carried a plant fixed cost of ₹14.2 lakh: ₹2.4 lakh of rent, ₹5.1 lakh of amortisation and power, ₹6.7 lakh of plant staff.

3. The industry around it

By 2026 the Indian recycling market had two halves that outsiders routinely confused. One half was the informal trade, moving material on cash without invoices. The other was a compliance market made by regulation. Under the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the Extended Producer Responsibility framework administered by the Central Pollution Control Board, brand owners must obtain certificates showing that an equivalent quantity of their packaging has been collected and recycled, filed on the CPCB portal. Hindustan Unilever, Dabur, Amul, the quick-commerce platforms and the sellers behind Flipkart and Meesho all carried obligations, and certificates were periodically audited.

Ogha sat between three kinds of buyer: recyclers wanting cheap clean feedstock, brand owners wanting documentation an auditor would accept, exporters wanting volume to a specification. Banyan Nation and Lucro Plastecycle had built processing depth, Nepra in Ahmedabad collection scale, Attero the same in electronics. Reliance Industries’ polyester recycling arm made the point that at scale this was a petrochemical business.

Global exposure arrived through one contract. From 1 April 2026 Ogha supplied Kitano Resin Trading in Fukuoka with high-density polyethylene flake: 60 tonnes a month, take-or-pay, for eighteen months at ₹61,000 a tonne, contamination not above 1.5 per cent, shortfall penalty ₹9,000 a tonne. That price stood roughly 17 per cent above the ₹52,000 a tonne mixed post-consumer flake fetched from Dakshin Polymer Industries in Coimbatore, and it was the single reason Siddhesh Amonkar, the finance lead, could show a gross margin at all.

4. What was believed, and when

Shalaka’s one methodological victory was a document. On 20 May 2026, before a four-month test running from 1 June to 30 September, she made the team write four beliefs as claims that could fail, each with a number agreed in advance. Exhibit 1 reproduces them with what the test returned.

Through 2025 tonnage grew and they assumed the society channel was growing with it; in fact, as Lotte Vermeiren in Antwerp established only in August 2026, almost all growth after the line opened came from industrial scrap Jignesh Tarsadia was buying in Rajkot and Surat to keep the line fed. 6. The people

Shalaka Vartak, Ahmedabad, chief executive. She wants to run the company on evidence and has the memo of 20 May to prove it. She does not say that the industrial business, which the evidence favours, is not the company she set out to build.

Pritesh Mogre, Pune, co-founder and head of engineering, with six engineers. The society channel failed on execution, he argues, not principle: the scheduling flow was rebuilt only in July, so H1 was tested against unfinished onboarding. His team has little to do in a trading business. Two of his engineers have been interviewing elsewhere, which he has not mentioned.

Jignesh Tarsadia, Surat, head of the generator network. He has built the industrial channel almost single-handedly and thinks Ogha should stop apologising for it. His quarterly payout is computed on declared tonnage, the column in Exhibit 3 that exceeds the weighbridge. He does not volunteer that six units supply 61.8 of September’s 96.4 industrial tonnes, or 64.1 per cent, and that two also sell to a Vapi processor whenever asked.

Lotte Vermeiren, Antwerp, data scientist, four and a half hours behind Ahmedabad. She produced Exhibit 4 and the reconciliation that exposed the 28.4-tonne gap, and holds that the company measures commitments rather than behaviour. On a six-month contract, she has no authority over the roadmap.

Niamh Doherty, Belfast, product designer. From fourteen interviews in August she reports that the society secretary who signs up rarely hands over the material; that is the housekeeping contractor, whose incentive is the kabadiwala who pays cash today. The app, she says, has never had a user, only a signatory.

Siddhesh Amonkar, Mumbai, finance. He notes ₹2.9 crore of cash on 30 September, gross monthly cash costs of ₹41 lakh, and September’s net burn of ₹18.55 lakh, implying about 15.6 months against about 7.1 if contribution collapsed. He favours whatever fills the line.

Rukhsar Dhanani, Narol, plant manager, measured on utilisation and cost per tonne. Society material is the enemy of both: small, wet, mixed loads that occupy the line for a third of the output. She says the plant can take 300 tonnes; she does not say that at 250 she would need a second shift.

Aparna Vaidyanathan, Mumbai, Palash Ventures, board member. Her bridge of ₹3.5 crore is conditional on 250 monthly active generators; September’s count was 141, being 97 societies and 44 industrial units. She invested in a network business and must explain to her partners what she now owns.

7. Voices

"We did not fail H1. We tested an onboarding flow I had told you was half-built, called the hypothesis dead, and now we are discussing becoming a scrap trader."

Pritesh Mogre, Monday call, 5 October 2026

"Every month I bring in more tonnes, and every month somebody in Europe explains why the tonnes are not real. My slips are not wrong."

Jignesh Tarsadia, in the same call

"I am not saying the slips are dishonest. I am saying 1,366 tonnes committed and 142.6 tonnes received cannot both describe the same business, and the board has only seen the first."

Lotte Vermeiren, chat thread, 6 October 2026

"We can sign for 120 tonnes a year at ₹7,500. What my auditor will ask is where each tonne came from. If the answer is an app used by a watchman, we have a problem, and so do you."

8. The options as Shalaka frames them

Option A: repair and re-test the society channel. Ship the rebuilt flow, add a deposit forfeited for a missed pickup, pay the housekeeping contractor directly, and re-run H1 on a fresh cohort. It keeps the platform story the bridge is priced against, and Niamh’s findings suggest the earlier test may have been of the wrong design rather than the wrong idea. It also spends a quarter on a channel worth ₹5,880 a tonne.

Option B: become, openly, an industrial scrap business. Put working capital behind Jignesh, raise the Kitano quantity at renewal, run the line at 250 tonnes a month, and tell the board that Ogha processes rather than intermediates. The economics are the best on the page; the engineering team becomes support staff, the moat is a purchase price any Vapi processor can beat, and the bridge does not apply.

Option C: build the traceability product for brand owners. Sell documented tonnage at ₹7,500, convert the Panchvati Home Care letter of intent at ₹6,800 for 200 tonnes into a contract, and build chain-of-custody software an auditor will accept. It is the only option in which software is the product, and the only one whose supply rests on the channel that just failed two hypotheses.

Option D: run four minimum experiments and decide in six weeks. Reconcile the 28.4 tonnes, pay the contractor directly in one ward, price documented tonnage to a second brand owner without building anything, and have Jignesh try to sign ten moulding units on a written volume agreement. It commits least, which is either its virtue or the reason the board will read it as drift.

Exhibit 6 prices the four. Shalaka is aware her framing may itself be the problem: the options are organised around which channel to feed, when the question Niamh and Lotte keep raising is who the customer is. A fifth possibility, in none of her slides, is that the line was the mistake of January 2025 and the asset is now choosing the strategy.

Source: departmental estimates compiled by S. Amonkar, 9 October 2026. The bottom row adds the four options for comparison only; the company would fund one, or one plus D. Against ₹2.9 crore of cash, A is 16.6 per cent, B 26.9 per cent, C 15.2 per cent and D 6.2 per cent.

9. The deadline and the constraints

Four things are fixed. The Kitano contract runs to September 2027, renewal decided in January, shortfall ₹9,000 a tonne. The Narol lease runs to December 2029 and costs ₹14.4 lakh to break, so the ₹14.2 lakh of monthly fixed cost stands whatever the board decides. The bridge of ₹3.5 crore is conditional on 250 monthly active generators against 141 today. And the compliance market has its own clock: documented tonnage must be filed on the CPCB portal with records an auditor can follow, yet because housekeeping contractors and kabadiwalas are not GST-registered, every rupee paid up that chain breaks the invoice trail the EPR channel’s credibility rests on. The DPDP Act raises a further question about resident-level data in the app.

On Thursday, Shalaka must put one page in front of the board. On Monday morning she must tell twenty-three people what they are working on, and a team cannot be told to hold four hypotheses open. Pritesh wants a decision by Monday evening; Jignesh has a trip to Rajkot booked for Tuesday and a verbal commitment on 40 tonnes he intends to accept.

It was past eleven when the watchman asked whether the gate could be locked. The first page of the memo still read Scaling the Ogha Network, a title she had written in June and could no longer read without wincing, and under it, in pencil, the question she had not yet put into a sentence: whether the company had spent two years failing to serve a customer, or two years serving one it never agreed to have.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the hypotheses in Exhibit 1 were genuinely tested, and which were tested badly? What would a fair test of H1 have required?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree about September. Which is the better record of the business, what explains the 28.4-tonne gap, and whose behaviour does each number reward?
  3. Exhibit 4 shows the September cohort ahead of July and August in month one. What would you have to believe for that to be good news?
  4. Using Exhibit 5, state the smallest experiment that could falsify the EPR hypothesis in six weeks under ₹10 lakh, and what result you would accept as proof.
  5. If the app has had a signatory rather than a user, which options survive, and does the January 2025 line look like a mistake or like the only reason the company has revenue?
  6. What should Shalaka do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board on Thursday, including what she tells Aparna about the 250-generator condition and which belief she will now state as falsifiable?
case20v1-pm.lean:
Nuskha Refill Network: Who Is the Customer?

A teaching case on hypothesis-driven product development

1. Opening

On Monday, 6 October 2025, Ishita Bhonsle sat in the glass cabin of a co-working floor in Baner, Pune, with a printout of three weeks of pilot data and a board meeting eleven days away. Diwali was on 20 October, three days after that meeting.

Ishita was co-founder and chief executive of Nuskha Refill Network, a company of 31 people that helped patients with long-term conditions remember to buy their medicines. The founding plan was a patient app. The pilot had just ended with mixed numbers. By Friday, 17 October she had to tell her board what to build with the next 90 days of money, and which customer the company was really serving.

2. Company background

India has over ten crore people with diabetes, and many more with hypertension. These patients buy the same tablets every month from the same neighbourhood chemist, and many run out for days at a time. Doctors call this an adherence gap; the chemist sees a regular who did not come in.

Ishita, a former insurance product manager, started Nuskha in 2023 with Tanmay Revankar, an engineer from Bengaluru. In September 2025 they closed a ₹3.6 crore seed round led by Rekha Sundaresan of Chennai. The belief was simple: a patient who is reminded, and can reorder in one tap, will stay on therapy and pay a small monthly fee.

The market was crowded at the top. Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo Pharmacy sold medicines online and offline, and Netmeds and MedPlus ran large chains. Nuskha avoided discounts. It wanted to sit between the patient and the independent chemist, and to hold the reminder relationship, while respecting the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

3. The situation

Before the pilot, Ishita had insisted on writing the plan as hypotheses rather than features. She and Tanmay stated three beliefs, each with a number below which it would be called false. First, that a patient who is shown a QR code at the chemist's counter will install the app: at least 25 per cent would. Second, that a patient who sets a reminder will refill through it: at least 40 per cent would. Third, that a patient who refills this way will pay ₹49 a month: at least 20 per cent would.

The patient pilot ran for three weeks, from 15 September to 5 October, across 40 chemists in Pune and Nashik. Exhibit 1 shows what happened. Installs reached 20 per cent against a threshold of 25. Only a quarter of those who set a reminder refilled through it, against 40. The third hypothesis passed: a quarter of refillers paid, against the 20 per cent bar. But twenty-one payers at ₹49 produced only ₹1,029 a month.

Then came an unplanned result. Suresh Kothawade, who owns four chemist shops in Nashik, was unimpressed by the app but liked the dashboard Nuskha had built for him, a list of overdue chronic patients. Unasked, he began sending those patients a WhatsApp message from his own phone. Nine other chemists copied him. Kamil Sobczak, the data scientist in Gdansk, compared their four weeks against the four before.

Exhibit 2 gives his findings. Across ten chemists and 1,800 patients, on-time refills rose from 45 to 63 per cent. At a monthly basket of ₹850, the extra refills were worth ₹2,75,400 to the ten shops in the month, or ₹27,540 each. The team saw it from their own places. Tanmay, in Bengaluru, wanted to ship a better onboarding flow and argued that a 20 per cent install rate on a first attempt was normal. Hannah Pryce, the designer in Bristol, had watched recordings of patients at counters; most were elderly and handed the phone to the chemist's assistant to register. Her view was that the app's user was not the one paying, or even holding the phone.

4. The people

Ishita Bhonsle, Pune, chief executive. She wants to be honest with the board about the evidence, but is reluctant to discard two years of patient-side work.

Tanmay Revankar, Bengaluru, chief technology officer. He believes in the patient app and leads nine engineers on it. He fears a pivot will look like failure.

Hannah Pryce, Bristol, designer, and Kamil Sobczak, Gdansk, data scientist. Both independently conclude that the chemist is the better customer. Neither controls the roadmap.

Suresh Kothawade, Nashik, chemist and early adopter. He wants a tool that keeps patients from drifting to online pharmacies, and has said he will not pay for an app aimed at his customers.

Rekha Sundaresan, Chennai, lead investor. She wants a plan she can defend to her partners, and a reason to believe the next money will teach more than the last.

5. The cost of the next 90 days

Exhibit 3 shows what each of the three courses open to Ishita would cost over the next 90 days. The company had ₹3.6 crore in the bank and a monthly burn of ₹30 lakh, or 12 months at current spending. Exhibit 3 shows budgets additional to payroll, drawn from the same cash. The patient-app option is dearest because counter incentives are its main lever; the test-first option builds almost nothing.

6. The options

Option A: scale the patient app. Take the new onboarding flow to Mumbai, Hyderabad and Chennai, as well as Pune and Nashik, and spend on counter incentives for chemists' staff. The upside is fidelity to the original vision, and the third hypothesis did pass. The cost is ₹72 lakh, and two of three beliefs failed; scaling would multiply a funnel that loses nearly all patients before they pay.

Option B: rebuild for the chemist. Stop the patient app, build a chemist workflow with a dashboard, templates and a WhatsApp integration, and sell it at ₹1,500 a month. The upside is the evidence in Exhibit 2. The cost is ₹54 lakh and a visible pivot resting on ten self-selected shops and three payers.

Option C: test the chemist hypothesis before building. Keep the existing dashboard, send reminders from the chemist's phone using templates, and recruit 30 new chemists in Pune, Nashik and Nagpur. Charge ₹1,500 a month from day one, and fix in advance what counts as proof. The upside is that ₹16 lakh buys an answer in six weeks. The cost is slower visible progress.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the three hypotheses did the pilot reject, and which did it support? How confident can you be, given Exhibit 1?
  2. Hannah says the app's user is not its payer. Who is the customer, and how would you test it?
  3. What besides the reminders could explain the 18-point rise in Exhibit 2?
  4. Using Exhibit 3, which option would you recommend, and what result would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

Hypothesis-driven development asks a team to write each belief as a claim that can be wrong, to set a threshold before the test, and to run the smallest experiment that could embarrass the claim. Nuskha did the first two well, which is why Ishita can say that two of her beliefs failed.

A well-reasoned answer separates three things the pilot mixes together. The problem, late refills, is real: Exhibit 2 shows 55 per cent of patients refilling late in the baseline month. The first solution, a patient app, fell below its bars. The second, chemist-led reminders, appeared by accident and is not yet proven, since the ten shops chose themselves and only three paid.

One defensible path is Option C, with Option B as the expected destination. Run the paid, no-build test with 30 fresh chemists for six weeks, and set the proof bar in advance, for example that at least 18 of them pay ₹1,500 and that their on-time refill rate rises by at least 10 percentage points over a matched baseline. If the bar is met, commit the ₹54 lakh of Option B with a much stronger case. If it is missed, Nuskha has spent ₹16 lakh rather than ₹72 lakh to learn the chemist hypothesis was wrong. Freeze, but keep, the patient app.

Ishita should tell Tanmay's engineers they are serving a different customer, not that their work failed.
exp40v2-pm.ai.shift:
How AI is reshaping the PM role

1. Two decisions, twenty days apart

On Monday 3 August 2026, Meenal Deshpande, vice-president of product at Udyot Credit Systems, received a one-page note from her chief executive, Sridhar Venkataraman. Udyot, founded in Chennai in 2017, sells loan-origination and collections software to 38 non-banking financial companies and 6 banks; revenue to March 2026 was ₹214 crore. Sridhar noted that Udyot's 54 engineers had used AI coding assistants since January, that requirement documents were now drafted by a model in minutes, and that he intended to take the product organisation from 11 product managers to 8 before the board met on 10 September, 38 days later. Fully loaded a Udyot PM costs ₹44 lakh a year; the 11 cost ₹4.84 crore, 2.26 per cent of revenue. Three fewer would save ₹1.32 crore, 0.62 per cent.

Meenal had instrumented the question before it was asked. From Monday 6 April to Monday 29 June 2026, twelve weeks, all 11 PMs logged their work against a fixed task list, recording separately the hours spent producing output, reviewing machine output, and redoing output that failed review. Rui Almeida, her engineering director in Lisbon, had separately forecast that Udyot could now ship 14 customer-visible releases a quarter against the 9 it managed in FY2026.

Twenty days before that board meeting, on Friday 21 August, Hiren Barot faced the inverse. Hiren runs product at Vihang Travel Network, an Ahmedabad consumer travel app with 1.9 crore monthly active users, gross bookings of ₹1,180 crore in FY2026 and net revenue of ₹96 crore, a take rate of 8.14 per cent. Vihang had budget for ten hires, and its founder, Nupur Chaturvedi, wanted all ten to be “product engineers” who write their own briefs with model assistance, rather than the 3 PMs and 7 engineers Hiren had requested. Vihang's 7 PMs cost ₹2.52 crore at ₹36 lakh each, 2.63 per cent of net revenue; an engineer costs ₹32 lakh. Nupur's plan was cheaper by ₹12 lakh, 3.6 per cent of Hiren's ₹3.32 crore — a rounding error, which told Hiren the argument was not about money.

Both turn on one question: which parts of the job does AI eliminate, which does it amplify, and which become more valuable because the rest got cheap?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Start from the job as defined, because AI's effect can only be measured against it. A product manager is accountable for deciding what a team builds and why, for a named set of customers, and for making the decision stick across engineering, design, sales and the executive. That accountability is discharged through a dozen recurring activities, and the serious move is to stop reasoning about the bundle and reason about the activities.

Each sorts into one of three classes. Eliminated activities are those where a model produces an acceptable artefact and the human hours largely vanish. Amplified activities are those where the model produces but a person frames the question and judges the answer, so the same hours buy more. Elevated activities the model does not perform at all, and they become the binding constraint once everything else gets cheap.

The lineage is the task-based account of automation in labour economics, which displaced an occupation-based account in the 2000s; the embarrassment it solved was that technologies meant to destroy occupations instead rearranged them. Applied here, it predicts that the bundle shrinks unevenly and that what remains is the part requiring accountability under uncertainty — which is where the teaching discipline of asking “what is the job?” before asking what the tools do also lands.

Four positions compete, and what separates them is the proposition each will sign. The task-substitution school signs “the bundle shrinks unevenly and the eliminated share is large” but refuses “headcount therefore falls proportionally,” because it says nothing about demand. The complementarity school signs “cheaper building raises the marginal value of deciding, so decision capacity per engineer must rise” but refuses “every PM job is safe.” The disintermediation school, which Nupur holds, signs “the role was partly an artefact of an expensive translation step between intent and code, and that step is collapsing” but refuses “product decisions stop needing an owner.” The measurement-sceptic school signs only “savings are self-reported, review cost is under-counted, and in regulated domains net savings may be near zero.” Meenal's log was built to test the fourth.

3. Mechanics: the delegation-yield calculation

Experts run a four-parameter calculation per activity, and the two usually left implicit decide it. Let B be baseline human hours a week; d the delegable fraction, the share of those hours whose production can be handed to a model at all; r the review ratio, review hours per delegated hour; f the rework fraction, the share of delegated output that fails review and is produced by hand anyway.

Delegated hours are D = B × d; hours saved are D × (1 − r − f), the bracket being the delegation yield, y; hours after delegation are B − D + Dr + Df. Three consequences are routinely missed. Yield, not delegable fraction, is what matters: a task can be 90 per cent delegable and save nothing. When r + f exceeds 1 the delegation loses money, the ordinary condition for first attempts in an unfamiliar domain. And the two have different cures: review scales with the consequence of error, rework with the quality of context given to the model.

Exhibit 1 is Meenal's log, averaged across the 11 PMs: a 44.0-hour week, 24.0 hours on six activities with delegable content and 20.0 on four with none.

Across 11 PMs the saving is 112.53 hours a week, at 44 hours 2.5575 PM-equivalents. Sridhar asked for 3: not a foolish instinct, but 17 per cent too aggressive, and the gap is the argument. To free three full roles, blended yield would have to rise from 70.07 to 82.19 per cent, meaning review plus rework falling from 29.93 per cent of delegated hours to 17.81 per cent. 4. The second-order effect, as testable claims

The supply calculation is the easy half, and stopping there is the commonest senior error here. The hard half is that elevated activities are not merely un-automatable; they are demanded in proportion to what gets built. Udyot's 11 PMs spent 20.0 elevated hours a week each, which over a 13-week quarter is 20.0 × 13 × 11 = 2,860 hours, or 317.78 decision-hours per release against 9 releases. Meenal chose to defend that number, which is itself a judgement: she was asserting that Udyot's historical release quality was adequate and its decision intensity therefore roughly right.

Now redeploy. If every freed hour goes into elevated work, each PM has 20.00 + 10.23 = 30.23 elevated hours a week, 392.99 a quarter, so eleven supply 4,322.89 decision-hours. At Rui's 14 releases that is 308.78 per release, 2.83 per cent below the historical 317.78 — a whole team's savings absorbed almost exactly by a 55.6 per cent rise in throughput, with no headcount change. At 8 PMs it is 3,143.92 hours, 224.57 per release, 29.33 per cent below history: not the same product shipped faster, but half again as much with each decision given 70.7 per cent of its former scrutiny.

Three testable claims follow, each applicable to both companies. One: the eliminated share is large only where the cost of error is low — true at Udyot for status notes, false for regulatory scanning, where a missed Reserve Bank of India circular reaches 44 regulated customers. Two: freed hours convert into headcount only in units of a whole role; 10.23 hours across 11 people releases two PMs only by reassigning product lines, which costs context. Three: decision demand scales with throughput unless the market cannot absorb the output. Udyot's 44 enterprise customers schedule upgrades quarterly and will not absorb 14 releases; Vihang's 1.9 crore users absorb experiments continuously. For Udyot, Exhibit 3 is therefore partly misleading, and Meenal said so in writing.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Vihang supplies the consumer and two-sided case. Hiren's log over the same twelve weeks covered 7 PMs on a 42.0-hour week: 20.0 hours delegable, 22.0 elevated — heavier than Udyot's, because consumer work spends hours on research and design judgement no model attends.

The aggregate is almost identical to Udyot's — 9.85 hours is 23.45 per cent of a 42-hour week against 23.25 per cent, and across 7 PMs 68.95 hours, 1.64 PM-equivalents — but the structural consequence is opposite. Vihang ran 22 experiments a quarter, decided inside 22 × 13 × 7 = 2,002 elevated hours, exactly 91.00 per experiment; Satyen Pillai, the engineering head, projected 34. With redeployment each PM supplies 31.85 × 13 = 414.05 hours. Hiren's 10 PMs yield 4,140.50 hours, 121.78 per experiment, 33.8 per cent above history; Nupur's 7 yield 2,898.35 hours, 85.25 per experiment, 6.3 per cent below. Six per cent is not a catastrophe, and Hiren could not honestly call it one. Nupur's steelman is stronger: if each of the 10 new product engineers gives 6 hours a week to elevated work, the pool becomes 2,898.35 + 780.00 = 3,678.35 hours, 108.19 per experiment, 18.9 per cent above history — at a cost of 780 of 5,460 engineer-hours a quarter, 14.29 per cent of their capacity.

At the seams the picture degrades in ways no table shows. In multi-product companies like Udyot, where 11 PMs cover 4 product lines, savings are stranded: Farhan Qureshi's co-lending PM cannot lend 0.9 freed hours to collections. In regulated products the review ratio is set by someone else: an audit trail does not care about yield. In AI-native products a new activity appears: at Ukti Support Labs, a Hyderabad firm whose product answers customer tickets, Devika Menon found her PMs curating evaluation sets for 6.50 hours a week, 15.1 per cent of a 43-hour week, on work that did not exist in 2024. Mature companies claim they redeploy freed hours into discovery; most let them absorb a larger backlog, which is why this analysis needs a second log later.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Yield, not delegable share, is the decision variable. The tell is a deck quoting “60 per cent of PM work is automatable.” At Udyot it is correct — 14.60 of 24.00 delegable hours — and overstates the saving by 43 per cent, since the true figure is 10.23.

Rework and review must be measured apart, because they have different cures. High review with low rework means output usually right but unverifiable: a traceability problem. High rework means the model was asked the wrong question or starved of context — Udyot's analysis row, at r 0.20 and f 0.15, is the second case: the PMs withheld the data dictionary. A uniform “checking tax” hides both.

Fluency is uncorrelated with correctness. A synthesis of 400 tickets invents a theme as confidently as it reports one. The tell is a PM who cannot trace a claim to a ticket in thirty seconds; the consequence is Exhibit 1's lowest yield, 0.60.

Savings arrive in fractions, redundancies in whole numbers. 10.23 hours across 11 people is 2.56 roles, and the 0.56 is unrecoverable without reorganising ownership. The expert converts it into a hiring pause.

The elevated set is a residual, not a sanctuary. It is defined by what today's tools cannot do — a claim about 2026, not about the nature of the work. The tell is a PM who says judgement cannot be automated without naming which judgement. Design judgement, Vihang's 5.00 hours, is the most exposed line.

Demand is endogenous. Treating release count as fixed while supply gets cheaper is the error behind Sridhar's note, and the tell is a capacity plan whose output figure equals last year's. At 14 releases Udyot needs 11.32 PMs, not 8.

Self-reported logs flatter the tools. Meenal audited 30 per cent of entries against calendars, pull requests and document histories, and found logged review time understated by about a fifth; Exhibit 1 carries the audited values. Ask how a baseline was produced.

The method sizes time, not value. Nothing in Exhibit 1 says whether Udyot builds the right things; a team could reach 0.90 yield and ship 14 excellent releases nobody wanted. The tell is an AI-productivity dashboard with no measure of decision quality.

7. Variation by product type and stage

In consumer products the elevated work is behavioural and aesthetic, and the model's contribution is volume: twenty variants raise rather than lower the weight of choosing one. The usual claim that enterprise work carries the larger elevated share is false here — Udyot's elevated hours are 20.0 of 44.0, 45.5 per cent, against Vihang's 22.0 of 42.0, 52.4 per cent. They differ in composition: Udyot's elevated hours are customer and stakeholder negotiation, Vihang's research and taste. In marketplaces every change lands on two populations at once, and model-drafted specs optimise the side whose data is richer; in hardware irreversibility widens the elevated set; in AI products Ukti's eval curation is a new elevated activity, not a reshaped old one.

By stage the differences are real but smaller than claimed. A seed-stage company with two PMs gains most proportionally from elimination and has no slack to cut; one of Vihang's size faces the composition question because it is hiring; one of Udyot's size has coordination hours that exist for control rather than inefficiency, so removing them without redesigning the control leaves the control unperformed. Yield itself barely varies by stage, being a property of the task and the tool.

8. Three worked outcomes, including one failure

Udyot, the supply side. 112.53 hours freed a week, 2.56 PM-equivalents against an ask of 3 — 2.01 under the pessimistic review assumption, 2.92 under the optimistic. No scenario supports 3 while holding 317.78 decision-hours per release.

Vihang, the composition side. 68.95 hours freed, 1.64 PM-equivalents, and a per-experiment decision budget 6.3 per cent below history under Nupur's plan, 33.8 per cent above under Hiren's. The arithmetic narrows the disagreement to whether product engineers will really spend 6 hours a week on elevated work when their reviews measure shipping.

Trinayan Device Industries, the failure. Trinayan, a Coimbatore maker of networked security cameras, cut its product team from 6 PMs to 3 on Monday 12 January 2026, on a gross-savings argument like Sridhar's. At ₹41 lakh fully loaded, three roles saved ₹123 lakh a year, and the board counted the saving from 1 January, so the nine months to 30 September 2026 are pro-rated as ₹123 × 9 ÷ 12 = ₹92.25 lakh. Balaji Ramanathan's remaining team shipped 19 features in the first half of FY2027 against 11 in the comparable half of FY2026, a rise of 72.7 per cent; 6 of the 19, 31.6 per cent, were withdrawn within 90 days. Engineering logged 1,480 hours of rework at a blended ₹2,600 an hour, ₹38.48 lakh, and one firmware release was rolled back across 24,000 devices at ₹310 each, ₹74.40 lakh. Identified cost ₹112.88 lakh against ₹92.25 lakh saved: a net loss of ₹20.63 lakh before warranty exposure nobody could price. Trinayan took back 2 PMs at ₹49 lakh each, a 19.5 per cent premium because the market had repriced the role, and named a release-decision owner able to refuse a shippable build. Balaji's account is that the cut was not the error; the error was cutting decision capacity while raising the build rate, measuring neither.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Quoting gross savings. Early sign: a plan citing 60.83 per cent with no review line. Diagnostic: “what is the yield, and who measured the review hours?” Caught late, it produces Trinayan's loss.

Holding demand constant. Early sign: next year's release target equals this year's while engineering velocity is up 55.6 per cent. Diagnostic: “decision-hours per release, before and after?” Caught late, quality failures surface two quarters on, when the causal link is deniable.

Letting freed hours vanish. Early sign: time saved is reported but no activity's hours rose. Diagnostic: re-run the log and compare elevated hours, not total hours. The organisation has banked a gain it cannot locate or defend.

Treating an artefact as a decision. Early sign: immaculate requirement documents for features no customer named. Diagnostic: “which customer sentence does line one answer?” Caught late, it appears as Trinayan's 31.6 per cent withdrawal rate.

Hollowing the junior rung. Early sign: the eliminated tasks are exactly the apprenticeship tasks and no associate PM has been hired in a year. Diagnostic: “where does our next senior PM come from?” The cost arrives beyond the planning horizon, which is why it is discounted.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Does the elevated set hold? The complementarity position says the residual is irreducible, because accountability cannot be delegated to a system that cannot be held responsible, its evidence is that review ratios have not fallen as fast as generation quality has risen. The disintermediation position says the residual is merely the current frontier, citing tasks elevated in 2023 and delegable in 2026, competitive scanning among them. It would be wrong if review ratios in high-consequence domains stayed flat for years; complementarity would be wrong if a model made better prioritisation calls on the same evidence, judged on realised outcomes.

Does decision demand scale with throughput? Exhibit 3 assumes it does. The opposing view is that throughput is capped by market absorption, and Udyot is its best evidence: 44 enterprise customers will not take 14 releases a quarter however fast they are built. If absorption binds, the freed hours are genuinely free and Sridhar is closer to right. The disagreement is empirical, and Meenal's board paper conceded it.

Is the PM role the right container? Nupur's position is not that product decisions vanish but that bundling them with document production was an efficiency of the era when documents were expensive. If documents are nearly free the bundle may be wrong, and the decisions may sit better with a senior engineer who owns the outcome. Her evidence is that Vihang's best-performing surface in FY2026 ran seven months without a PM. She would be wrong if quality there depended on an unusually product-minded engineer rather than on the structure.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can recite the three classes. Someone who has internalised it instruments before the question arrives, because a twelve-week log cannot be produced in 38 days; quotes yield, not automation potential; sets a demand number beside every supply number; and states the assumption that would overturn their own conclusion — for Meenal, that absorption rather than engineering binds — before an opponent does.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 10 September Meenal recommended against cutting 3 roles and against cutting none. She proposed holding 10 PMs by not filling the next departure, banking 1 of the 2.56 PM-equivalents, redeploying the rest into customer and prioritisation hours, and capping FY2027 at 12 releases a quarter rather than 14: at 12, ten PMs supply 3,929.90 hours, 327.49 per release, 3.1 per cent above the historical 317.78. She set a second twelve-week log for January, with the review ratio as the number to watch. Hiren accepted 2 PMs rather than 3 and 8 product engineers rather than 7, and asked Nupur to agree in advance that engineers' elevated hours be scheduled and logged, so the 6-hour assumption becomes a measurement rather than a hope.

Questions. First: if Udyot's blended yield reached 0.8219, freeing exactly 3 PM-equivalents, would you cut 3 roles, and what would you require of the remaining 8? Second: Vihang's two plans differ by ₹12 lakh and by 36.53 decision-hours per experiment; which should the board weigh more heavily, and what evidence would change that ranking? Third: whose interest is served by measuring gross savings rather than yield, and what would you change in Udyot's reporting so the honest number is the easy one to produce?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does is the baseline every figure here is measured against. AI-native teams and The AI-era PM skillset take up what the elevated hours should hold once freed; AI tools in the PM workflow is where review and rework ratios actually fall. Dividing work between PMs, engineers and agents is Nupur's argument taken seriously, and When building gets cheap and deciding does not is Exhibit 3 generalised. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't explains the 0.60 synthesis yield; Tokens and tokenisation prices a review ratio. For the history behind disintermediation: PM myths vs reality, Origins of product management, PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder. For why the two firms diverged: PM archetypes, How the PM job changes by company stage, The end-to-end product lifecycle.
case20v1-pm.ai.shift:
Kasturi Textile Exchange: The Backlog That Builds Itself

A teaching case on how AI reshapes the product manager's job

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Kanchan Subramaniam sat in a corner of the Bengaluru office of Kasturi Textile Exchange with two numbers on her screen that she could not reconcile. In the first half of the financial year, her product team had shipped 61 features, nearly three times the 22 it had shipped a year earlier. Over the same period, the platform's gross merchandise value had grown by barely five per cent.

Kanchan was Head of Product. By Friday, 23 October, she owed the founder-CEO a plan for how the product organisation of four product managers, nineteen engineers, two designers and one analyst would work through the festive quarter and into FY27's second half. Diwali fell on 8 November.

2. Company background

Kasturi Textile Exchange is a business-to-business marketplace that connects roughly 1,850 mills, traders and garment makers, concentrated in Surat, Tiruppur and Ludhiana, with about 38,000 small retailers in 410 towns. A retailer in Nashik or Guwahati can browse fabric and ready-made lots, compare prices, place an order and track dispatch on one app, with GST invoices generated automatically. In FY26 the platform processed ₹598 crore of orders and kept a little over three per cent as net revenue, about ₹18.5 crore.

Kailash Agrawal, whose family traded fabric in Surat, founded it in 2017. It competes with Udaan for small-retailer orders, with the wholesale arms of Flipkart and Meesho for the lower end, and, more quietly, with the WhatsApp groups and phone calls through which most textile trade in India still happens. Kasturi's advantage is trust: sellers are verified and payments are held until delivery.

Product work had always been constrained by engineering capacity. A good product manager at Kasturi was, in practice, a good rationer.

3. The situation

That constraint ended faster than anyone planned. In October 2025, Latha Rangarajan's squad in Pune began using AI coding agents on a pilot basis. By 1 January 2026 every squad used them (Exhibit 3 places these dates against the decision calendar). Exhibit 1 shows what the team's own time sheets recorded for a typical mid-sized feature: 33 person-days before the agents, 10 in the second quarter of FY27, a fall of 70 per cent. At a blended loaded cost of ₹9,000 per person-day, a feature that cost ₹2.97 lakh now cost ₹0.90 lakh.

Exhibit 1: Person-days to ship a typical mid-sized feature

Source: Kasturi engineering time sheets; blended loaded cost assumed uniform across roles.

The shipping rate followed the cost. But Exhibit 2 shows that adoption did not. Before the agents, 40.9 per cent of shipped features (9 of 22) carried a target agreed in advance; now 23.0 per cent (14 of 61) did. Six of 22 features, 27.3 per cent, were still used by a fifth of active buyers sixty days after launch. Eight of 61, 13.1 per cent, had passed it by 30 September, but features shipped after mid-August had not yet had sixty days, so this is a floor that will rise, not a settled like-for-like rate. On the counts so far, unused work at the typical size in Exhibit 1 cost about ₹47.52 lakh in H1 FY26 and ₹47.70 lakh in H1 FY27. Building was cheaper, yet the waste was no smaller; it was spread across more features, each needing support and a place in the app.

Kate Dunstan, the product analyst in Melbourne, who had compiled these figures, put it plainly in her note: the agents had removed the bottleneck that used to force the team to choose.

Exhibit 4 shows what had happened to the product managers' own week. Writing specifications had fallen from 14 hours to 5, but 10 new hours went to reviewing what the agents had built, and 12 hours, up from 7, went to prioritisation arguments. The one activity Kanchan thought most valuable, conversations with retailers and mills, had slipped from 4 hours a week per PM to 3.

4. The people

Kailash Agrawal, founder and CEO, in Surat, believes the company has finally been freed. The backlog stands at 112 items. He wants all of them shipped before Diwali and sees product managers as a queue.

Latha Rangarajan, engineering manager in Pune, is proud of her squads' speed and notes that her engineers now supervise agents more than they write code. She wants clear instructions and fewer reversals mid-build.

Kiran Mehendale, senior PM for sourcing in Coimbatore, is closest to the Tiruppur garment makers. Last month three of them told her their real problem was late payment, not the catalogue filters the backlog proposed. She fears her role is shrinking to an approver of machine output.

Lukasz Wrobel, a staff engineer in Warsaw who set up the agent tooling, thinks the PM role may need to change rather than disappear. His team's best experiments began with a PM who could state, in two sentences, what a buyer could not do today. He is willing to build a review gate if someone decides what it should enforce.

5. The options

Option A: Ship the backlog. Keep the four PMs as specification writers and let the agents clear all 112 requests. The upside is a satisfied Surat. The cost is that, at the 13.1 per cent rate measured so far, about 97 of those 112 items would go unused, and still most even if the final rate proves higher, and Kiran's retailer conversations would shrink further.

Option B: Shrink the PM function. Cut from four PMs to two, and let engineers and the founder decide directly, using the agents to prototype. At an average cost of ₹48 lakh a year per PM, this saves ₹96 lakh annually. The cost is that nobody would own the question of which problem deserves the next build, which is the very gap Exhibit 2 exposes.

Option C: Reposition the PMs around the decision. Keep all four, and move them from writing specifications to gatekeeping evidence. Any item above five person-days would need a one-page statement of the buyer problem, evidence from at least three conversations and a measurable target. Each PM would spend at least nine hours a week with buyers and sellers (36 hours across the four, against 12 now). Live experiments would be capped at 12. This would cost an extra ₹14 lakh a year for buyer visits and interview incentives, and it would slow the headline feature count. Kanchan estimates 30 features in H2 rather than 61, with a target use rate of 30 per cent: 9 used and 21 unused, costing ₹18.90 lakh at the Exhibit 1 size, against up to ₹47.70 lakh on the counts so far. Both projections are her assumptions.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what has AI eliminated in the product manager's job at Kasturi, and what has it left untouched?
  2. Exhibit 4 shows hours moving rather than vanishing. Which of the seven activities has been amplified, and which has become more important?
  3. Why did cheaper building not improve the use rate? What did the old queue do that nobody had noticed?
  4. Compare the three options on cost, risk and what each assumes about where the scarce contribution now lies. Which would you take to Kailash, and what would you ask him to accept?

7. A note for the learner

This case frames the topic as a question of what the job is for. AI automated the writing of specifications and a large share of building. It amplified anyone able to prototype, review and test quickly. What became more important was deciding which problem deserved building and knowing, from evidence, whether it worked. Kasturi's own figures show the point: the cost of an unused feature fell, yet the cost of unused work did not, because the old queue had been quietly doing the PM's rationing for them.

One defensible path is Option C, introduced in stages. Kanchan would run the gate for the festive quarter, protect the PMs' buyer hours first, and tell Kailash that a handful of his Surat requests would wait. She would not take Option A, because it multiplies the very thing Exhibit 2 shows failing. She would also avoid Option B, because it removes the capability the company now lacks and its ₹96 lakh annual saving is small beside the cost of building the wrong things. She should set two tests for January: the share of shipped features with a target above 80 per cent, and a 60-day use rate of at least 30 per cent. If the second test is missed, the gate has failed and Option C needs rethinking rather than abandoning.

The lesson is that when building is cheap, the product manager's scarce contribution is a defensible answer to why this, why now and for whom.
exp20v2-pm.ai.shift:
How AI is reshaping the PM role

1. The memo and the clock

On Tuesday 14 July 2026, Kavita Iyer, head of product at Jivika Rozgar Network, opened a message from her chief executive, Anand Kulkarni. Jivika, a Pune-based marketplace that matches blue-collar workers with small employers, had reached revenue of ₹86 crore in the year to March 2026. It competed with larger platforms such as Apna and WorkIndia, and its board would meet on 28 July, fourteen days away. Anand's message was short: engineers now shipped with AI coding assistants, product requirement documents could be drafted in minutes, and he wanted the product team cut from six product managers (PMs) to four. At ₹38 lakh a year fully loaded per PM, two fewer people saved ₹76 lakh, about 0.88 per cent of revenue.

Kavita did not dismiss the idea. Between 11 May and 3 July, eight weeks, all six of her PMs had logged how they spent their time while using AI tools on a defined set of tasks. Tomasz Wrona, a staff engineer in Krakow, had separately told her that his team could now build a first version of a feature in days, not weeks. If she defended all six jobs on instinct, she would lose the argument and perhaps the credibility of the function. If she conceded two jobs on instinct, Jivika might ship eighteen features a quarter with nobody sure which twelve mattered. This page follows the question she faced: which parts of a PM's job does AI automate, which does it amplify, and which become more valuable?

2. The idea

A product manager is the person accountable for deciding what a team builds and why, for a defined set of customers. That job is a bundle of activities, and the useful way to ask about AI is to unbundle it. Each activity can be sorted into one of three groups. Eliminated activities are those where AI produces an acceptable result with little human effort, so the hours largely vanish. Amplified activities are those where AI does the heavy lifting but a person still frames the work and judges the result, so the same hours buy more. Elevated activities are those AI does not touch, but which become the binding constraint once everything else gets cheaper.

The framing descends from older thinking about automation in economics, in which technology substitutes for tasks rather than for whole occupations. Teaching programmes now apply it on day one of product courses by asking "what is the job?" before asking what the tools do; the habit is to start from a customer problem, not a backlog. Kavita's sentence for the board was this: "AI makes producing things cheap, so the scarce part of our work is deciding what is worth producing, and that is the part we cannot cut."

3. How it works, step by step

The method has five steps, and practitioners often leave the third and fourth implicit. First, list the activities that make up a typical week, with hours, so the baseline sums to the real working week. Second, classify each as routine production (writing, summarising, querying), or judgement and relationship work (choosing, persuading, listening). Third, estimate for each routine activity the fraction of time AI saves. This must come from measurement, not vendor claims, which is why Kavita's eight-week log mattered.

Fourth, and most often forgotten, add the cost of checking. An AI draft is not finished work. A PM must read it, test it against what she knows of the customer, and correct what is plausible but wrong. That checking is new work created by the tool. Fifth, compare the net hours freed with the demand on the team, remembering that demand itself changes when building becomes cheaper. The result is a capacity picture, not a verdict on any individual.

4. A worked example, line by line

Kavita's log, averaged across six PMs, produced the baseline in Exhibit 1. A PM's working week was 45 hours. Five activities were routine and AI-assisted; three were not.

Drafting specs and PRDsEliminated (first drafts)7.050%3.53.5
Status notes, release notes, minutesEliminated6.070%4.21.8
Synthesising tickets and interviewsAmplified5.060%3.02.0
Analysis and dashboardsAmplified4.050%2.02.0
AdministrationEliminated3.050%1.51.5
