Exhibit 1. Hours per PM per week, exact values, pilot average 11 May to 3 July 2026. Checking is set at 20 per cent of the 25.0 hours in the five routine rows (7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3), which is 5.0 hours. Net saving is 14.2 minus 5.0, or 9.2 hours.

Read the exhibit from the left column. Specs fall from 7.0 to 3.5 hours because half the typing disappears. Status work falls furthest, by 70 per cent, because it is mostly reformatting. Across the five routine rows, AI saved 14.2 of 25.0 hours, or 56.8 per cent, which is why Anand's instinct was not foolish. But checking costs 5.0 hours, so the net saving is 9.2 hours, 20.4 per cent of a 45-hour week. Across six PMs that is 55.2 hours, or 1.23 PMs' worth of time (55.2 divided by 45).

Now the demand test. Before AI the team needed 6 × 45 = 270 hours. After the net saving it needs 270 minus 55.2, or 214.8 hours. Five PMs supply 225 hours, so load would be 95.5 per cent; four PMs supply 180, so load would be 119.3 per cent. Two cuts require 90 hours of savings; the measurement offers 55.2.

Second pass. Change one input: suppose checking costs 40 per cent of the routine hours, not 20. Checking becomes 10.0 hours, net saving falls to 14.2 minus 10.0, or 4.2 hours, and across six PMs to 25.2 hours. Demand becomes 244.8 hours. Five PMs run at 108.8 per cent of capacity; four at 136.0 per cent. One assumption, how much to trust the machine, swings the answer from "one role is spare" to "none is."

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Tasks are not jobs

AI acts on tasks. Whether a task disappears matters less than whether the hours it frees can be converted into a smaller team. In Exhibit 1 the freed hours are scattered across five activities, at 1.5 to 4.2 hours each per PM per week, and fractions of a week do not make a redundancy.

Cheaper building raises the demand for deciding

Tomasz's team could move from twelve features a quarter to eighteen, an increase of 50 per cent. With six PMs that is three features each, up from two; with four PMs, 4.5 each. Every feature still needs a customer problem, a priority and an owner.

Checking is a skill, not a tax

The 20 per cent assumption is a measurement, not a law. It depends on the domain, the quality of the context given to the tool and the cost of a wrong answer. Where an error would reach a worker's wages, checking cost rises sharply.

Fluent is not correct

AI output reads equally confidently whether it is right or wrong. A synthesis of ticket themes can invent a theme. The test is whether the PM can trace each claim back to a ticket or a conversation.

Elevated does not mean safe

Stakeholder alignment and customer conversations are not touched by the tools today, but a PM who stops doing them well will find the tools make her visible deficiency more, not less, expensive.

Self-reported hours are noisy

Pilot logs flatter tools, since people like to report success. Kavita sampled 30 per cent of entries against calendars and pull requests. Ask how the baseline was measured before relying on it.

The edge of the method

The table says nothing about which features to build, whether the customer problem is real, or how quality of decisions changes. It sizes time, not value. Treat it as a floor for a conversation.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the elevated work is taste and behaviour: knowing why a user abandons a screen. AI floods the team with variants, and the PM's decision about which to ship, and what to measure, grows in weight. In B2B products, stakeholder and account work dominates, so the elevated share is larger and the savings smaller; a PM spends a day each week with customers' procurement teams, which no assistant attends. In a marketplace such as Jivika, every change affects two sides at once. A spec written by a machine often optimises one side, and the PM's value is noticing the other side's reaction before launch.

By stage, an early-stage company with one or two PMs gains most from elimination, because the founder-PM drowns in documents, but has no slack to cut. A large company has process layers, so the eliminated hours are real, though many sit in coordination that exists for reasons of control. Cutting there requires redesigning the process, not removing a headcount.

7. Common mistakes

Subtracting gross savings. Symptom: a headcount plan quoting "56.8 per cent time saved". Misunderstanding: ignoring the checking cost. Diagnostic: ask for the net figure, 9.2 of 45 hours, and who verified the output.

Treating a spec as a decision. Symptom: beautifully formatted PRDs for features nobody requested. Misunderstanding: confusing output with judgement. Diagnostic: ask for the customer evidence behind the first line.

Holding demand constant. Symptom: capacity plans with the same feature count as last year. Misunderstanding: assuming cheaper building yields the same amount of building. Diagnostic: compare features per PM before and after; 2 versus 3 or 4.5 shows the pressure.

Starting from the tool. Symptom: a roadmap titled "AI initiatives". Misunderstanding: starting from a backlog rather than a customer problem. Diagnostic: ask which customer sentence each item answers.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Kavita's decision opens with the table, not with a defence. It shows gross and net savings, tests a pessimistic checking cost, expresses load as a percentage of capacity and sets the demand forecast beside it. It names which hours are redeployed, for instance from status writing into customer conversations, and by how much. It states what would change the conclusion, such as checking cost falling below 20 per cent after three more months. A board reading it can disagree with an assumption, but cannot say it was hidden.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Kavita told the board on 28 July that she would not cut two roles. Net savings of 55.2 hours covered one role's 45 hours with 10.2 to spare, at the 20 per cent checking cost, and none at 40 per cent. She proposed leaving one vacancy unfilled when a PM left, which kept load near 95.5 per cent in the base case and 108.8 per cent in the pessimistic one, and moving the freed hours into customer conversations. She also set a review in January, with checking cost as the number to watch. Her reasoning was that a 50 per cent rise in features was a bigger risk to Jivika than a ₹38 lakh saving was an opportunity.

To go further, study how teams divide work between PMs, engineers and agents, then how discovery changes when synthesis is cheap but evidence is not, and finally the vocabulary of tokens, since the cost of the tools is metered in them.

Questions to sit with. First: if checking cost were 0 per cent, would you cut two roles, and what would you still need the remaining PMs to do? Second: which of your own weekly hours would you move to the elevated group, and what evidence would convince a sceptic you are doing it well?
case40v1-pm.ai.shift:
Taalmel Ticketing Network: Everyone Can Ship Now

A case on what a product manager is for when building stops being the hard part

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At a quarter to eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Shalini Thakurdesai sat on the floor of her flat in Bengaluru's Cooke Town with six printed exhibits around her and a board paper due on Friday. As Chief Product Officer of Taalmel Ticketing Network, she was trying to decide whether her own function should be half its size, twice its size, or something nobody in the company had built before.

The exhibits did not agree. In the six months to 30 September 2026, Taalmel shipped 278 changes against 48 a year earlier. Only 58 came from her product squads; the rest were built by the organiser-success team in Pune, the growth-marketing team two floors below her, the venue-operations desk in Gurugram and the platform guild — none of which reported to her. All of them now shipped code, because AI coding agents let a payout analyst with a fortnight's training put a working screen in front of 4,406 organisers.

Gross ticket value had grown 41.0 per cent in the half; conversion from session to paid order had fallen from 4.20 to 3.39 per cent; incidents had cost ₹44.8 lakh, one claim disputed and one exposure her risk head would not price. On Monday morning the founder expected a product operating model at the leadership offsite; on Thursday 22 October the board would vote on it.

2. The company, and the decision of 2021

Taalmel was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by Bhupesh Raikwar, who had ticketed Pune college festivals with a spreadsheet and a payment link. For four years it was a thin layer over comedy rooms, Sunday gigs and two Kochi theatres.

The decision that shaped everything since was taken in March 2021. To win stadium business, Taalmel built its own seat-inventory and on-sale transaction core rather than licence one, because nothing then available in India could hold a queue of four lakh concurrent buyers against a single seat map at the instant an on-sale opened. The build took fourteen months and most of a funding round. On its strength Taalmel signed five-year exclusive contracts with venue operators in Ahmedabad and Navi Mumbai, carrying 99.95 per cent monthly uptime and a penalty of ₹1.5 lakh for every minute of degradation inside a published on-sale window. They expire on 31 March 2027; renewal talks open on 1 November 2026.

The core is thus both moat and locked room: the one surface nobody outside two senior platform squads may ship to — a rule written in 2021 for engineering reasons that has become the de facto boundary of Shalini's authority.

In FY26 Taalmel processed 22,40,000 paid orders at a blended average order value of ₹1,436: gross ticket value ₹321.66 crore, net revenue at a 7.0 per cent take ₹22.52 crore, loss after tax ₹26.8 crore.

3. The industry

Indian live events barely existed at scale in 2019 and now sell out stadiums. BookMyShow remains the default verb for buying a ticket; District, Zomato's events arm, arrived with a food-delivery app's distribution; Paytm Insider owns a particular festival audience. Taalmel's claim against them is operational: its on-sales do not fall over, and organisers get their money and their data faster.

Three forces press on the product. NPCI's UPI Autopay and the RBI's card-on-file tokenisation rules govern how fast a buyer clears checkout, so every change to that path is regulated territory. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes a buyer's phone number something a company must have a recorded consent basis to share — which matters to a growth team that can build an audience export in an afternoon. And organisers expect GST on admission computed correctly in every state.

Seasonality is brutal: Navratri in Vadodara, Durga Puja in Kolkata, the Goa and Shillong circuits and the December–March stadium tours compress most of the year into a few on-sale mornings. A Manila pilot for regional Southeast Asian tours contributed ₹8.90 crore of the half's gross ticket value, 4.3 per cent, and gave Taalmel a second regulatory regime and a staff engineer ahead of Bengaluru's clock.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The platform guild piloted AI coding agents in November 2025; on 1 February 2026 the tooling opened to every engineer. The guild estimated a mid-sized change had gone from about nineteen person-days to five.

What nobody planned for happened on 14 April 2026, when Meher Zachariah's organiser-success team shipped a payout dashboard with no product ticket, no design review and no roadmap entry. A payout analyst and one seconded engineer built it in nine days, and it was good; organisers asked for it by name, and Shalini approved it retroactively. On 1 May Bhupesh told an all-hands that anyone who understood a customer problem could now build the answer, and declared a Build Week (Figure C). Everyone read this as a change to engineering throughput, not to the product organisation.

Four things have since turned out to be unsafe to believe.

First, conversion. On 14 July the analytics SDK was migrated, and from that date a "session" included push-notification opens the old SDK excluded, so the fall from 4.20 to 3.39 per cent (Exhibit 3) compares two denominators across a break. The stage rates unaffected by it tell a weaker but real story: selection-to-checkout fell from 35.0 to 32.5 per cent, checkout-to-paid from 60.0 to 58.0 per cent.

Second, attribution. Exhibit 2, circulated by the growth team, shows organiser success generating ₹5.17 lakh of incremental net revenue per change against central product's ₹3.69 lakh. But ₹178 lakh of its ₹486 lakh — 36.6 per cent — falls in the nine days from 26 July to 3 August, the window of a two-night Ahmedabad stadium on-sale that was also the first to run on a queueing change central product shipped on 19 July. And the attributed total, ₹1,043 lakh, is 72.2 per cent of the half's net revenue of ₹14.45 crore, which cannot be incremental in any ordinary sense.

Third, safety. The 26 July on-sale degraded for eighteen minutes under a checkout-banner experiment the growth team had shipped the previous evening; the Ahmedabad operator claims twelve of those minutes as downtime, ₹18.0 lakh, disputed. On 9 August a marketing audience export was found to carry buyer phone numbers with no recorded consent basis; counsel has billed ₹4.5 lakh and will not estimate the rest.

Fourth, and hardest to say aloud: Exhibit 6 shows where the 278 changes went. The ten largest organisers, 47.6 per cent of gross ticket value, got 142. The 4,106 in the tail — the entire growth thesis, 9.8 per cent of gross ticket value — got 19.

5. The people

Shalini Thakurdesai, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru: nine PMs, three designers, two analysts, and the roadmap discipline the company now routes around. She wants a bounded way for anyone to ship without endangering the core or the DPDP obligation. Unsaid: she doubts her function, as staffed, is worth ₹8.34 crore a year, and thinks two of her nine PMs write specifications an agent now writes better.

Bhupesh Raikwar, founder and CEO, Bengaluru, calls 1 May his best decision since 2021 and cites Exhibit 2 to every investor; he needs a January Series D story that looks structural, not seasonal. Unsaid: the Ahmedabad operator's general counsel wrote to him on 31 August about the eighteen minutes. On Thursday he sits beside Nandita Agashe, the 2024 round's lead investor, who sits on three boards that have each shrunk their product function.

Meher Zachariah, Head of Organiser Success, Pune, shipped ninety-four of the half's changes. Her team ships well, she argues, because it sits with organisers all day and needs nobody to tell it what organisers want; her variable pay rides on retaining the top fifty. Unsaid: two of her four builder-analysts have offers, the work has no test coverage, and her proudest dashboard duplicated a payout file on 27 April at a cost of ₹6.2 lakh.

Sudhanshu Vaze, VP Engineering, Bengaluru, runs seventy-four engineers and is woken at two in the morning when Pune's work breaks something near the core — three times since April. He wants shipping rights tied to on-call duty. Unsaid: his squads look slow beside the distributed teams because they do the regulated, invisible work: tokenisation, GST rounding, the queue.

Ritika Dhanraj, Head of Growth Marketing, Bengaluru, owns both the uplift model behind Exhibit 2 and the SDK migration behind Exhibit 3, and treats both as settled instrumentation. Unsaid: she knew in July the session definition had changed and thought it immaterial, and the 9 August export was built on her team, with an agent, in forty minutes.

Abhijat Kurulkar, Head of Risk and Compliance, Bengaluru, wrote to the board on 6 October that he could no longer produce, on demand, a list of every system processing a buyer's phone number — "in July I could" — and wants pre-ship review of anything touching personal data or money. Unsaid: he cannot run one, being one man with one analyst.

Jomar Salcedo, staff engineer in Manila, built the agent tooling and the self-serve deploy path and coined "paved road" inside Taalmel; he would rather fund bounded safe surfaces than argue about permissions. Unsaid: the road needs seven engineers for a year, he has two, and he has an approach from elsewhere.

Inês Carvalho, Design Lead, Porto, watches the distributed teams ignore her design system — organisers now meet four date pickers — and wants design review restored as a gate. Unsaid: her team is the slowest step in any change that does come through product, and she knows it.

7. Voices

Bhupesh Raikwar, all-hands, 1 May 2026: "For nine years the answer to every good idea here was 'it's in the backlog'. That sentence is retired. Describe the problem and you can build the fix."

Meher Zachariah to Shalini, chat, 28 September: "I'm not trying to take your job. The organisers told us what they needed, we built it in nine days, it works. What would a PM have added?"

Sudhanshu Vaze, engineering review, 2 October: "Ninety-four changes and not one runbook. When that payout file duplicated, three of my people lost a Saturday. Build what you like — but carry the pager."

Ritika Dhanraj, email to Shalini, 7 October: "The dip is mix, not quality. I'd rather not open the SDK question in a board paper; it will read as if we don't know our own numbers."

Jomar Salcedo, pull-request comment, 8 October: "Everyone argues about who is allowed to ship. Nobody argues about which thing we should have shipped. Those are different arguments and we can fund only one."

8. The options as Shalini sees them

Option A: formalise the distributed model. Cut to five product managers embedded as decision partners — one each with organiser success, growth, venue operations, the core and Manila — and move outcome accountability to the teams that build. ₹720 lakh a year, ₹114 lakh below the run-rate. The risk sits in Exhibits 4 and 6: the incidents and the neglected tail are both what happens when whoever has the loudest customer builds next.

Option B: recentralise. Route every change through product review, grow to eleven product managers and two risk reviewers, restore design review as a gate. ₹1,052 lakh, inside budget, and it would probably have prevented three of the five incidents. It would also, on H1 FY26 evidence, return the company to roughly 48 changes a half, and Meher's best builders would likely resign.

Option C: build the paved road. Keep the core locked, define bounded surfaces on which anyone may ship behind automated checks for consent, payments and GST, and staff the guild at seven. ₹1,429 lakh, including ₹165 lakh a year of amortised build. Jomar estimates nine months to a usable road — landing after the December–March season and the venue renewals.

Shalini has written the three on a page and does not trust the page. All three answer the question of who writes the code. None answers Jomar's, or the one buried in Exhibit 6: in a half of 278 changes, nobody held the question of which customer — the organiser who signs the contract, or the buyer who abandons the checkout — the next change should serve. The 2021 rule drew a boundary around the core; nothing has ever drawn one around that.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board paper is due Friday 16 October; the board votes on Thursday 22 October. The FY27 envelope approved for the lines in Exhibit 5 is ₹1,150 lakh, so Option C is ₹279 lakh over and needs the budget reopened in the same meeting that hears about ₹44.8 lakh of incidents. Renewal talks open on 1 November, weeks before the heaviest on-sales of the year, with the ₹18.0 lakh claim on the table; the contracts expire on 31 March 2027. Abhijat's consent-register gap must be closed whichever option wins, and he has one analyst. Diwali falls on 8 November, after which the organisation historically ships nothing material until January. Jomar has an offer; so do two of Meher's four builder-analysts. And Bhupesh has told three investors, in writing, that Taalmel is a company where anyone can ship.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what part of the PM's work has AI eliminated, and what part has merely moved to a different job title?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 are the most quoted inside the company. For each, state what it does and does not establish, and what you would need before relying on it.
  3. Cost per change fell 78.5 per cent while the share carrying a measured target fell from 68.8 to 30.9 per cent. Are those facts related, and by what mechanism?
  4. Exhibit 6 shows 19 of 278 changes going to 4,106 organisers. Is that a failure of the operating model, a correct response to concentration, or both — and whose job was it to notice?
  5. Options A, B and C differ by ₹709 lakh a year. If the board will fund any of them, which does least damage when its central assumption proves wrong, and what is that assumption?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October. What does Shalini do first, and what does she tell the board on 22 October — about what her function is for, and what she cannot yet prove?

At midnight she typed one line at the top of the blank board paper: "The constraint has moved. I do not yet know where to." Then she deleted it, unable to tell whether it was an admission of failure or the most useful thing she could say to them, and the offsite was in nine hours.
exp20v2-pm.hardware.vs.software:
Software, Hardware and Physical-Goods PM Compared

1. Eleven days before the tooling order

On Monday 3 August 2026, Farida Kothari opened a spreadsheet that she had hoped never to need. Eighteen months earlier she had joined Bhojan Kitchen Industries, a Pune-based maker of connected kitchen products, from a Bengaluru payments start-up where she had shipped a release every fortnight. At Bhojan she now owned the Rasoi Pod, an induction cooktop that reads a QR code on a spice-pod pack, sets its own heat profile, and talks to a phone app. It had three parts: a cooktop (hardware), an app (software) and the pods (packaged consumer goods, called CPG).

The decision was due by Friday 14 August. That was the date by which the company had to release the order for production tooling, the steel moulds that stamp out the cooktop housing. Bhaskar Rege, the hardware head in Pune, had told her that tooling takes nine weeks to cut. A release on 14 August meant tooling complete on 16 October, a first batch of 20,000 units, and shelves stocked before Diwali on 8 November. Bhaskar admitted that the temperature sensor sat 4 millimetres from where the thermal tests now suggested it belonged.

Lakshmi Narvekar, the app lead in Bengaluru, had a different instinct. Her team could ship a fix in two days, and she saw no reason to delay. Jaideep Sathe, who ran the pod business from Mumbai, worried about something neither of them mentioned: whether distributors would stock a pod pack whose cooktop might arrive late. Each was right inside a different world, and Farida had to make one decision for all three.

2. The idea: atoms change the cost of change

A software product is made of bits, copies of which cost almost nothing and can be replaced after delivery. A hardware product is made of atoms: components, tools and inventory that must be paid for before a customer ever sees them and cannot be edited afterwards. A physical consumer good such as a packaged food is also made of atoms, but it adds a third element, a channel of distributors and retailers who hold stock and take a margin between the maker and the buyer. The central claim is that atoms and bits change the cost of change and the speed of iteration, not the responsibilities of the product manager. In all three worlds the PM still owns the customer problem, the priorities and the trade-offs.

The vocabulary comes from several sources. The "cost of change curve" was drawn in Barry Boehm's software-engineering work in the early 1980s, which argued that defects become more expensive the later they are found. Agile methods, formalised in the 2001 manifesto, set out to flatten that curve for software. Manufacturers had learned the steeper version long before, in the stage-gate processes of the 1980s that Robert Cooper popularised, where a design is reviewed and then frozen at fixed gates.

The sentence Farida could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: "Every product decision is a decision about how expensive it will be to change our minds, so we should spend our certainty where changing is dearest."

3. How it actually works

Begin with the cycle: the loop of building something, putting it in front of a customer and learning from the result. Figure 2 shows how many complete loops each part of the Rasoi Pod can run in a year. The app runs 26, because a fortnightly release needs only code and a store review. The cooktop circuit board is respun about three times a year, because each spin means ordering boards, assembling them and testing them. The spice pods are reformulated about twice a year, because a new recipe must be tested for taste and shelf life, and must clear the old stock from the channel.

Three mechanics follow from this, and practitioners often leave them implicit. First, the PM must decide which decisions are one-way and which are two-way. A one-way decision, in the phrase Amazon's leaders popularised, cannot be reversed cheaply; a two-way decision can. In software, nearly everything is two-way, so a PM may decide quickly and learn afterwards. In hardware, tooling, certification and component commitments are one-way, so the PM must learn first and decide afterwards.

Second, the PM must pull learning forward. Because late learning is dear, the hardware PM buys cheaper learning early: prototypes, 3D-printed housings, pilot batches, and field trials with fifty households in Nashik before the moulds are cut. Third, the PM must read the channel as a constraint on timing. Distributors set their stocking calendar months ahead, and a shelf that is missed in one season is not recovered by being excellent in the next.

Table 1 states the contrast.

Table 1. The three worlds at a glance
DimensionSoftware (the app)Hardware (the cooktop)CPG (the pods)
Learning cycleDays to weeksMonthsMonths to a season
Fix after releasePatch, same weekRecall or reworkWithdraw and relabel stock
Marginal cost of a unitNear zeroBill of materials plus assemblyIngredients, pack, freight
ChannelApp stores, directRetail, e-commerce, service networkDistributors, kirana and modern trade
First feedback signalUsage within hoursReturns and service calls after weeksSell-through and repeat after months

4. A worked example: freeze or test once more

Farida had two options. Option A: release tooling on 14 August and accept the sensor as it stands. Option B: fund one more prototype round, which Bhaskar costed at ₹6 lakh and five weeks, and release tooling on 18 September (14 August plus 35 days). Tooling then completes on 20 November, after Diwali. She needed four inputs.

The first input was the cost of a flaw found late. Table 2 shows Bhaskar's estimate by stage; the post-production figure comes from reworking 20,000 units at ₹310 each, which is ₹62,00,000, or ₹62 lakh. The second was the chance that the sensor position really is flawed: Bhaskar put it at 30 per cent if the design froze now, and 10 per cent after another round. The third was the cost of missing Diwali. Bhojan expected to sell 400 units a week at a contribution (price less variable cost) of ₹2,500 a unit. Five weeks of delay therefore defers 5 x 400 x 2,500 = ₹50,00,000, or ₹50 lakh of contribution. Jaideep judged that 30 per cent of this would never be recovered, because buyers who miss the festival purchase do not wait: 30 per cent of ₹50 lakh is ₹15 lakh.

Table 2. Cost of the sensor change by stage (₹ lakh)
StageCost (₹ lakh)Multiple of design-stage cost
Design (CAD file)0.51x
Working prototype36x
Production tooling1836x
After 20,000 units built62124x

The arithmetic runs line by line. Option A: expected cost of a late flaw is 30 per cent of ₹62 lakh, which is ₹18.6 lakh, with no delay cost. Option B: ₹6 lakh for the round, plus 10 per cent of ₹62 lakh (₹6.2 lakh) for the smaller residual flaw risk, plus the ₹15 lakh Diwali loss, totalling ₹27.2 lakh. On these inputs Option A is cheaper by ₹8.6 lakh. Figure 3 sets the two side by side.

Now change one input. Suppose the thermal data had been worse and Bhaskar had put the flaw chance at 60 per cent if the design froze now. Option A becomes 60 per cent of ₹62 lakh, which is ₹37.2 lakh, and Option B stays at ₹27.2 lakh. The answer reverses, and Option B is cheaper by ₹10 lakh. The break-even is the chance at which the two are equal: 27.2 divided by 62 is 0.4387, so about 43.9 per cent. Below it, freeze; above it, test again. The debate about being careful is really a debate about one number, which can be investigated cheaply.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Responsibilities are constant; costs are not

Hardware PMs do not do a different job; they still discover the customer problem and prioritise. What differs is the price of being wrong, and therefore the proportion of time spent on risk reduction before commitment.

The one-way line moves with technology

Over-the-air updates make heat curves patchable through firmware; a sensor's physical position stays fixed. Ask of every decision, "what exactly is fixed once we ship?"

Channel economics are part of the product

Take a Rasoi Pod pack with a printed price (maximum retail price, or MRP) of ₹240. If the retailer keeps 18 per cent (₹43.20) and the distributor 8 per cent (₹19.20), Bhojan receives ₹240 less ₹62.40, which is ₹177.60 before its own costs. The price on the pack is not the price the company earns.

Inventory is a bet made before demand is known

Software carries no stock; hardware and CPG do. The 20,000-unit batch is a forecast converted into steel, boards and working capital.

Quality has a legal edge

Electrical products must meet Bureau of Indian Standards requirements and food pods FSSAI rules. A bug in a to-do app inconveniences; an overheating cooktop is a safety event.

What the idea cannot tell you

The cost-of-change view says where to concentrate care. It does not say whether the product should exist, which customers want it, or what price they will pay.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Ask which cost figures are measured and which guessed, whether the probability came from tests or confidence, and whether a cheaper way of learning exists.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early-stage and large

In consumer products, as with the Rasoi Pod, the buyer is a household, feedback arrives through reviews and returns, and the brand carries the risk of a bad batch. In B2B hardware, such as a restaurant chain buying fifty commercial induction units, the contract can specify changes, pilots are normal, and one customer's acceptance test acts as a stage gate. A marketplace, such as a platform listing other sellers' cookware, has mostly software costs but a physical-world problem: it cannot control the quality of goods it does not make, so its PM works through seller standards and return policies instead of tooling.

Size matters too. An early-stage company has little cash for steel, makes small batches by outsourced assembly, and cannot survive a single failure. A large company can fund several prototype rounds but carries distributor commitments and a brand, so a recall costs more than the units.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the hardware roadmap like a backlog

Symptom: a long list of features with weekly re-ordering, while the tooling date quietly approaches. Misunderstanding: that all work is reversible. Diagnostic: mark every item "one-way" or "two-way" and see how many one-way items have no dated decision.

Ignoring the shelf calendar

Symptom: a launch date set by engineering readiness alone. Misunderstanding: that the channel will take stock whenever the product is ready. Diagnostic: ask distributors for their last date to accept new lines for the season.

Believing a single probability

Symptom: a go decision resting on one confident estimate. Misunderstanding: that the number is a fact. Diagnostic: compute the break-even, as in section 4, and ask how far the estimate is from it.

8. What good looks like

Done well, Farida's week looks like this. She asks Bhaskar for the cost-by-stage table before the meeting, not during it. She asks for the 30 per cent flaw estimate to be backed by a three-day thermal test on a 3D-printed housing, which costs a fraction of ₹6 lakh. She asks Lakshmi to move the heat-curve logic into updatable firmware. She asks Jaideep for the distributors' cut-off date for Diwali stocking. The team spends its certainty on the irreversible item and its speed on the rest.

9. Closing: what Farida decided

She ordered a three-day test, not a five-week round. The test showed that 3 of 20 sample cooking runs overshot temperature, and all three traced to a heat curve that Lakshmi's team could correct in firmware. Farida therefore released the tooling order on 14 August, froze the housing, and kept the sensor position fixed while moving the heat logic into updatable firmware. Her reasoning was the one the arithmetic suggested: the flaw chance sat below the 43.9 per cent break-even, and the part that could be changed later was deliberately left changeable.

To go further, read next about hardware product management in detail, where certification, bills of materials and supplier lead times take the place of sprint velocity, and then about physical goods and CPG product management, where pricing ladders and distributor calendars govern the work. Two questions to sit with. First, in a product you know, which three decisions are truly one-way, and who owns each date? Second, if your most confident estimate were wrong by half, which of your current commitments would you regret most?
case40v1-pm.hardware.vs.software:
Ikaai Sensor Works: Atoms at the Collection Centre

A case for discussion. Anand, Gujarat, October 2026.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Sharvari Lokhande was still at the long table in the Ikaai Sensor Works office in Anand, two devices in front of her. On her left an Ikaai M1: a grey polycarbonate box with a thermal printer, a keypad and a stainless probe that dips into a 20-millilitre milk sample and returns fat and solids-not-fat in forty seconds. On her right a 3D-printed mock-up of the M2, lighter, with a colour screen and a 4G module. Taped to her laptop lid was a slip from a society near Bhilwara: a member number, 4.3 per cent fat, and a rupee figure smudged by a thumb.

The board's product sub-committee met at ten. Three clocks were running. Thanh Loi Precision, the contract manufacturer in Hanoi that would mould the M2 housings, was holding a tooling slot until Friday, 16 October, at ₹168 lakh for the tool set. The Turin sensor supplier had written on 24 September that its ultrasonic heads would rise 14 per cent for orders placed after 31 October. And Ikaai still owed the Mewar Milk Union 1,650 M1 units by 31 March 2027 under a contract signed in February 2024.

Lokhande had joined eighteen months earlier from a payments company in Bengaluru, where she shipped twice a week and killed features without ceremony. What she had not expected in Anand was how much of the job was deciding irreversibly, in advance, on evidence she did not trust.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Ikaai Sensor Works was founded in March 2023 by Chandrahas Pendse, a former instrumentation engineer, with two colleagues from the dairy equipment trade. The premise was that village-level collection ran on measurement nobody believed: an analyser bought on price, a ledger register, a payment ten days later the farmer could not reconstruct. Ikaai would build an analyser that was accurate, printed a slip and sent every reading to the cloud.

The first M1 shipped in April 2023. By 30 September 2026 Ikaai had shipped 41,200, employed 112 people across Anand, Pune and Hyderabad, and held ₹14.2 crore of cash against a burn of ₹58 lakh a month. FY26 revenue was ₹17.03 crore: 13,900 devices at an average ₹12,100, which is ₹16.82 crore, plus ₹21.4 lakh of subscriptions.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken on 14 February 2024, when Ikaai won the Mewar Milk Union tender: 9,000 M1 units by 31 March 2027 at a fixed ₹11,800 per device, with a seven-year spares obligation and liquidated damages of 0.5 per cent of order value per week of delay, capped at 5 per cent. Order value is ₹10.62 crore, so weekly exposure is ₹5.31 lakh and the cap ₹53.1 lakh. The tender made the company; it is also why Ikaai cannot reprice. At the old sensor quote the M1 cost ₹10,950 and earned ₹850, a margin of 7.2 per cent; after the Turin increase it costs ₹11,349 and earns ₹451, or 3.8 per cent. Ikaai delivered 7,350 units to Mewar between April 2024 and September 2026, an average of 245 a month. The remaining 1,650 must go out in six months, which is 275 a month, about 12 per cent above any rate it has achieved.

3. The industry

India collects more milk than any other country, and most of it passes through a village society before a chilling centre. The cooperative structure Amul made famous — village society, district union, state federation — still sets the rules of the sale, and the National Dairy Development Board's automatic milk collection specifications are what a procurement officer reads before a brochure. Mother Dairy and the private processors buy on similar terms. Ikaai competes with established equipment houses and with dairy-technology firms such as Stellapps and Prompt Equipments, which reached the same village from the software side and sell analysers, weighing and dashboards as a bundle.

Three forces bear on the product. First, legal metrology: any new model of a measuring instrument used in trade needs model approval, and Ikaai's consultant budgets sixteen to twenty-two weeks for the M2. Second, food safety: FSSAI's standards govern what a reading means, and a union's interest in adulteration testing is not a farmer's interest in a fair fat reading. Third, data: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has every union's legal adviser asking who the data fiduciary is when a farmer's milk record and bank-linked payment sit in Ikaai's cloud. Connectivity is no longer the obstacle of 2019 — Jio reaches most societies Ikaai serves — which is why the software argument is harder to dismiss.

Ikaai is also exposed abroad. A processor in Bandung has run eleven M1 units since March 2026 and wants 400; Pendse reads that as proof of a global market. Sensor heads come from Turin on a twenty-week lead time, minimum order 5,000, and the housings would be moulded in Hanoi.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Figure A. Red markers: commitments or findings the team now reads differently.

In April 2026 the sub-committee approved the M2 concept on three beliefs: the buyer was the union's procurement officer, the differentiator was accuracy and cycle time, and the subscription would follow the devices into the field. Tooling was quoted on 6 April at ₹168 lakh for a first batch of 6,000.

Between 4 and 18 August 2026 Lokhande ran a field study with two engineers, visiting 60 societies across Mewar and Saurashtra and pulling eighteen months of telemetry. Exhibit 1 is what came back, and it is why the M2's case feels thinner than it did in April. Of 41,200 devices shipped, 18,540 have ever paired, 9,270 sent data in the previous thirty days, 1,854 had a secretary who logged in during September, and 927 were on a paid subscription. The subscription meant to follow the hardware reaches 927 of 41,200 devices, or 2.25 per cent.

The secretaries who had stopped pairing were not indifferent; they were busy. Pairing needed a menu sequence they performed once at installation and forgot. The farmers complained of something else. They asked for neither a better sensor nor an app: they asked why the slip they held and the amount credited ten days later did not correspond, and why a disputed reading could not be re-taken.

Fifty-five days later, on 12 October, the sub-committee is asked to approve tooling for a device premised on beliefs the August study did not support — and Annika Strandberg's drift analysis from Gothenburg adds a third complication. Fitting a model to eighteen months of readings from the 9,270 active devices, she found 2,781 of them, or 30 per cent, apparently drifted beyond ±0.05 fat points from their commissioning baseline. If so, Ikaai's installed base is itself producing the disputes the farmers complain about, and no mould fixes that.

5. The people

Sharvari Lokhande, head of product, Anand. She owns the recommendation, and believes Ikaai has defined its product by what it is good at making rather than by any problem someone pays to solve. Unsaid: she cannot say what Ikaai is, commercially, if it stops being an instrument company.

Chandrahas Pendse, co-founder and chief executive, Anand. He wants the tooling committed on Friday: credibility with unions, with Bandung and with Turin rests on being a manufacturer that ships new models. Unsaid: in the Series B he is raising for early 2027, one term sheet has already asked why hardware revenue should earn software multiples.

Trupti Hundekari, head of hardware, Pune. Thirty-one of her thirty-eight engineers have been on the M2 for six months. She argues, with justice, that the Hanoi slot is a place in a queue, not a date, and the next costs 6 per cent more. Unsaid: she disbelieves Strandberg's drift finding, because if it is real her team's calibration is the cause.

Zaheer Mukadam, platform lead, Hyderabad. He wants the M2 shelved for a year and the retrofit kit of Exhibit 3 shipped instead: a ₹1,300 dongle reading the serial port of any analyser already in a society, Ikaai's or a competitor's. His objectives are written in recurring revenue. Unsaid: the consent architecture he needs does not exist, and two union legal advisers say the data is the union's.

Lakshman Boruah, head of institutional sales, Jaipur. He produced Exhibit 4 and is paid on tender value. Unions buy instruments, not subscriptions, and a kit that works on a rival's analyser helps that rival keep the socket. Unsaid: he has not reconciled his counts with Exhibit 5, calling the audit "a sample, not the territory".

Lan Pham, manufacturing engineer at Thanh Loi Precision, Hanoi, holding the slot as a favour to a small customer. The housing geometry, she notes, needs a side-action tool that limits later changes; she has twice asked whether Ikaai wants a simpler two-part housing. Nobody has answered.

Annika Strandberg, data scientist, Gothenburg, three days a week. Her drift model is the most interesting thing anyone at Ikaai produced this year and she knows it. She wants a field calibration study with reference samples. Unsaid: without one, her 30 per cent cannot be defended.

Sohini Mazumdar, investor, Mumbai. At each of the last three meetings she has asked who the customer is. She will back either direction if the answer is evidenced, and has an unstated interest in a clean Series B.

7. Voices

"The slot is not a date, it is a queue. Let it go and the next tool is 6 per cent dearer and we are behind two other customers. I can give you a device in July. I cannot give you one in July if we decide in March."Trupti Hundekari, sub-committee call, 6 October 2026
"Procurement officers buy instruments. There is no line in a union budget called software. Ask them for ₹250 a month and they will ask you to take ₹250 off the device."Lakshman Boruah, email to Pendse and Lokhande, 29 September 2026
"We shipped 41,200 instruments to prove a point about accuracy and 927 people pay us for the data. Either the data is worth nothing or we have never once sold it to the person who wants it. I do not think we know which."Zaheer Mukadam, internal chat thread, 2 October 2026
"My thirty per cent is a model, not a measurement. Give me 120 devices and reference samples in Mewar and in six weeks you will know whether the base is drifting. Until then please do not put that number in a board deck."Annika Strandberg, note to Lokhande, 8 October 2026
"The union asks me for the register, the farmer asks me why his slip says one thing. I have no time to log in anywhere. If the machine printed what the farmer finally gets paid, half my morning would be free."Shankar Lal Gurjar, society secretary near Bhilwara, field interview, 11 August 2026

8. The options as Lokhande sees them

Option A. Commit the tooling. Pay Hanoi on Friday and build the M2 for the tender channel. The first batch costs ₹720 lakh at the March quote, or ₹743.94 lakh after the sensor rise — ₹743.94 lakh of the ₹1,420 lakh of cash, which is 52.4 per cent, leaving 11.7 months of runway. The hypothesis bought is April's: the customer is the procurement officer and the problem is the instrument.

Option B. Shelve the M2 and ship the retrofit kit. Six thousand kits cost ₹78 lakh and Mukadam's platform work needs ₹96 lakh of engineering over seven months, so ₹174 lakh in all, which is 12.3 per cent of cash and leaves 21.5 months. The hypothesis is that the value is in the data and the buyer is whoever suffers the disputes. It also puts Ikaai's software on rivals' hardware, which Boruah calls arming them.

Option C. A paid pilot of 600 units in 60 societies. Three hundred hand-built M2 units at ₹13,329 each — the ₹8,439 of materials, less the ₹610 moulded housing, plus a ₹3,400 machined housing and ₹2,100 of hand assembly and calibration — is ₹39.99 lakh; 300 retrofit kits at ₹1,300 is ₹3.90 lakh; ₹22 lakh buys a field team for fourteen weeks. Total ₹65.89 lakh, leaving 23.3 months. It forfeits the Hanoi slot and the 6 per cent, ₹10.08 lakh on the ₹168 lakh tool, and delays M2 revenue to FY29.

Lokhande wrote all three on the whiteboard and sat looking at them, because the list bothered her. Every option assumes the payer is an institution. None tests what Gurjar said — that the slip should show what the farmer finally gets paid, a change living in firmware and a payment integration, costing almost nothing, needing neither mould nor subscription. None addresses Strandberg's possibility that the binding constraint is calibration in the field, which would make Ikaai a service business and both devices beside the point. The hardware-versus-software framing is the one her team finds natural. It may also be why the question has had three answers.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Friday, 16 October, is when Hanoi releases the tool; Saturday, 31 October, is when the sensor price protection lapses. The Mewar balance of 1,650 M1 units must ship by 31 March 2027 whatever happens, and the Turin minimum order is 5,000 heads, so Ikaai must buy 5,000 to finish a contract needing 1,650. If the M2 does not proceed, 3,350 surplus heads at ₹3,249 are ₹108.84 lakh of inventory with no product to go into; ordering all 5,000 before 31 October at ₹2,850 costs ₹142.5 lakh instead of ₹162.45 lakh, a saving of ₹19.95 lakh, but commits the cash now.

Cash is ₹14.2 crore against a burn of ₹58 lakh a month, so Ikaai has about 24 months if it commits to nothing. Model approval for the M2 takes sixteen to twenty-two weeks and cannot start before the housing is frozen. Thirty-one of Hundekari's thirty-eight engineers have no other project, and the DPDP consent framework Option B needs has not been designed, let alone agreed with a union.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Who is Ikaai's customer? Separate buyer, user and beneficiary in each option, and say which the April 2026 M2 concept was designed for.
  2. Restate the problem in the words of the person who has it. Of those on the table — accuracy, pairing, disputes, payment transparency, drift — which will someone pay to have solved, and on what evidence here?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 cannot both be right. How would you establish which is closer to the truth before Friday, and how should the chance that both are wrong change the recommendation?
  4. Exhibit 6 favours the retrofit; Exhibit 1 undermines it. Which assumption in Exhibit 6 would you test first, and what would a cheap test look like?
  5. Hundekari and Mukadam are each right about the cost of being wrong in their own layer. What does the cost of change imply about the order in which Ikaai decides things — and which decision due this month is genuinely irreversible?
  6. What should Lokhande do on Monday morning, and what exactly would she say to the sub-committee: what she believes, what she no longer believes, and what she will spend to find out?

It was past midnight. Lokhande turned the smudged slip over. On the back, in pencil, were a member number and two amounts, one crossed out. She had asked Gurjar and he had shrugged: the first figure was what the machine said, the second what the union paid. She had assumed an arithmetic difference. She no longer assumed that. In nine hours she would tell a sub-committee which of the two devices in front of her Ikaai should build, and she was no longer sure it was either of them.
case20v1-pm.hardware.vs.software:
Hastkala Lock Works: The Mould or the Pilot

1. Opening

On Monday morning, 12 October 2026, Himani Rane sat in the glass-walled meeting room of Hastkala Lock Works in Baner, Pune, with a prototype door lock in front of her and a deadline on her phone. Zhang Wei, the company's contract-manufacturing contact in Shenzhen, had written the night before: the injection-mould slot reserved for Hastkala would be released to another customer unless a deposit arrived by Friday, 16 October. The mould was priced at ₹95 lakh. Hastkala had ₹2.4 crore left from its seed round.

Rane had spent six years as a software product manager before founding the company, and her instinct was to ship something small and learn. She had four days to decide what Hastkala would build first, and for whom.

2. Company background

Hastkala Lock Works was founded in 2024 to make connected door locks for Indian homes. The pitch was simple: a lock that opens by fingerprint, phone or a time-limited code, so that a household no longer depends on a bunch of metal keys. The company has fourteen employees: eight in Pune, four in Bengaluru, and two contractors abroad.

The market is crowded at the mechanical end and thin at the connected end. Godrej Locks and Yale sell smart locks through hardware dealers and on Amazon and Flipkart, and Urban Company technicians are often the people who actually fit them. Prices in the metros run well above what an ordinary landlord will pay for a door. Hastkala's planned retail price was ₹9,999.

3. The situation

Over August and September, Rane's team held forty customer interviews in Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The founding assumption had been that the customer was the owner-occupier of a flat who wanted the convenience of a fingerprint lock. The interviews told a different story. Fourteen of the forty, or 35 per cent, were owner-occupiers, and they said they were broadly content with keys. Eighteen, or 45 per cent, were landlords or non-resident owners who let flats to tenants, and their pain was acute: handing keys over, copying keys, and changing locks at every tenant turnover. The remaining eight, or 20 per cent, ran paying-guest accommodation and wanted to give and revoke access for many rooms.

The problem that people paid to solve, then, was not "a nicer lock". It was "I cannot be at the door, and I do not want to cut a new key for every tenant". That is a sharing problem, and much of it could be solved in software.

The team's views depend on where they sit. In Bengaluru, Meenal Shetye, who leads the app, argued that the shared-access software could be tested within weeks on locks that customers already owned. In Pune, Tushar Nikam, the hardware lead, pointed out that the sample lock was good and that the mould slot would not come again cheaply. In Shenzhen, Zhang Wei was courteous and clear: the next mould window opened on 1 March 2027, at a price 5 per cent higher. In Rotterdam, the industrial designer Joost Verbeek had finished a body design that only made sense if tooled in full.

Exhibit 1 explains why the software people and the hardware people were talking past each other. The same change, discovered after launch, costs wildly different amounts depending on where it lives.

Source: Hastkala internal estimates, including supplier quotes from Shenzhen. A mould modification costs 180 times an app change (18 ÷ 0.1).

4. The people

Himani Rane, founder and chief product officer, Pune. She owns the decision and the cash. She wants evidence of who the customer is before spending most of the seed round.

Tushar Nikam, head of hardware, Pune. He wants the mould deposit paid now. A missed slot, in his view, signals to engineers and suppliers that the company cannot commit.

Meenal Shetye, app lead, Bengaluru. She wants to test sharing and revocation of access first, using the app on off-the-shelf locks, and to treat Hastkala's own lock as a later question.

Nandini Rao, a seed investor in Mumbai. She has not demanded tooling, but she has asked twice when "the product" will be in homes. She will back either course if the reasoning is clear.

5. The cost of building a first lock

Exhibit 2 sets out the bill of materials for one lock at engineering-sample quality, and what 300 such units would cost. This is the volume the team believes it could assemble by hand in Pune. The metal body here is a bought-in housing, not a tooled plastic part, so the pilot lock is heavier and plainer than the lock Verbeek designed.

6. The options

Option A: Pay the deposit and commit to tooling. Hastkala would fund the mould and a first batch of 2,000 locks. The upside is a finished, attractive product in about nine months, and goodwill with the supplier. The cost is the commitment: the mould and batch together would absorb ₹184.6 lakh, about 77 per cent of the remaining cash, on the strength of a customer guess that interviews had just contradicted.

Option B: Software first. Hastkala would drop its own lock for now and ship the shared-access app on third-party smart locks, selling a subscription to landlords. The upside is speed and low cost, ₹22 lakh over ten weeks. The cost is that Hastkala would be dependent on other firms' hardware, and the lock may well be the part that makes the experience reliable.

Option C: A hand-built pilot with the real lock. Hastkala would assemble 300 locks in Pune, install them in landlord and PG homes in Pune and Bengaluru, and measure use. The upside is real behaviour from real doors, for ₹23 lakh. The cost is that the pilot lock is rough, that 300 hand-built units strain the Pune team, and that the mould slot would be lost.

Scale: 10 pixels per week.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Rane began with an owner-occupier and the interviews pointed to landlords. What is the real customer problem, and which layer of the product (app, firmware, board, body) does each part of it live in?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, explain why Nikam and Shetye each feel the cost of being wrong differently. How does the cost of change change what a product manager should decide early, and what can be left open?
  3. Which hypothesis is Option A betting on, and what would have to be true for 2,000 locks to sell? What would Options B and C teach that A cannot?
  4. What would you tell Zhang Wei by Friday, and what evidence would you give Nandini Rao to justify it?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about why the product manager's job is the same in hardware and in software, while its rhythm is not. In both worlds the PM must find the customer's real problem, state a hypothesis and test it cheaply. What changes is the price of a wrong answer. An app screen can be rewritten by Tuesday; a mould is a one-way door. A software PM can ship and then learn. A hardware PM must learn enough before the irreversible step, and that step must be placed as late as the schedule allows.

A defensible path is Option C, with the tooling decision deliberately deferred. Rane should tell Zhang Wei that Hastkala will take the 1 March 2027 window, accepting a price rise of ₹4.75 lakh (5 per cent of ₹95 lakh), which brings the mould to ₹99.75 lakh. Against that known and modest cost, the pilot buys what the interviews could not: whether landlords share and revoke access every week, which is the behaviour that justifies a ₹9,999 lock. The pilot finishes on 22 January 2027, with five weeks to spare before the March decision.

Rane should set the test before the pilot begins. If at least 60 per cent of the 300 homes, which is 180, use remote sharing every week, she should commit the mould in March, with Verbeek's design adjusted by what the pilot reveals. If fewer do, she has spent ₹23 lakh, not ₹184.6 lakh, to learn that the real business may be the software of Option B. Meenal Shetye's app belongs in both cases, because the pilot depends on it. Nikam's concern about signalling is real and should be answered by giving his team the pilot, with a clear date for the tooling decision, rather than a missed slot. The skill on display is sequencing: learn on the cheap layers first.
exp40v2-pm.hardware.vs.software:
Atoms, Bits and the Price of Changing Your Mind

Software, hardware and physical-goods product management compared: iteration speed, cost of change and channel as the three variables that reshape one job.

1. Two gates, twenty-one days apart

On Tuesday 10 February 2026, in a shed off the Avinashi Road in Coimbatore, Ketaki Raikar asked Murali Chidambaram a question she half-regretted. Raikar was product manager for the Himvaahak CL-4 at Rupantar Device Works: a reusable cold-chain logger that rides inside a vaccine carrier, records temperature every two minutes and uploads over Bluetooth. Rupantar had bid for 60,000 loggers over twenty-four months on a state health tender, first lot due 30 June.

Chidambaram, who ran mechanical engineering, needed the mould tool released to Shikhar Moulding Services in Rajkot by Friday 27 February, eleven weeks before first shells. That put them in Coimbatore on 15 May, leaving six weeks for assembly, calibration at Sahasra Calibration Labs in Pune and BIS paperwork. Seventeen days of float, and one open question: whether the probe should sit in a boss moulded into the shell, as drawn, or on a carrier the shell clamps. The boss was cheaper and harder to change.

Twenty-seven days later, Aniruddh Sabnis faced the mirror image in Ahmedabad. On Monday 9 March he had eleven days before Sumeru Personal Care Industries' council on 20 March — twenty-one days after Raikar's tool deadline — to recommend reformulating its flagship 100 gram toothpaste, sold at ₹95, by replacing an imported humectant. The saving was ₹2.35 a tube on 1.80 crore tubes a year. Nobody doubted the arithmetic; they doubted whether the paste would feel the same, and new artwork took twelve weeks to flush through the channel. Both decisions turn on one quantity: what it costs to change your mind, and when the chance closes.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

State it precisely. For any product decision there is a commitment gate: the moment after which reversal costs materially more than before. Define the reversibility coefficient R as the cost of a change just after the gate divided by its cost just before. Software layers sit near 1, the hardware layers tabulated below run 3 to 4, and physical goods in a channel carry an R modest in rupees but brutal in time, the gate belonging to someone else's stocking calendar. The claim is narrow: atoms and channels change R and the learning cycle, not what a product manager is responsible for.

Two intellectual streams met late. The software stream begins with Barry Boehm's 1981 cost-of-change curve, defect cost rising an order of magnitude per phase, and runs through the 2001 agile manifesto, whose project was to flatten that curve rather than respect it. The manufacturing stream was never romantic about flattening: Robert Cooper's stage-gate work, Kim Clark and Takahiro Fujimoto's 1991 study of automotive lead times and Karl Ulrich and Steven Eppinger's 1995 textbook treat the freeze as physics to be scheduled. Set-based concurrent engineering, documented by Allen Ward, Durward Sobek and Jeffrey Liker in 1995, showed Toyota deferring the gate by carrying several designs forward. Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck's 1994 work on investment under uncertainty supplied the language: an irreversible commitment destroys a priced option.

Three schools disagree. The universalists hold the differences to be parameters: they sign "both run the same loop at different frequencies," and refuse "a software PM can be dropped into a tooling decision after a week's orientation." The specialists hold these are different professions sharing a title, the binding skill being supplier and systems engineering: they sign "the deciding competence is knowing what the tool can be modified to do," and refuse "the hardware PM need not run discovery." The commercial school holds that the channel is the divide: they sign "resold software behaves more like toothpaste than like a self-serve app," and refuse "tooling is unimportant."

3. Mechanics in depth

Experts do four things usually left implicit. First, they decompose the product into layers and measure each layer's cycle rate separately, because one cadence for a layered product is a category error. Table 1 is Raikar's decomposition of the CL-3, still in the field, for the year to 31 March 2026.

Table 1. One product, four cadences: CL-3, year to 31 March 2026

The layers that absorbed one-seventh of the money produced four-fifths of the learning — an asymmetry invisible to anyone reporting a single velocity.

Second, experts compute R rather than argue. The web dashboard's gate is deployment, which is also its rollback; the app's is store review plus the upgrade lag; firmware's is the over-the-air campaign; the board's is the purchase order; the enclosure's is the tool release.

The ₹104.56 lakh is ₹34.00 lakh to cut a replacement tool plus ₹70.56 lakh of contribution deferred by a nine-week slip, at 700 units a week and ₹1,120 a unit. Blended R is 147.34 divided by 45.33.

Third, they turn the argument into an expected-cost comparison over a stated demand distribution, because in hardware the tooling choice and the volume forecast are one decision. The hard tool cost ₹34 lakh at a unit cost of ₹1,180; a bridge tool in aluminium cost ₹6 lakh at ₹1,300 a unit and wore out after 25,000 shots. Bharat Sankhe in supply chain gave three scenarios: the full tender at 60,000 units with probability 0.45, a split award at 24,000 with 0.35, and a loss leaving only private pharma at 9,000 with 0.20. Expected volume is 27,000 plus 8,400 plus 1,800, or 37,200 units.

At 60,000 units the hard tool costs ₹34 lakh plus ₹708 lakh of unit cost, or ₹742 lakh, against three bridge tools at ₹18 lakh plus ₹780 lakh, or ₹798 lakh. At 9,000 the bridge wins, ₹123.0 lakh against ₹140.2 lakh. Weighted, the two come to ₹472.96 lakh and ₹495.00 lakh: an advantage of ₹22.04 lakh to committing.

Fourth, and this separates the practitioner from the expert, they price design risk apart from demand risk, because only the first is reducible by testing. Let q be the probability that the probe geometry must change after the gate. If it does, the hard-tool route forfeits the ₹104.56 lakh of Table 2, the bridge route ₹6 lakh of tool plus two weeks of deferred contribution at ₹7.84 lakh a week, or ₹21.68 lakh. The difference, ₹82.88 lakh, is what the hard tool stakes on the geometry; against the ₹22.04 lakh advantage the break-even is 26.6 per cent. Chidambaram's estimate was 20 per cent.

Twenty against twenty-six point six is not comfortable, and the expert buys information rather than argues. Dr Latika Ghatge, who ran quality and regulatory, proposed a two-week pilot inside the float: twelve printed shells in live vaccine carriers at three Assam district stores, ₹3.5 lakh. Chidambaram put its resolving power at a 70 per cent chance the geometry holds, leaving q near 0.05, and a 30 per cent chance of showing the clamped carrier necessary, pushing q to 0.55 — consistent with his prior, since 0.70 times 0.05 plus 0.30 times 0.55 is 0.20.

Software managers rarely build this, and are rarely wrong not to: when R is 1, the experiment is the decision.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three testable claims hold the framework up. First, the gate is identifiable and dated: for Raikar, 27 February, written into Shikhar's purchase order; for Sabnis, the day the cartons are printed, because Rangoli Distribution Network in Indore and three hundred like it will not hold two artworks for one stock-keeping unit. Second, the cost on either side is estimable within a factor of two. Third, the probability is reducible by an experiment that fits inside the float. Here it most often fails: a twelve-week stability study cannot be compressed, and no panel of 420 users tells you what 1.80 crore tubes will do.

It misleads in three cases: when a soft gate is treated as hard, so teams buy certainty they did not need; when the irreversible commitment is a customer commitment — a contract, a published interface, a regulatory filing — so a team with R near 1 on its code carries R near 8 on its promises; and when the real uncertainty is whether anyone wants the product, in which case arithmetic over tooling is precision applied to the wrong question.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Hardware-plus-software products have a gate that moves, and the movement is a design decision. The CL-4's offsets, thresholds and upload protocol sit in firmware, which is why Chidambaram's nine-week exposure covered only the probe's position. The tell is a bill of materials with a dearer microcontroller than the feature list justifies.

Regulated products invert the ordering. The CL-4 required BIS conformity and, for pharma, documentation aligned to the World Health Organization's prequalification scheme. R is then set by the certificate, not the atoms: Raikar's board revision cost ₹38 lakh after its gate because a changed board meant a re-test.

Marketplaces have almost no tooling, yet face the highest R of all on the rules: one that changes its seller commission cannot roll it back, because sellers have repriced. Platform managers from pure software find their R on policy nearer Sumeru's than their own code's.

AI-native products are re-steepening a curve the industry spent twenty years flattening. A model's behaviour emerges from weights, prompts, retrieval and evaluation sets, not code. Changing a prompt is cheap; changing the evaluation suite that tells you whether it helped is not, and a regression suite over 4,000 graded examples has the feel of a tool cut.

At the seams the pattern is rarely admitted. Mature companies run a hardware stage-gate and a software cadence side by side, with a weekly joint freeze review. What they say they run is "one agile programme." What they run is two calendars and one argument.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

The gate is a negotiated date, not a physical constant. Chidambaram's eleven weeks included four of queue at Shikhar, and a manager who asks the price of a reserved slot often finds two purchasable — the cheapest float there is. The tell is a supplier quoting a round number.

Unit cost and tool cost trade against each other, and the exchange rate is the forecast. The obvious reading is that cheaper units win; the expert reads a bet on volume. At 9,000 units Rupantar would rather pay ₹120 more per unit than ₹28 lakh more in steel, and at 60,000 the reverse. The tell is a team that quotes unit cost to the rupee but cannot say where the choice flips.

In physical goods the channel owns the clock. Sabnis's twelve weeks of stock in trade — three at the factory, four at distributors, five on shelves — is 41.5 lakh tubes at a weekly offtake of 3.46 lakh, worth roughly ₹22.4 crore at a realisation of ₹54.04 a tube. The tell is a launch date set in a factory meeting.

The price on the pack is not the price the company earns. Table 3 traces all ₹95. A ₹2.35 ingredient saving is 11.3 per cent of Sumeru's ₹20.84 contribution, which is why a change invisible to consumers can dominate a quarter. The tell is a manager quoting maximum retail price in a margin discussion.

Reversibility is a property of the decision, not of the industry. Hiring, pricing, public commitments and data schemas are high-R decisions inside pure software businesses, and where such companies get stuck. The tell is a team that ships twice a week and has not touched its pricing page in three years.

The cheapest learning is almost never the obvious experiment. Ghatge's twelve shells cost a tenth of a prototype round and answered the one question that mattered, being instrumented for it alone. The tell is a test plan costed in proportion to the product rather than the uncertainty.

Panel evidence on sensory change is weaker than it looks. Payal Dastane's blind test of 420 users returned 176 preferring the new formulation, 192 the old and 52 indifferent — 41.9, 45.7 and 12.4 per cent. The 3.8-point adverse gap feels like a finding, but its standard error on 420 paired respondents is 4.6 points, so the gap sits inside one standard error of zero. The tell is a gap reported with no interval.

Mature teams freeze in layers, not all at once. The practised sequence is interfaces, then geometry, then behaviour, then content. Rupantar froze the mounting interface in January, the geometry in February, the alarm logic in April and the dashboard copy on launch morning. The tell is one dated "design freeze" milestone on a layered product.

7. How the practice differs by product type and company stage

Across consumer, business and enterprise software the difference is smaller than folklore suggests: consumer software has R near 1 and abundant signal, while enterprise software has R near 1 on code and 5 or more on contracts, pilots and migrations, which is why enterprise managers behave more like hardware managers than they admit. Hardware and physical goods differ from each other more than either differs from software: Raikar's constraint is capital committed to steel, Sabnis's is time committed to a pipeline, so she buys information inside her float and he buys reversibility by sequencing.

By stage the honest differences are two. An early-stage company cannot absorb a wrong tool, so it over-pays per unit for optionality and should. A large company can absorb the tool but not the channel disruption, so its high-R decisions migrate from capital to reputation. What does not change is the arithmetic: Sankhe's table is the same instrument at ten crore of revenue and at ten thousand.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

The first is Rupantar's CL-2, built in 2023 and 2024 by a team that had read about agile hardware and resolved to iterate. Over sixteen months they modified the tool four times, at ₹7.5, ₹11.0, ₹19.5 and ₹6.0 lakh, and re-tested to BIS three times at ₹3.2 lakh each, ₹9.6 lakh in all. The ₹53.6 lakh spent changing the tool was 2.44 times the ₹22 lakh the tool had cost, with seven weeks of slip. The lesson was not "iterate less" but "iterate where iteration is cheap" — hence the CL-3's 41 dashboard releases and one tool change.

The second succeeded. Sumeru's previous launch, a herbal variant, went out as a ₹1 five-gram sachet in 1,420 Vidarbha outlets for nine weeks before any tube was printed: 4.6 lakh sachets, about 36 per outlet per week, repeat purchase at day 45 of 31 per cent. The test cost ₹38 lakh against a national launch budget of ₹6.4 crore, and its finding was unwelcome — fragrance, not the claim, drove repeat.

The third failed. Srijan Commerce Exchange, a Bengaluru seller-software firm, acquired a thermal label printer line in 2024 and ran it on its software cadence, with no freeze register. Nidhi Talpade, its product head, shipped 14,000 units before anyone established that the print-head mount flexed under continuous duty; 2,180 of the 14,000 units failed in the field within ten months, 15.6 per cent. The ₹113.41 lakh of Table 4 consumed 49.1 per cent of the ₹231 lakh of lifetime contribution earned at ₹1,650 a unit. The recovery, led by Pradyumna Kale from Chennai, was unglamorous: a dated freeze register, a rule barring mechanical changes inside eight weeks of a tool release, and a ₹14 lakh rig. The next model shipped 31,000 units at a field-failure rate of 0.9 per cent, 279 units.
