9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of late detection

The backlog-shaped hardware plan is commonest. Its sign is a re-ordered list in a product whose tool date has not moved in three months; the diagnostic is "which items are irreversible after a date, and what date?"; caught at the design review it costs nothing, caught after the tool is cut it costs Srijan's ₹113.41 lakh. The single-point probability failure is a go decision resting on one confident estimate; the diagnostic is to compute the break-even, as Raikar did at 26.6 per cent, and ask how far the estimate sits from it. The false freeze is the opposite error, known-wrong details tooled; its sign is engineers saying "we'll fix it next revision," and its cost is a second tool.

In physical goods the characteristic failure is pipeline blindness: a change authorised with no plan for the stock already in trade. Its early sign is a plan whose last milestone is "new artwork approved"; the diagnostic is "how many rupees of old stock exist, and who eats them?"; caught before printing it costs a conversation, caught after it costs a quarter of relabelling. The fourth, shared by all three worlds, is treating the cost of change as fixed: a team that never asks whether a parameter could move into firmware has conceded the framework's only lever.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The flatten-the-curve position holds that most hardware irreversibility is self-inflicted. Its evidence is real: additive manufacturing, modular architectures, bridge tooling and shared tool banks have cut hardware iteration cost by an order of magnitude in a decade. It would be wrong if the residual irreversible core — certification, channel commitment, capital at scale — dominated the cost, as Rupantar's ₹38 lakh board revision suggests, the money sitting in the re-test.

The respect-the-gate position holds that iterating through a physical commitment destroys more value than it creates, citing Clark and Fujimoto's finding that the fastest automotive developers were not those who changed designs most but those who front-loaded problem-solving. It would be wrong if front-loading needed information that does not exist before a real product meets real users — the software industry's central claim about itself.

The channel-primacy position holds that both over-index on the factory. Harshvardhan Mestry, Sumeru's sales head, put it bluntly in the 20 March council: formulation could change in six weeks and artwork in four, and neither mattered, because the channel moved in twelve-week blocks. It would be wrong if direct-to-consumer distribution made the trade optional, which in Indian oral care it has not.

A fourth disagreement is unsettled: whether AI-native products have R closer to software or to hardware. One camp notes that prompts are edited in minutes; the other that fixing a behaviour means changing the evaluation set, the data pipeline or the fine-tune, and that finding a regression takes weeks of traffic. Nobody has published Table 2's equivalent for a model.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this says hardware iterates slowly. Someone who has internalised it arrives at the design review with gate dates collected from suppliers, costs on either side of each, a probability with its source named, and an experiment costed to fit the float. They argue about which number is soft rather than whether to be careful, and ask the distributor for his cut-off date before asking engineering for a launch date. When the arithmetic is close, as Raikar's was at 20 against 26.6 per cent, they treat the closeness itself as the signal to buy information.

12. What each of them decided

Raikar authorised Ghatge's pilot on 11 February and held the 27 February release. The twelve shells went to Assam on 13 February; by 25 February nine had logged clean, two showed a 0.4 degree offset traceable to firmware averaging, and one failed on a cable strain. She released the hard tool on 27 February with the moulded boss, moved the averaging window into firmware, and added a second, unused mounting pad — ₹1.2 lakh of extra steel that bought a clamped-carrier option without a second cut. Her reasoning was Figure 3: the pilot was worth ₹7.06 lakh against ₹3.50 lakh of cost, and once it returned favourable, 5 per cent sat far below the 26.6 per cent break-even.

Sabnis recommended something the council had not asked for. He accepted the reformulation, because the break-even was severe in his favour: 1.80 crore tubes at ₹20.84 is ₹37.512 crore of contribution today, and at ₹23.19 after the saving it is ₹41.742 crore, so volume could fall 10.1 per cent before value was destroyed, and nothing in Dastane's panel supported a fall that large. But he refused the national roll-out, proposing Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh only, both cartons held one twelve-week cycle at a cost Sharmila Deodhar put at ₹19 lakh, with repeat read at day 90. He was, in effect, buying a bridge tool.

Three questions. First, was Sabnis's roll-out a genuine experiment or an expensive deferral of a decision already made? Second, the bridge tool would have cost ₹22 lakh more in expectation while preserving ₹82.88 lakh of downside protection — when does paying for optionality become an unwillingness to decide? Third, in a product you know, name the three highest-R decisions and the dates their gates close; if you cannot, who in your organisation can?

13. Going deeper

What a product manager does — the responsibilities this page holds constant. Hardware product management: what's different — bills of materials, lead times, certification and design for manufacture. Physical goods and CPG product management — Table 3's ladder expanded into pack architecture and distributor economics. PM myths vs reality — why "ship fast and learn" has a domain of validity. Origins of product management — the brand-management lineage behind Sabnis's job. PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder — who owns the freeze date. PM archetypes — which archetype a high-R product rewards. How the PM job changes by company stage — section 7 worked through. The end-to-end product lifecycle — where the gates sit from discovery to sunset.
case20v1-pm.sixps:
Hitkari Dukaan Systems: A Quarter's Plan Built on the Wrong Spine?

A case on the Six Ps framework

1. Opening

On Thursday 29 October 2026, Tanishka Pethe sat in a corner of the Bengaluru office of Hitkari Dukaan Systems with a printed backlog of 61 items and a blank slide titled "Plan for January to March". She was the head of product. On Monday 2 November she was due to present the quarter's plan to the chief executive, Dhruv Khosla, and the board, six days before Diwali, when neighbourhood shops across India do a large share of their annual sales.

But two weeks earlier Tanishka had asked her customer-success lead to sit behind the counters of twenty stores, and what came back made her unsure that the team had been building for the right person at all. She had a weekend and a Monday morning to decide what to propose.

2. Company background

Hitkari Dukaan Systems, founded in 2019 by Dhruv Khosla and a former distributor-sales manager, sells a mobile and WhatsApp-based shop-management app to India's neighbourhood general stores, the kiranas. Industry estimates put the number of such stores at around 1.2 crore. The app records customer credit (the "udhaar" that regulars run up and settle at month-end), tracks stock, and accepts UPI payments through a QR code tied to the shop's bank account.

The market is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the digital ledger habit; PhonePe for Business and Paytm put a payment device on the counter; Udaan and Jumbotail pursue the wholesale-ordering relationship; JioMart's partner programme and ONDC-linked buyer apps are courting the same owners with delivery. Hitkari offered a free tier and a ₹300-a-month paid plan with stock and reporting tools.

By October 2026 the app had 1,80,000 registered stores, of which 54,000, or 30 per cent, opened it at least once in the month. The team numbered 8 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a designer in Lisbon, a data scientist in Melbourne, a customer-success lead in Lucknow and a sales head in Gurugram.

3. The situation

The base was not uniform, and Exhibit 1 shows how. Of the 54,000 monthly-active stores, 60 per cent were small neighbourhood shops selling under ₹3 lakh a month, a quarter were mid-sized, and 15 per cent were large stores, typically selling about ₹12 lakh a month, which is ₹1.44 crore a year. The heavy users and the payers were not the same group: small stores were the majority but only 30 per cent opened the app three or more times a week, while 75 per cent of large stores did. Large stores were 15 per cent of active stores and yet produced 43.35 per cent of subscription revenue.

The backlog, shown in Exhibit 2, had grown in the way backlogs do. Nobody had ever written beside each item which kind of shop it was for. The two largest, a GST invoicing and filing module, and a distributor-ordering integration, came almost entirely from Jatin Wadhwani's sales team in Gurugram. Of fourteen large-store owners his team had spoken to that quarter, twelve asked for GST help.

Exhibit 2 makes the first difficulty plain: 100 engineer-weeks of wishes against 84 of capacity. The deeper difficulty came from Lucknow. Shabnam Siddiqui had visited twenty small and mid-sized shops over ten days. In thirteen of them, 65 per cent, the person who actually entered the day's credit sales was not the owner but a spouse, a son home from college, or a shop assistant who did the books in the evening. The owner decided whether to pay ₹300; the assistant decided whether the app was pleasant enough to open. Hitkari's research had been written about "the kirana owner" as if one person did both.

The GST module also gave her pause. E-invoicing is mandatory only above ₹5 crore of annual turnover. Even a large Hitkari store, at ₹1.44 crore, was well below it. Anirudh Subbaiah, the data scientist in Melbourne, confirmed that among the twelve GST-seeking large stores, usage of the existing stock tools was lower than the base average. They wanted GST help, but it was not clear they were the stores that would use the product.

4. The people

Dhruv Khosla, chief executive in Bengaluru, wanted a plan that raised revenue before the next funding conversation and distrusted anything that sounded like research. Jatin Wadhwani, sales head in Gurugram, wanted GST and ordering shipped, since large-store owners had told him that was the price of renewal. Shabnam Siddiqui, customer-success lead in Lucknow, argued that small shops were the future and that the assistant was a user nobody designed for. Matilde Ferraz, the designer in Lisbon, had been quietly sketching a voice-first ledger screen for months, and wanted a chance to test it with someone other than colleagues.

5. The options

Tanishka reduced the weekend's thinking to three distinct courses, compared in Exhibit 4. Exhibit 3 shows the calendar they all had to fit.

Option A: Follow the backlog's loudest demand. Build the GST module and the distributor integration, 52 engineer-weeks and ₹62.4 lakh. If the paying share among large stores rose from 25 to 40 per cent, there would be 3,240 payers instead of 2,025, an extra 1,215 stores and ₹3,64,500 a month, or ₹43.74 lakh a year. Payback would be about 17 months, if the lift happened, and the ceiling is the 8,100 large stores.

Option B: Pivot to the small shop. Build voice ledger entry and spend on vernacular onboarding: 14 engineer-weeks (₹16.8 lakh) plus ₹18.2 lakh of marketing, ₹35.0 lakh in all. If weekly-regular small stores rose from 30 to 45 per cent, that is 14,580 stores, 4,860 more than today. But at the current 4 per cent paying rate, roughly 194 of them would pay, about ₹58,000 a month. It builds the base and not the revenue.

Option C: Spend six weeks establishing the spine first. Run a structured discovery sprint from 9 November to 18 December with three people (a product manager, the Lisbon designer and one engineer), 18 person-weeks at ₹1.2 lakh, ₹21.6 lakh, plus ₹3.4 lakh of field costs, ₹25.0 lakh in all. Choose the persona and the problem, then commit the build quarter to what the evidence supports. The cost is that nothing ships in November, and Dhruv must accept a plan with a question mark in it.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, who is the "customer" for Hitkari today? Is "kirana owner" a persona or a segment, and what does Shabnam's finding add?
  2. For the GST module, state the persona, the problem and the proposition in one sentence each. Where does the chain break?
  3. Option A pays back in about 17 months and Option B barely pays at all. Does that make Option C the safe choice or only the slow one? What would change your answer?
  4. If you were Tanishka on Monday, what exactly would you ask the board to approve, and what would you tell Jatin?

7. A note for the learner

The Six Ps are Persona, Problem, Proposal, Proposition, Priority and Plan, in that order. The point of the order is that the later checkpoints inherit the quality of the earlier ones. Hitkari's team had started at the fifth, Priority, ranking features by cost and by who shouted loudest, and had a plan before anyone had agreed on a persona.

Read the case through the spine. The Persona is blurred: the owner pays and the assistant uses, and these are different people with different jobs. The Problem is not yet stated; "needs GST" is a request, not a problem, and the e-invoicing threshold suggests the stated need may belong to a minority. The Proposal, the GST module, therefore has no proposition behind it. Priority, the engineer-week arithmetic in Exhibit 2, was done well, but on a list with no persona attached.

One defensible path is Option C, with discipline. Tanishka should propose a plan that is explicit about its question: a six-week sprint from 9 November, costing ₹25.0 lakh, whose exit is a written persona (owner and assistant treated separately), a single ranked problem and a proposition tested with at least ten stores, with the decision readout on 18 December. She should commit 4 January onward, 84 engineer-weeks, to whichever proposal survives. Dhruv's worry about revenue is met by giving the sprint a revenue test: it must say which segment can plausibly add paying stores faster than Option A's 1,215. Jatin's twelve GST accounts become interview subjects.

Why not A? Its best-case return of ₹43.74 lakh a year on ₹62.4 lakh depends on a persona the evidence does not yet support. Why not B? It addresses a real user but pays almost nothing unless the paying rate also rises, which nothing in the case says it will. Option C is not a refusal to decide. It is a decision about which checkpoint to spend money on first, and a student who can say why that checkpoint is Persona has understood the framework.
exp20v2-pm.sixps:
The Six Ps framework

Persona, Problem, Proposal, Proposition, Priority, Plan: keeping a whole product effort in your head.

1. A backlog of 143 items

On Monday 6 July 2026, Bharati Venkatesan, product manager at Deepmala Home Care Network, opened the planning document for the quarter ending 30 September and counted the backlog. It held 143 items. Deepmala runs an app through which households in Pune, Nagpur and Indore book trained cleaners for kitchens, bathrooms and full-flat deep cleans. Its founder and chief executive, Chirag Oberoi, had asked for a roadmap by Friday 24 July. Everyone had a favourite: a referral scheme, a subscription plan, a new rating screen, a Hindi interface, a loyalty wallet.

The numbers made the choice uncomfortable. Deepmala had spent ₹2.4 crore on performance marketing in the previous quarter, and only 22 per cent of new customers booked a second time within 90 days. The squad Bharati could draw on had 7 person-months of engineering capacity after maintenance. If she spent it on features that did not move repeat booking, the company would burn another ₹2.4 crore filling a leaking bucket and Chirag would be raising money in the autumn on a flat curve.

Divya Nambiar, the design lead, offered a different way to start. She wrote six words on a whiteboard in a row and said that a roadmap should be the last of them, not the first. This page follows Bharati as she works through those six words: what each one asks, how they connect, and where the framework stops being able to help her.

2. The idea

The Six Ps is a checklist of six checkpoints that a product effort passes in order, and that a product manager revisits whenever evidence arrives. The Persona is the specific kind of person the product is for. The Problem is the difficulty that person has, stated in their terms and supported by evidence. The Proposal is the candidate solution, or set of solutions, that might relieve it. The Proposition is the promise the customer hears: why this, from you, is worth choosing. The Priority is the decision about which proposals get resourced first. The Plan is the sequence of work, owners and dates that turns the priority into delivery.

No single author owns the framework. It descends from the older marketing habit of the “four Ps” (product, price, place, promotion), which McCarthy popularised in 1960 and which starts from what the firm sells. Product teams in the following decades, and the teardown-led courses at business schools that teach the role, reversed the direction: begin with the person and the problem and let the product be a late answer. The six-part version is a teaching spine, not a standard, and different teams swap in different labels. Its value lies in the ordering.

The problem it was invented to solve is the backlog that Bharati faced: a list of solutions with no recorded reasoning about whom they serve. The sentence she could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this one: “Before we argue about what to build, can we say who it is for, what is hard for them, and how we would know?”

3. How it works

Bharati took the checkpoints in order, writing each answer in a single sentence before she was allowed the next.

Persona. Deepmala’s analytics showed three kinds of buyers: dual-income couples in rented two-bedroom flats, older households with a regular maid who wanted a quarterly deep clean, and landlords preparing flats for tenants. She chose the first, because they booked most often and tolerated the least slack. She described them as a person, not a demographic: a couple in Pune’s Baner area, both working, who book a deep clean once a quarter and are at home for a one-hour window only.

Problem. The team had surveyed 1,200 customers from the previous quarter. Of these, 372 named the cleaner arriving late or not at all as their worst experience, which is 31 per cent. That is a stated frequency, not yet a cause. The implicit step practitioners skip is to ask what the customer does today instead: these couples stayed home and waited, or cancelled and rebooked on a rival platform.

Proposal. The team’s ideas that touched the problem were live arrival tracking (so the customer sees the cleaner’s progress), a referral reward and a subscription plan with a fixed cleaner. Another step usually left implicit: proposals are hypotheses about how the problem will be relieved, so each should be written with the measure it is expected to move.

Proposition. Here the team stated the promise to the customer: “A trained cleaner at your door in a confirmed 60-minute window, or ₹300 back.” A proposition is not a slogan. It is a commitment that the operations team must be able to keep, and it disciplines the proposals, since tracking helps keep the promise and a referral scheme does not.

Priority and Plan. Only now did the team weigh the options and sequence them, the subject of the next section.

4. A worked example

For Priority, Bharati used RICE scoring, a convention developed at Intercom. Reach is the number of customers affected in a quarter; Impact is a judged score of 0.25 (minimal), 0.5, 1, 2 or 3 (massive) for each of them; Confidence is how sure the team is of both estimates; Effort is in person-months. The score is Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. It is a ranking device, not a forecast.

 Table 1. First pass. A: 60,000 × 2 × 0.8 ÷ 4 = 24,000. B: 20,000 × 3 × 0.5 ÷ 6 = 5,000. C: 90,000 × 0.5 × 0.8 ÷ 3 = 12,000.

With 7 person-months available, the ranking funds A (4) and C (3), which together use exactly 7. B, at 6 person-months, does not fit. A decision that looks like a debate about taste has become an arithmetic one, and the assumptions, not the scores, are where the argument now lives.

Now change one input. Dhruv Wagh, the operations head, warned that most late arrivals came from cleaners who accepted overlapping jobs, which tracking would display but not fix. Bharati lowered A’s confidence from 80 to 50 per cent, and, because a tracking feature that also had to alert dispatchers would need more work, raised its effort from 4 to 6 person-months.

The order flips: C leads at 12,000, A follows at 10,000. But A now costs 6 person-months, and after funding C (3) only 4 of the 7 remain. Neither A nor B fits. Two conclusions follow. The score is sensitive to a single honest correction, which is the point of showing it; and the Plan checkpoint has something to say, because the fix is to cut A into a 4-person-month first slice that is genuinely shippable, not to quietly overspend.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

The order is a logic, not a schedule

Nobody finishes Persona in week one and never returns to it. The order says which answer depends on which. If the Persona changes, every later answer is suspect.

Persona is not a market segment

A segment is a group defined by attributes the company can count; a persona is a described representative whose behaviour you can reason about. “Women aged 25 to 40 in tier-1 cities” is a segment. The couple in Baner is a persona. The next topic in this series, market segments versus personas, develops the distinction.

A problem is not an absence of your solution

“Customers lack a tracking screen” is a proposal wearing a problem’s clothes. A test: could someone propose a different solution to the same sentence? If not, it is not a problem statement.

Proposal and Proposition are different audiences

The proposal is addressed to the team and says what might be built. The proposition is addressed to the customer and says what they get. Teams that merge the two ship features that cannot be described to anyone outside.

Priority needs a stated currency

Scoring only ranks options against a chosen outcome. Bharati’s outcome was repeat booking within 90 days. Had it been gross bookings, the referral reward would have scored differently.

Estimates carry the bias of their owners

Impact is a judgement. People score their own proposals higher. Cheap protection: have someone who does not own the idea score it, and record the evidence behind each number.

The framework cannot tell you whether the Persona is the right one

It organises thinking; it cannot supply the insight that a different customer might be a bigger business. Choosing the persona is a strategic bet.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Which checkpoint is weakest in evidence? Which answer would, if wrong, invalidate all the later ones? Who in the room has seen the persona at home?

6. How it varies by product and by stage

In a consumer product, like Deepmala, the persona is a person and the buyer and user coincide. In B2B, the person who pays, the person who uses and the person who approves differ, so Persona becomes a small set, and a proposition that delights the user may fail the purchasing committee. In a marketplace there are two personas at once, here the household and the cleaner, and a proposal that helps one can hurt the other; Dhruv’s overlapping jobs exist because cleaners were paid per job.

Early-stage companies run the six quickly and loosely, often in a single sitting, and revisit constantly. A large company has the opposite risk: the checkpoints become a document template filled in to justify a decision already taken. The remedy is the same in both: each checkpoint needs a named piece of evidence.

7. Common mistakes

Starting from the backlog

Symptom: the roadmap reads as a list of features with no customer named. Misunderstanding: that the backlog is the input. Diagnostic: pick any item and ask, “For whom, and what is hard for them?” If the answer takes more than a sentence, stop.

A persona nobody could meet

Symptom: a persona with a stock photograph and invented hobbies. Misunderstanding: that a persona is a creative artefact. Diagnostic: name three real customers who fit it and when you last spoke to one.

A proposition the operations team cannot keep

Symptom: refunds spike after launch. Misunderstanding: that the promise is a marketing line. Diagnostic: ask the delivery owner to sign the promise before it is published.

Treating the score as the decision

Symptom: the highest number wins without discussion. Misunderstanding: that RICE is objective. Diagnostic: change one input by a plausible amount, as the second pass did, and see if the order holds.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Bharati’s week produces a single page. It names the Baner couple and the 1,200-customer survey behind the 31 per cent. It states the problem without a solution in it, lists three proposals with the metric each should move, carries the 60-minute promise signed by Dhruv, shows both scoring passes, and ends with a plan in which each slice is shippable inside the 7 person-months. Anyone joining the team on Monday can read it in ten minutes and say what the team is doing and what it is not.

9. Closing

On Friday 24 July, Bharati presented the page to Chirag. She recommended funding the referral reward in full (3 person-months) and a 4-person-month first slice of arrival tracking limited to confirmed slots, with dispatch alerts held back until Dhruv’s team had changed the job-acceptance rules. Her reasoning was that the leak was operational, so the proposal that treated it as a display problem deserved only a part of the capacity, and that a promise Deepmala could not keep was worse than none.

To go further, read about market segments versus personas, and then about why personas matter, since the Persona checkpoint is where most of the later error originates.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of your own current projects could you take back to the Persona line and describe in one sentence without naming a feature? Second, if your highest-scoring item lost half its confidence tomorrow, would your plan survive?

The Six Ps framework

Persona, Problem, Proposal, Proposition, Priority, Plan — read not as a checklist but as a dependency order, and as a register of what a team has not yet earned the right to decide.

1. Two decisions, four weeks apart

On Monday 12 January 2026 Kalyani Dharwadkar had nineteen engineer-months of demand in front of her and eleven to spend. Maapdand Metering Systems of Ahmedabad, where she is senior product manager, makes ultrasonic bulk water meters and the district-metering software that reads them; Table 1 is its installed base. Lohit Chaubal, the engineering head, had three engineers for the five months to end-May — fifteen engineer-months, four pre-committed to firmware for a Bureau of Indian Standards recertification.

Table 1. Installed base at 31 December 2025. Revenue is meters × annual rate. The last row sums Contracts, Meters and Revenue, and averages the rate: ₹2,85,27,000 ÷ 1,42,000 = ₹200.89 a meter.
SegmentContractsMetersSoftware ₹ per meter per yearSoftware revenue (₹ lakh a year)

Total (average rate)971,42,000200.89285.27

Four proposals competed for the eleven free months: a non-revenue-water analytics module for utility engineers, a household billing portal, cheaper-meter firmware, and a tamper-detection alert. Mukund Khaparde, the chief executive, wanted a decision by Friday 30 January; two tenders, closing 31 March and 30 June, turned on it.

Four weeks later, on Tuesday 10 February 2026, Malvika Chitnis had a harder problem in Pune. Laukik Learning Network sells a maths-practice subscription for Classes 9 to 12 in Marathi and Hindi; in the quarter to 31 December 2025 it spent ₹1.92 crore for 3,20,000 installs, ₹60 each. Keya Bhagat, the growth analyst, traced that cohort to end-January: 80,000 accounts, 28,000 completing a practice set in week one, 3,500 paying ₹1,200 within sixty days, 1,400 paying again next quarter. That is ₹5,486 of acquisition cost per payer against ₹1,680 of revenue (₹1,200 plus 40 per cent of a second ₹1,200) and ₹1,176 of contribution at a 70 per cent margin. Lalit Barhate had capital for two quarters.

Both believed they had a prioritisation problem. Neither did: Kalyani's best proposal did not fit her capacity, and Malvika could build nothing to repair the arithmetic above. The Six Ps earns its keep by exposing which earlier answer was assumed rather than evidenced — call it evidence debt.

2. The idea, and the five schools that disagree about it

The Six Ps are six questions answered in an order fixed by dependency, not calendar. Persona: for which described person is this? Problem: what is hard for them, in their units, measured? Proposal: what might relieve it, and what measure should each candidate move? Proposition: what promise does the customer hear, and who signs it? Priority: given capacity and the cost of delay, what is funded first? Plan: who does what, by when, in slices.

The framework is clearer once you see what it reacts against. Its oldest ancestor runs the other way: McCarthy's four Ps of 1960 — product, price, place, promotion — organise the brand man created by Neil McElroy's 1931 Procter & Gamble memorandum, and every item in that mix is a company action. The reversal came the same year, with Levitt's railways, which declined by defining themselves by what they operated rather than what customers needed. Christensen's jobs-to-be-done, Blank's customer development, Ries's build-measure-learn loop, Cagan's discovery and Torres's opportunity solution tree all push one way: begin with the person and the difficulty. The Six Ps compresses that into six words, taught on day one because the dominant habit is to begin with a backlog.

Table 2. Five schools and the commitments that separate them; no synthesis is offered because none is held.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Problem-first discovery (Christensen, Cagan, Torres)No solution before the problem has evidence.That a promise can be fixed before its proposals are tested.
Proposition-first (Amazon's working-backwards release and FAQ)Write the promise first; proposals are whatever keeps it.That the proposition summarises what discovery produced.
Capability-first (hardware, frontier model work)Some products exist because a capability became cheap.That every effort begins at the Persona line.
Flow economics (Reinertsen)Priority is economics under a capacity constraint.That Priority is downstream of a good Proposition.
Strategy-first (Rumelt)The Persona is chosen, not discovered.That one may start at the Persona line without a market.

What all five would sign is load-bearing: a later answer is only as good as the earliest it rests on. Changing the Persona puts all five later answers in question; the Problem four, the Proposal three, the Proposition two, Priority one, the Plan none. Debt at the top of that ladder is the expensive kind.

3. Mechanics in depth: Kalyani's eighteen days

Persona. Maapdand had three candidates: the municipal engineer accountable for non-revenue water, the household that receives the bill, and the procurement officer who signs. Kalyani chose the first: all three are real, and the question was which Maapdand could serve best. Her note read: "the deputy engineer (water) in a corporation of 15 to 25 lakh residents, accountable for a non-revenue-water figure reported upwards each quarter. Not the household. Not procurement."

Problem. The arithmetic must be done in the customer's units. One corporation in western India, serving 19 lakh residents and tendering under the national urban water programme, pumps 300 million litres a day and bills against 189. The 111 MLD of the 300 MLD pumped that is never billed — 37.0 per cent — is non-revenue water. A pilot across 48 district metered areas split it 62 per cent physical leakage, 38 per cent commercial loss: 68.82 MLD and 42.18 MLD. At ₹8.40 a kilolitre of production cost, leakage is 68,820 kilolitres a day, 2,51,19,300 a year, ₹21.10 crore never sold. Commercial loss is delivered but unbilled, so it carries the ₹11.00 metered tariff: 1,53,95,700 kilolitres, ₹16.94 crore a year.

Two steps are usually left implicit. First the recovery fraction: nobody eliminates leakage, and the pressure-management literature supports about a fifth of physical loss in year one, so a fifth of ₹21.10 crore is ₹4.22 crore. Second Maapdand's share, 8 per cent of verified saving — ₹33.76 lakh a year here. The commercial side, at a cautious 10 per cent recovery, gives ₹1.69 crore saved and ₹13.55 lakh of licence. A smaller council at 0.6 of the first adds ₹20.26 lakh and ₹8.13 lakh. Revenue at stake: ₹54.02 lakh from leakage analytics, ₹21.68 lakh from tamper detection.

Proposal. Each candidate was rewritten with the measure it should move, which demoted the billing portal: it touches customer satisfaction, for which nobody was accountable, not non-revenue water.

Proposition. Kalyani drafted one sentence: "we will find your lost water, zone by zone, with evidence a third-party auditor will accept, and we will be paid out of what you recover." A proposition is not a slogan but a commitment someone must sign. Madhavi Sarnaik, who runs field service, signed only after a verification protocol was added, because a share-of-saving contract makes revenue depend on a measurement the customer's auditor controls.

Priority. Maapdand does not score in points. Because tenders close on dates, delay has a rupee cost, so it uses cost of delay divided by duration — Reinertsen's rule — treating a month of delay as a third of first-year revenue, the tender calendar moving in quarters.

Table 3. Priority pass, 12 January 2026. Cost of delay = revenue at stake ÷ 3; score = displayed cost of delay ÷ duration, in ₹ lakh avoided per engineer-month. The last row sums the displayed column (18.01 + 4.20 + 14.47 + 7.23) and the durations.

Read naively the table says: fund C, then D, then stop. C and D take six engineer-months; A needs seven and five remain, B six. Five months idle, and the module the Proposition depends on unbuilt. Two observations rescue it. C's 3.618 and D's 3.615 differ by three thousandths, noise in inputs judged to one significant figure. And a Proposition constrains the proposal set rather than competing within it: without A there is no "lost water" promise to sell.

Plan. The Plan checkpoint then did what the framework's linear presentation hides — it changed the Priority. Kalyani and Lohit took A apart and found two of its seven engineer-months were a bespoke mapping integration and a printed-report builder, both on the tender's wish-list, neither producing a rupee of saving. Dropped, A became a five-month slice, A′, with the same cost of delay and so a score of 3.602, level with C and D. Five plus four plus two is exactly eleven.

4. When the framework applies, stated as tests

The conditions under which the Six Ps helps are testable.

Table 4. Four testable conditions, applied to Maapdand (January 2026) and Laukik (February 2026).
ConditionMaapdandLaukik
Measurable in the persona's own unitsHolds. The engineer already reports non-revenue water.Fails. The parent's unit is "will my child pass".
No harm to another persona neededHolds, bar work for Madhavi's crews.Fails. What holds a teenager, a parent distrusts.
Capacity is the binding constraintHolds. Eleven engineer-months against nineteen.Fails. Willingness to pay is what is scarce.
Value verifiable before the next paymentHolds. Reconciliation precedes renewal.Fails. A quarter cannot show a change in marks.

Where three or four fail, the framework is working the wrong layer: it organises a conversation about features when the live question is whether this persona can be reached and charged at all. It can also mislead. In capability-first work the Proposal precedes the Problem, and forcing a persona narrative onto it produces fiction. In regulated products the Plan holds statutory dates Priority cannot move — Maapdand's four reserved months are imposed, not chosen.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company the six are answered at two altitudes. Problem and Proposal belong to the squad; Proposition is owned at brand level, because a promise the whole company makes cannot be redrafted by one team. The seam shows as a feature defensible on its own evidence that violates a promise made elsewhere. Mature firms run a forum on propositions, and call it alignment.

In two-sided businesses the honest move is to run all six twice, once per side, reconciling at the Proposition line, where the promises must be compatible rather than identical. A blended persona is the characteristic error, and the weaker side is what gets averaged away.

Hardware plus software breaks the assumption that the Plan is the most flexible checkpoint. Proposal C was four engineer-months of firmware, but the cheaper meter needed an injection mould with a fourteen-week lead time, validated by a contract engineer, Lena Kowalczyk, in Kraków. No re-cutting of software shortens fourteen weeks. Here the Plan constrains Priority, which is why hardware product managers look conservative and are usually just numerate.

AI-native products invert the order honestly: a capability that reads a photographed handwritten sum and returns a worked solution arrives before any persona is named. The disciplined response is to run the six backwards once, from Proposal to Problem to Persona, then forwards with evidence. The extra obligation at the Proposition line is to state the failure mode — "a worked solution in seconds" is incomplete without "and when unsure, it says so", because a confidently wrong step destroys more trust than a slow answer.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The order is a dependency graph, not a schedule. The competent practitioner works through the six and considers them done; the expert asks which earlier answer is load-bearing now. The tell: if we were wrong about who this is for, what else here dies?

The Persona is chosen, not discovered. Research describes people you have already decided to serve; it cannot tell you which market to be in. The tell is that an expert's note records a rejection, as Kalyani's did. A persona excluding nobody is a market description.

A problem stated in your units is not a problem. "Customers lack arrival tracking" names a proposal; "non-revenue water is 37.0 per cent and is reported upwards quarterly" names a problem, because several proposals could address it. The test: could a rival propose something entirely different to the sentence?

The Proposition is a constraint, not a summary. The proposal set faces inward and says what might be built; the proposition faces outward and says what the customer gets. Once a promise is made, the proposals under it stop competing for funding; they are its price.

Priority has a currency, and the currency is usually time. Dimensionless points rank options but cannot say whether delay costs money. Where delay has a date attached — a tender, a deadline, a festival season — cost of delay divided by duration is stronger because its output has units. The tell: can the team price a month?

Scope is an input to Priority. The competent practitioner estimates effort, then ranks. The expert ranks, sees what does not fit, and re-cuts the scope of what matters until it does, as A became A′. Treating estimates as given is how a correct model yields a wrong plan.

A near-tie is information, not a tie-break problem. At 3.618 against 3.615 the model has said the two are indistinguishable, and further argument is about rounding. The expert then decides on a criterion the model does not contain — sequencing risk, team learning, April leave.

Evidence debt accrues interest. A weak answer at checkpoint one is a liability settled later at a multiple, because every downstream commitment compounds it. The expert's artefact is therefore one page with an evidence column, where a revision at the Persona line marks the answers below it provisional. Teams without that column revise quietly, and nobody can later say which commitments rest on an abandoned belief.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products buyer and user usually coincide, which is why single-persona discipline works there — and why Laukik is instructive, its user a teenager and its payer a parent. In B2B and enterprise the persona is a set — user, buyer, approver — and the winning promise often addresses the approver. Platforms and marketplaces run the framework twice; in hardware lead times dominate; in AI products the Proposal space is nearly free to explore, which makes measured Problem evidence the scarce good.

Two things do not differ: the Problem line everywhere demands a measured figure in the customer's units with a named source, and a Proposition everywhere needs a signatory who can be held to it.

Stage changes the difficulty, not the content. At seed stage a team runs all six in one sitting and expects the Persona to change within the quarter; the risk is attachment, not sloppiness. At Laukik's and Maapdand's stage Priority is the visibly hard checkpoint, Persona the quietly expensive one. In large companies all six are filled in as a template, ratifying a decision already taken.

8. Three worked examples

Mandali Freight Exchange, a Nagpur marketplace matching shippers with truck owners, had run the six Ps once, on the shipper. Manali Pujari, its product lead, ran them again on the truck owner and found the problem was not load availability but unpaid waiting at the loading point. The proposal: a confirmed loading slot with a driver penalty. In the quarter ended 30 June 2026, 18,240 of 48,000 posted loads were matched, 38.0 per cent; in the quarter ended 30 September 2026, 28,080 of 52,000, 54.0 per cent. At ₹1,450 a matched load that is ₹2.64 crore rising to ₹4.07 crore, up ₹1.43 crore across two comparable quarters.

Kshemkari Benefits Services of Chennai administers employee health benefits for 42 enterprises covering 2.9 lakh employees at ₹640 per covered employee a year, ₹18.56 crore of annual recurring revenue. Of 1,46,000 claims in FY2026, 23,360 were rejected, and 14,016 of those 23,360 rejections — 60.0 per cent — were for missing documents. Kartik Bhave's team chose the chief financial officer's proposition over the employee's: not "claims filed in a minute" but "benefits spend audited to the rupee". One checklist served both. In FY2027, 12,640 of 1,58,000 claims were rejected, 8.0 per cent, and renewals moved from 36 of 42 to 40 of 43 enterprises.

Lohpath Equipment Industries of Coimbatore is the failure. It makes industrial pumps and in 2024 instrumented 1,800 of them at ₹9,400 a unit — ₹1.69 crore — to sell monitoring at ₹24,000 a pump a year. Mihika Chiplunkar's team completed all six checkpoints fluently, and the persona, the plant maintenance engineer, had a real problem: unplanned downtime. But he held no budget; procurement, which approved purchases, saw a subscription on a machine already paid for. Against a target of 460 subscriptions, 38 sold — 8.26 per cent of target, ₹9.12 lakh of annual revenue against ₹1.10 crore planned.

Table 5. Lohpath: failed and recovered propositions. Energy per pump per year: 37 kW × 5,100 hours = 1,88,700 kWh; at ₹7.60, ₹14,34,120; a 6 per cent saving is ₹86,047; 15 per cent of that, ₹12,907, is rounded to ₹12,900.
CheckpointOriginal (2024–25)Recovered (2025–26)
PersonaPlant maintenance engineerPlant energy manager
Problem, in their unitsDowntime, in hoursEnergy cost per pump, ₹ a year
PropositionFewer breakdowns, flat fee15 per cent of verified saving
Price per pump per year (₹)24,00012,900
Pumps subscribed38640
Annual revenue (₹ lakh)9.1282.56

The recovery, driven by Kishore Dhume against internal resistance, was not a feature but a return to the Persona and Problem lines: the energy manager did hold a budget and did report a number upward. Repricing at 15 per cent of verified saving, ₹12,900 a pump, was lower per unit, but 640 pumps subscribed against 38 — ₹82.56 lakh against ₹9.12 lakh, a payback on the sunk ₹1.69 crore of 2.05 years.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Starting from the backlog. Early sign: items described by what they are rather than whom they are for. Diagnostic: ask who it is for and what is hard for them. Caught late it costs a quarter of capacity and credibility for the next re-plan.

Choosing the persona by reachability. Early sign: acquisition cost per payer rising while engagement looks healthy. Diagnostic: who actually pays, and when did we last speak to one? Laukik's ₹1.92 crore in a quarter is the late-catch cost.

A proposition with no signatory. Early sign: the promise lives in marketing copy and no operations owner has agreed it. Diagnostic: who signs this, and what happens to them if it is not kept? Caught late: refunds, penalties, a lost audit.

Prioritising in the wrong currency. Early sign: items with a dated cost of delay losing to items with none. Diagnostic: what does a month of delay cost? At Maapdand the answer for A was ₹18.01 lakh a month.

Completing the template. Early sign: all six answered fluently, no source named. Diagnostic: point at the data behind line two.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the Proposition precede or follow the Proposal? The working-backwards school holds that writing the promise and the objections first disciplines everything after, citing products so specified that shipped coherently. The discovery school holds that a promise written before any proposal is tested is a commitment to a hypothesis, citing launches that kept a promise nobody wanted. Each fails where the other's evidence generalises: the first when the team lacks intuition about the problem, the second when exploring proposals is expensive.

Is Priority an economic calculation or a strategic judgement? The flow-economics position is that teams misjudge sequencing systematically, that cost of delay divided by duration corrects it, and that most priority disputes are about estimates in disguise. The strategy position is that such models optimise within a frame and say nothing about the frame — Lohpath's model would have ranked features for the maintenance engineer. For the second to suffice alone, framing would have to prevent idle capacity, which it does not.

Is single-persona discipline clarity or distortion? One camp insists on one persona per effort, because a product serving two people serves neither. The other holds that most businesses are multi-sided and the rule hides the weaker side until it collapses. The test is whether the gains are complementary: Kshemkari's were, Mandali's were not until each side was run separately.

Does the framework survive capability-first products? The strong claim is that the Six Ps is a general spine and running it backwards costs nothing. The counter-claim is that this is a retrofit, and that dressing a capability as a persona story teaches new managers to fabricate. The compromise, which neither camp holds, is to keep the artefact and state which checkpoint was answered first.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the framework produces six filled sections. Someone who has internalised it names the checkpoint weakest in evidence, treats the artefact as a liability register rather than a plan, and locates a disagreement on the ladder. Kalyani's dispute with Lohit over A was never about effort but about whether the Proposition was a candidate or a constraint — which, said aloud, dissolved it.

12. Two decisions

On Friday 30 January 2026 Kalyani recommended exactly eleven engineer-months: A′ at five, the meter firmware C at four, tamper alerts D at two, the billing portal deferred. The Proposition bound A′ in regardless of score; C and D, indistinguishable on the model, were sequenced by the mould lead time; and the ₹54.02 lakh of licence revenue needed Madhavi's protocol. She flagged the figure she least trusted: the 20 per cent recovery fraction on which the cost-of-delay column rests.

Malvika's decision was harder, because the honest answer was to stop doing something. Keya's pilot of a weekly parent report was clean: of 2,400 practice-completers split evenly, 198 of the 1,200 treated paid within sixty days (16.5 per cent) against 150 of the 1,200 controls (12.5 per cent) — a four-point lift, two-sided p about 0.005. Applied to all 28,000 practice-completers that is 1,120 extra payers and ₹13.44 lakh a quarter — yet it moves acquisition cost per payer only from ₹5,486 to ₹4,156, against ₹1,176 of contribution. So Malvika shipped the report, then recommended cutting paid installs to near zero and re-running the Persona checkpoint on the tuition-centre owner as a distribution persona. The first eleven centres carried 180 students each: 1,980 students at a bulk ₹600 a quarter is ₹11.88 lakh of revenue and ₹8.32 lakh of contribution against ₹99,000 of field cost.

  1. Kalyani's ranking rests on a 20 per cent recovery fraction. If the true figure were 10 per cent, which rows of Table 3 change order, and would her plan change?
  2. Laukik's pilot produced a sound four-point lift that does not fix the business. What does that say about the Proposition and Persona checkpoints?
  3. Lohpath completed all six checkpoints and still lost ₹1.69 crore. Design the one column you would add to their document, and say who signs it.

13. Going deeper

The end-to-end product lifecycle places the six checkpoints along a timeline. Market segments vs personas attacks the load-bearing distinction here: Kalyani chose a persona; "municipal corporations in western India" is a segment. Why personas gives the standard a usable one meets. What a product manager does and PM myths vs reality name who owns each checkpoint; origins of product management extends section 2; PM vs PMM vs TPM vs project manager vs founder matters because the Proposition is where those roles collide; PM archetypes and how the PM job changes by company stage explain why two managers weight the six differently.
case40v1-pm.sixps:
Libaas Linen Works: Sixty-Nine Sites and No Agreed Customer

An ambiguous case for discussion. Pune, November 2026.

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

The Libaas Linen Works office in Baner, Pune, was empty except for Sharanya Rajagopal and a humming server cabinet. It was a quarter to ten on Sunday 15 November 2026. On Wednesday she would face the board's product committee and say what her engineers would build between Monday 4 January and Friday 2 April 2027, the thirteen weeks the budget documents called the product quarter.

Three documents were open. Taufiq Vora's pipeline sheet: eighteen qualified opportunities worth ₹156.7 lakh of annual contract value, with a margin note reading all gated on job-work. Anju Pappachan's field report of 14 October: at eleven of the fourteen sites she had visited, the person who opened Chihna most often was a delivery-van driver nobody had asked for an opinion. And a telemetry note Hana Jeong had sent from Seoul nine days earlier, on 6 November, beginning: I do not think we can tell who is using this product.

Sharanya had joined fourteen months earlier to turn an internal tool into a business. She had sixty-nine live sites, ₹83.31 lakh of annual recurring revenue, nine engineers for the quarter ahead, and a board thesis requiring that revenue to multiply just over thirtyfold by FY2029. What she did not have was a sentence she believed about who the customer was.

2. How Libaas got here

Libaas Linen Works was founded in August 2017 by Abhiraj Kanekar, who had run operations for a hotel-supplies distributor, and Jayashree Mulgund, an industrial engineer from Nashik. Their proposition, ordinary in Europe and unusual in India: rather than wash a hotel's bedsheets, Libaas would own them. The hotel paid per piece delivered, clean and counted, and never bought linen again. The model tied up capital in cotton but made Libaas care how long a towel lasted.

The first plant was at Chakan, outside Pune; Nashik followed in 2019. The pandemic reshaped the company: hospital linen, until then a side business, became the whole business for eighteen months, and its discipline became Libaas's competence. Goa and Jaipur opened in 2021, Hyderabad in April 2025, Kochi in June 2025, taking the group to six plants. In the year to 30 September 2026 they issued 6.10 crore pieces at an average realisation of ₹11.00: laundry-services revenue of ₹67.10 crore, EBITDA of ₹6.71 crore, or 10.0 per cent.

The decision that now constrained everything was made in November 2023, when linen loss — pieces that left a plant and never came back — was running at 0.40 per cent of pieces issued. Jayashree wanted tags sewn into every piece and a system that could say where each one was; she and Abhiraj, with four engineers, built it in-house and called it Chihna. To get it live across four plants in five months they made one simplifying assumption, written into the schema and never revisited: every piece of linen has exactly one owner, and that owner is Libaas.

In February 2025 a growth fund led a ₹118 crore round. Devraj Pandit's memorandum valued the laundry business on its plants and contracts, and everything above that on a second thesis: Chihna, sold to other people, reaching ₹25 crore of annual recurring revenue by FY2029.

3. The industry

Institutional laundry in India is large, fragmented and almost entirely unbranded. A few organised operators serve the branded chains — IHCL's properties, Lemon Tree, the inventory Oyo aggregates — and hospital groups such as Apollo, Manipal and Narayana Health. Beneath them sits an enormous layer of family-run dhobi ghat operations and single-boiler plants doing job work: the hotel owns the linen, the laundry washes it for a fee, and nobody can tell you where the sheets are.

That distinction — rental against job work — is the fault line of this case. Libaas is a rental operator; nine in ten of the laundries that might buy its software do job work, and their pain is not lost cotton, because the cotton is not theirs. It is the month-end argument about how many pieces went out and how many came back, which they usually lose.

Three outside forces pressed on the product. GST e-invoicing is mandatory above ₹5 crore of annual turnover, and 17 of the 23 paying laundries are above that line, so a billing export that reconciles to the invoice is not optional. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bears on the hotel-side features, which record which named attendant signed for which trolley: that makes the hotel a data fiduciary and Libaas a processor, and the standard contract was not drafted for it. And the 865–867 MHz tag band is delicensed by the Wireless Planning and Coordination wing, so prospects own readers from several vendors and expect Chihna to talk to them.

Exhibit 1 is less a map of competitors than of substitutes. Hospitality software firms such as IDS Next, and systems like Oracle's OPERA, already sit on the hotel's desk; Reliance Retail's uniform-rental business runs its own tracking. The commonest competitor is a spreadsheet.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Chihna Open's first external site went live in September 2025: an unpaid pilot at a Ludhiana job-work laundry, Sopan Dhulai Works, persuaded to put Libaas-owned trial linen into its own circulation so the schema would work. Nobody registered this as a workaround, not a sale. Commercial launch followed in January 2026; Taufiq joined in February and sold hard. Third-party deployments reached scale in May 2026, the first hotel-side deployment — where the hotel, not the laundry, held the licence — in June. Exhibit 2 lays out the sequence.

By 30 September 2026 the base looked like Exhibit 3: sixty-nine sites, six of them Libaas's own plants and unpaid, and ₹83.31 lakh of recurring revenue across the other sixty-three, ₹1.32 lakh a site. Recognised product revenue for the year was lower, ₹61.40 lakh, because most contracts began part-way through it. The product organisation — ten engineers, a designer in Manchester, a data scientist in Seoul, two customer-success staff and Sharanya — cost ₹618.40 lakh, a net drag of ₹557.00 lakh against ₹6.71 crore of laundry EBITDA.

That last ratio had set Hana off. If one seat is shared by two or three people, the role recorded against a session is the role of the seat, not of the human holding the handset. Exhibit 4 is usage as the system reports it.

Read one way, Exhibit 4 is the most important fact in the company: drivers and floor supervisors open the product 72.0 and 58.0 times a month, while the people who sign the cheque open it twelve. The person Taufiq's deck calls "the customer" is 10.2 per cent of users and 2.4 per cent of sessions. Read another way, that is what field software always looks like. The housekeeping row sits between the two readings: at 42.0 sessions it is 41.7 per cent below the driver row, yet those features are the newest in the product and the ones Taufiq says prospects ask for. Imogen read that as broken screens; Hana read four months as too short to read at all.

Anju's report questioned the problem, not the user: what people argued about was not where a sheet was but who should pay for it. In September 2026 the 31 hotel properties raised 2,480 discrepancy claims; 1,612, or 65.0 per cent, were accepted, and of those 1,209, or 75.0 per cent, were settled inside the seven-day contractual window — so 48.75 per cent of claims raised were settled on time. The 1,271 left over averaged 14 pieces each: 17,794 pieces, worth ₹32.92 lakh at the ₹185 blended replacement cost Libaas uses. Chihna records the claim and does nothing about the argument. Exhibit 5, Taufiq's pipeline, was built on none of this, but on what buyers said they wanted.

Exhibit 6 is the evidence for the proposition itself — that Chihna reduces linen loss. Loss rate is pieces unaccounted for in a period divided by pieces issued in that period.

Jayashree read Exhibit 6 as proof: loss at the Libaas plants more than halved, 0.40 to 0.18 per cent, a difference of ₹212.01 lakh of cotton between the two years. Hana pointed out that those rows are three years apart and two plants opened in between, so the comparison carries three years of other operational work as well as the software. The third-party row, 0.35 per cent over five months, is barely better than the pre-Chihna baseline; the hotel-side row, 0.40 per cent over four months, is identical to it.

Exhibit 7 is the supply side: nine engineers for thirteen weeks is 117 engineer-weeks, 26 of which run the system the six Libaas plants depend on, leaving 91.

5. The people

Abhiraj Kanekar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. He made the one-owner-per-piece decision in 2023 and has never regretted it; he wants signable contracts. Unsaid: the ₹118 crore round was raised on the product thesis, and a flat quarter changes the next one.

Jayashree Mulgund, co-founder and chief operating officer, Nashik. Her plants are Chihna's largest user and pay nothing; she opposes item A because configurable ownership complicates screens her supervisors have finally learned. Unsaid: her bonus runs off the plant loss targets Exhibit 6 shows she is beating.

Taufiq Vora, head of sales, Gurugram, paid on quoted contract value — the only incentive here indifferent to whether a feature exists. He says twelve of the eighteen accounts asked for the hotel-side app. Unsaid: in six of them the asker was a purchase manager comparing feature lists.

Anju Pappachan, customer-success lead, Kochi, measured on renewals. She says the product has three candidate users and has chosen none. Unsaid: two of her laundry accounts have stopped reconciling, which she logged and did not escalate.

Nilay Bhanushali, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He estimated item A at 38 engineer-weeks and privately thinks 50 once the six own plants are migrated; he wants item E, because hardware tickets consume his team. Unsaid: one of his ten engineers has resigned, effective 31 December, leaving nine, and he has not said who.

Imogen Hartley, product designer, Manchester. She cannot get her offline-first driver app prioritised against anything carrying a rupee figure, and argues the heaviest user is the one whose errors create every dispute downstream. Unsaid: she has never spent a day in an Indian laundry.

Hana Jeong, data scientist, Seoul, the only person with no stake and the only one who will not endorse any exhibit as causal. Unsaid: she built the loss comparison Jayashree quotes, in July, and flagged the window mismatch in a comment nobody read.

Devraj Pandit, growth-fund partner, Mumbai, board member, author of the ₹25 crore thesis. He has begun asking in writing whether the product should be a separate company — which solves his problem and creates a different one for Sharanya.

7. The options as Sharanya sees them

She had written four on the pipeline sheet. Each spends all 91 engineer-weeks, because the ₹95.94 lakh of engineering payroll is committed whatever she decides.

Option 1: unblock the pipeline. Items A, D and E are 72 engineer-weeks, ₹59.04 lakh, leaving 19 for a cut-down hotel-side app to meet the Udawatta clause. It treats the buyer as the customer, bets ₹70.4 lakh of pipeline against Nilay's suspicion that A is a 50-week job, and gives the driver nothing.

Option 2: build for the hotel estate. Items B, C and D are 62 engineer-weeks, ₹50.84 lakh, with 29 left for a partial start on A that would not finish. Taufiq's twelve requests point here, and Exhibit 5 says it is already serviceable: 1,89,000 of 2,10,000 hotel pieces are trackable today. It also walks into the DPDP question.

Option 3: build for the heaviest user. Items C, B and E are 66 engineer-weeks, ₹54.12 lakh, with 25 for reliability and migration. It treats the driver and floor supervisor as the users and the owner as a buyer who will pay to stop the month-end argument. Weakest revenue story, strongest usage evidence — which is Exhibit 4, at 2.55 devices a seat.

Option 4: spend five weeks finding out. Discovery from 4 January to Friday 5 February 2027 across all three candidate users, with one engineer, Imogen and Sharanya, then commit the remaining 86 engineer-weeks on Monday 8 February 2027. Discovery consumes 5 engineer-weeks: the first five weeks yield 35 net engineer-weeks of which 30 stay free, and the last eight yield 56, making the 86. Field cost is ₹4.60 lakh of the ₹32.06 lakh non-engineering budget, leaving ₹27.46 lakh. It commits nothing until February, and the Udawatta date is 31 March.

All four allocate engineer-weeks. None asks whether Libaas is selling a tracking system, an arbitration service for a monthly argument, or a financing product for linen it owns.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The product committee meets on Wednesday 18 November 2026, the full board on Friday 12 February 2027. The build quarter runs 4 January to 2 April 2027.

Money: the product budget is ₹1.28 crore, of which ₹95.94 lakh is engineering payroll, leaving ₹32.06 lakh for travel, hardware, certification and customer success, and no contingency. People: nine engineers, after one Pune resignation effective 31 December 2026 that the hiring freeze will not backfill. Imogen is five and a half hours behind Pune in winter and Hana three and a half ahead, so Seoul's day ends about when Manchester's begins.

Contract: Udawatta Resorts Group's agreement, covering nine of the 31 hotel properties, commits Libaas to a multi-property discrepancy dashboard live by 31 March 2027, two days before the quarter ends, failing which it may terminate on sixty days' notice. Udawatta is ₹8.64 lakh of ARR, 10.4 per cent of the total, and the only international reference the company has.

Regulation: the GST export matters to 17 of 23 paying laundries; the hotel-side features need a data-processing agreement Libaas has not drafted.

And one constraint nobody wrote down: the six Libaas plants are Chihna's largest user, pay nothing, and can veto any change to the plant screens — if those stop, the ₹67.10 crore business stops.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. In one sentence each: who is Chihna Open's user, and who is its buyer? Now answer for the hotel-side deployments. Where do the answers diverge?
  2. Those who authorise the purchase are 10.2 per cent of users and 2.4 per cent of sessions. Defect, or normal for field software? What evidence would settle it?
  3. Taufiq reports a pipeline of ₹156.7 lakh and Anju ₹86.3 lakh, both computed correctly from the same eighteen accounts. Which belongs in the committee pack, and what does choosing it do to the incentive of whoever produced it?
  4. Exhibit 6's weighted loss rate of 0.29 per cent is arithmetically right. What would it take for that exhibit to support the claim that Chihna reduces linen loss, and what do the two external rows tell you now?
  5. The 2023 decision to model one owner per piece bought five months of speed and now costs 38 engineer-weeks, or 50 by Nilay's reckoning. Was it wrong, and how would you have known then? What is its equivalent now?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November, two days before the committee. What does Sharanya do first, what goes on the one slide the committee will remember, and what does she say when Devraj asks whether Chihna Open should be a separate company?

10. Sunday night, continued

At half past eleven Sharanya did the arithmetic that was in none of the three documents. Sixty-nine sites. Nine hundred and ninety-five devices opening the application every month. Eighty seats able to authorise a rupee, at twelve sessions a month each.

She typed a slide title — Who is Chihna Open for? — and sat looking at it, because every answer she could defend to Taufiq she could not defend to Hana, and the one she could defend to Hana would take five weeks. Outside, the last Chakan van turned onto the highway with tomorrow's sheets, driven by someone who would open the product seven times before Wednesday and had never been asked about it.

She closed the laptop without deleting the slide.
